title: Computer-Use Agents Gain Little Benefit from a World Model When Conditioned on Tutorials

paper.title: Computer-Use Agents Gain Little Benefit from a World Model When Conditioned on Tutorials
paper.abstract:
Abstract Recent work has improved computer-use agents (CUAs) by combining retrieved task-relevant tutorials and look-ahead planning using world models with MLLM judges.
However, the contribution of each component—tutorials, the judge, and the world model—to overall improvement has not been evaluated in isolation.
To fill this gap, we first construct OSWorld-Tutorial and ScienceBoard-Tutorial: two datasets for CUAs with curated multimodal tutorials, covering everyday and scientific domains.
We then propose RAG-PolicyJudge (RAG-PJ), a policy-judge framework for CUAs conditioned on task-specific tutorials: the policy proposes candidate actions, and the judge selects among them.
To isolate the effect of world models given tutorials, we compare RAG-PJ with and without common world models: using either zero-shot text-based descriptions of next states or an oracle that returns ground-truth visual observations.
We find that RAG-PJ gains little benefit from these rollouts when tutorials are present, even with perfect visual futures .
This suggests prior world-model gains in tutorial-conditioned methods come mainly from tutorial understanding and the judge’s ability to select the proposed actions, rather than from predicted rollouts.
Error analysis reveals that the bottleneck is not rollout fidelity, but the judge’s ability to reason over future states and recognize task completion.
This highlights the need to improve not just next-state prediction in world models, but also reasoning over their predicted rollouts. 1 1 1 Datasets and code are available at github.com/realjoenguyen/RAGPJ-official .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: People rely on desktop and web software for day-to-day tasks and scientific workflows. Computer-use agents (CUAs) aim to automate these tasks by interacting with computer interfaces given natural-language user instructions. Modern CUAs are typically built on top of multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) trained on static offline data. As software is updated and user interfaces shift, these MLLM-based CUAs may lack current procedural knowledge about new environments, resulting in degraded performance Ishmam and Marino (2026) . A natural approach to address this gap is to provide CUAs with up-to-date task-specific tutorials. These readily available tutorials, contain environment descriptions and step-by-step instructions in the form of text and screenshots. 2 2 2 An example tutorial is given in Appendix G . Figure 1: Success rate on OSWorld-Tutorial (Qwen3-VL-32B) of RAG-PJ, a policy–judge CUA, whose judge sees no rollout, a predicted text rollout (R-WoM Mei et al. (2026) ), or an oracle visual rollout (real future screenshots). Rollouts help RAG-PJ without a tutorial but add almost nothing with one. Full results in § 6 and Appendix C . Recent work has integrated tutorial retrieval as a component in CUA systems Yang et al. (2026a) ; Xu et al. (2025a) . However, these systems do not compare against alternative tutorial-use approaches, leaving their effectiveness unclear. A parallel body of work has considered test-time scaling for CUAs through a policy-judge approach with look-ahead planning Luo et al. (2026) ; Chae et al. (2025) . These methods use a world model to predict the outcome of action candidates under a policy, over one or many steps. They then use an MLLM-as-a-judge to select the best action among the candidates, conditioned on these predicted rollouts. Recently, tutorial-augmented methods of this approach have been introduced Mei et al. (2026) . However, these methods conflate the contributions of the tutorial, the judge, and world-model rollouts without proper evaluation. To fill this gap, we study the effect of tutorial information on CUAs with and without look-ahead planning, while retaining the MLLM-as-a-judge framework. Intuitively, high-quality tutorials already provide guidance for the policy to generate actions and demonstrations of their effects that can be used by the judge. This can potentially reduce the need for costly world model training and inference. With this motivation, we propose a simple yet effective method: RAG-PolicyJudge (RAG-PJ), a retrieval-augmented policy-judge framework for CUAs. RAG-PJ provides a task-specific tutorial to both (1) the policy, which proposes action candidates, and (2) the judge, which selects the best action among them. To evaluate tutorials for CUAs across domains, we build curated tutorials for existing datasets: OSWorld-Verified for day-to-day tasks Xie et al. (2024) and ScienceBoard for scientific workflows Sun et al. (2026) , resulting in two new tutorial benchmarks: OSWorld-Tutorial and ScienceBoard-Tutorial. The two original datasets are widely adopted for CUAs, facilitating easy adoption and reuse by the research community. To study the effect of world models on policy-judge frameworks in these two tutorial datasets, using the same base MLLM for both the policy and the judge, we compare RAG-PJ with two types of world models for CUAs: text-based and visual. First, zero-shot text-based rollouts Mei et al. (2026) (i.e., the text description of what the predicted next state would look like). Second, oracle visual rollouts (i.e., the real screenshot of the next state). We argue that these oracle rollouts are an upper bound on the next-state fidelity a learned visual world model (like ViMo Luo et al. (2026) ) could achieve. We find that RAG-PJ matches both rollout variants when tutorials are present. This indicates that current zero-shot MLLM-as-a-judge models gain little extra benefit from a world model, even with oracle visual futures, when conditioned on tutorials (Figure 1 ). Analyzing failures of the oracle rollout, we find that the agent’s failure to understand task success and progress , even when the oracle future is available, is a primary bottleneck to higher performance. This suggests that progress in CUAs may require not just better world models, but also stronger reasoning over the futures these world models simulate. In summary, our contributions are as follows: – We introduce RAG-PJ, a simple yet effective tutorial-conditioned policy-judge method for CUAs (§ 4.2 ). – We build OSWorld-Tutorial and ScienceBoard-Tutorial, two curated tutorial datasets with existing tasks from OSWorld Xie et al. (2024) and ScienceBoard Sun et al. (2026) (§ 3 ), facilitating tutorial study for CUAs. – We propose an oracle visual rollout infrastructure for CUAs, providing an important ablation on the effect of visual world-model rollouts with perfect future information (§ 5 , Appendix F ). – We provide a controlled comparison of tutorial-only judging, text-based rollouts, and oracle visual rollouts-demonstrating that current MLLM-as-a-judge models gain little benefit from world models given task-specific tutorials (§ 6 ).

sections.heading: World model evaluation for CUAs.
sections.text: Several works find that zero-shot rollouts from pretrained MLLMs used as world models Ha and Schmidhuber (2018) are not yet faithful or consistent proxies for real environments Li et al. (2026) ; Xu et al. (2026) ; Fu et al. (2026) . Beyond MLLMs as world models, other works use oracle world models to study upper-bound look-ahead performance in embodied tasks Qian et al. (2026) and, at the first step only, in computer-use tasks Gonzalez-Pumariega et al. (2026) . We extend these analyses to (1) oracle image-based rollouts with task-specific tutorials and (2) look-ahead planning at every step of computer-use tasks. Concurrent to our work, Tang et al. (2026) show that code-based visual world model add little benefit if agents can already have a well-trained MLLM-as-a-judge. Our work complements theirs by studying the benefit of world model rollouts against zero-shot MLLM-as-judge, in the presence of task-specific tutorials. Further, we study two types of common world models: we adopt (1) text-based, and build (2) visual ground truths, which is the upper bound of current visual world models.

sections.heading: CUAs that use tutorials (or manuals).
sections.text: Prior work uses tutorials either to create training data Ou et al. (2024) ; Xu et al. (2025b) ; Zhang et al. (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2025b) ; Song et al. (2026) ; Lu et al. (2026) or as guidance at inference time Liu et al. (2026b) ; Xu et al. (2025a) ; Agashe et al. (2025a) ; Mei et al. (2026) ; Yang et al. (2026a) , where the tutorial guides action generation (policy) or selection (judge). RAG-GUI Xu et al. (2025a) and Agent S Agashe et al. (2025a) retrieve text-only tutorials to extract guidance for policy-only agents. 3 3 3 See Appendix D.3 for a comparison with RAG-GUI. Liu et al. (2026b) retrieve tutorial videos at inference time as in-context guidance for the policy. Similar to our benchmarks, there are two recent multimodal tutorial datasets for CUA/GUI: WebOne Long et al. (2026) and DocOS Liu et al. (2026a) , where agents must search the open web for documentation before executing a task. However, WebOne is only for web agents and tutorials are not task-conditioned, but rather than software documentation in general. DocOS is not publicly available, preventing direct comparison. In contrast, our work focuses on task-specific multimodal tutorials for general CUAs and test-time scaling approach with a MLLM-as-a-judge, which is evaluated against world model rollout methods. We also release our benchmark and trained agents for reproducibility. Most similar to our approach are OS-Symphony Yang et al. (2026a) and R-WoM Mei et al. (2026) . OS-Symphony couples retrieved tutorials with a multi-agent history-reflection policy, but does not compare against other tutorial-using baselines. Our tutorial-conditioned judge is orthogonal and could be combined with its policy. Like R-WoM, we focus on settings where multimodal task-specific tutorials are available, but R-WoM’s results do not disentangle the tutorial, the MLLM-as-a-judge, and the rollout, and it is evaluated on a non-public subset of ∼ 85 {\sim}85 OSWorld tasks. R-WoM reports that its rollouts improve over a no-tutorial baseline, but never compares against a tutorial-conditioned judge without rollout. We add that comparison with our method RAG-PJ, and find the judge alone matches R-WoM; we further test oracle visual rollouts. See Appendix D for a more detailed discussion of related work.

sections.heading: Tutorial dataset domains.
sections.text: To evaluate tutorials and tutorial-conditioned CUAs across domains, we pair existing tasks with newly collected tutorials to build two datasets: (1) OSWorld-Tutorial, from general-purpose desktop tasks in OSWorld-Verified Xie et al. (2024) , and (2) ScienceBoard-Tutorial, from scientific-software workflow tasks in ScienceBoard Sun et al. (2026) . General-purpose tasks from OSWorld-Verified reflect everyday computer use, with abundant online tutorials. Scientific software from ScienceBoard is harder on both fronts. First, its applications are niche: step-by-step task tutorials are scarce, and even ScienceBoard’s annotators relied on official documentation (Table 6 of Sun et al. (2026) ). Second, current open MLLMs still struggle on these tasks, with as low as ∼ \sim 30% success rate with Qwen3.8-27B (Table 9 ). This makes it a natural testbed for whether tutorials, even scarce ones, can compensate for limited MLLM familiarity with these specialized domains.

sections.heading: Generating tutorials.
sections.text: We pair each task with one multimodal tutorial (text and possibly images) drawn from web sources. The tutorial type depends on what is available online for that task. First, human-verified online tutorials : we search Google with the task instruction, and when a retrieved tutorial covers the task, one of three annotators experienced with Ubuntu environments selects the most helpful one and verifies it by following its instructions to complete the task; we keep the pair only when this succeeds. This accounts for 31% of OSWorld-Tutorial tasks and none of the ScienceBoard-Tutorial tasks, as the latter’s scientific software is niche and lacks task-level tutorials online. These tutorials rule out retrieval errors, letting us measure the effect of tutorials independently of the retrieval pipeline. Second, MLLM-generated tutorials : when no single online tutorial covers the task (none exists, or the task requires combining several), we launch the task in a virtual machine and prompt Google Gemini 3.8 Flash Google DeepMind (2026) with the task instruction, the initial screenshot, and the tutorial-generation prompt in Appendix H ; Gemini searches the web and writes a task-specific tutorial, which we keep without human verification. The screenshot lets it refer to the actual files, columns, and menus of the task instead of inventing names. MLLM-generated tutorials mirror practical real-world guidance: users rarely have a curated tutorial database and instead ask a search-augmented MLLM for task-specific instructions. MLLM-generated tutorials cover 69% of OSWorld-Tutorial tasks and all ScienceBoard-Tutorial tasks.

sections.heading: Dataset statistics.
sections.text: We create total 529 tutorials across both original datasets. OSWorld-Tutorial contains 360 existing OSWorld-Verified tasks 4 4 4 OSWorld-Verified at commit 83e8534 (Jun 24, 2026), excluding 9 tasks that require Google Drive credentials or are blocked by website bot detection (Appendix H ). : 110 with human-verified and 250 with MLLM-generated tutorials (examples in Appendix H ). ScienceBoard-Tutorial pairs all 169 existing ScienceBoard tasks with MLLM-generated tutorials (examples in Appendix I ).

sections.heading: 4 Tutorial-conditioned CUAs
sections.text: Figure 2: Overview of RAG-PJ. Given the instruction, current screenshot, and trajectory history, a tutorial-conditioned policy proposes candidate actions, a tutorial-conditioned judge selects one, and a grounding model maps it to keyboard/mouse inputs.

sections.heading: CUA architectures.
sections.text: A CUA is a policy π ⁡ ( a t | o ≤ t , a < t , L , M ) \pi(a_{t}\,|\,o_{\leq t},a_{<t},L,M) over screenshots o o , actions a a , instruction L L , and tutorial M M . See Appendix J for the full problem formulation. Typically, CUA architectures are built on MLLMs. Designs are either end-to-end, with one MLLM mapping inputs directly to actions Qin et al. (2025) , or modular, combining multiple MLLMs and specialized models Agashe et al. (2025b) ; Yang et al. (2026a) . We follow the common two-stage modular design. A policy π ( a ^ t | ⋅ ) \pi(\hat{a}_{t}\,|\,\cdot) outputs a natural-language action (e.g., click(the red button) ). A grounding model g ( a t | a ^ t , ⋅ ) g(a_{t}\,|\,\hat{a}_{t},\cdot) then maps it to a low-level action (e.g., click(731, 244) ).

sections.heading: Judges and world models.
sections.text: Other work samples K K action candidates a ^ t 1 , … , a ^ t K ∼ π ( a ^ t | ⋅ ) \hat{a}^{1}_{t},\ldots,\hat{a}^{K}_{t}\sim\pi(\hat{a}_{t}\,|\,\cdot) and introduces a judge model that selects the index of the best candidate, k ∗ = j ( a ^ t 1 , … , a ^ t K | o ≤ t , a < t , L , M ) ∈ { 1 , … , K } k^{*}=j(\hat{a}^{1}_{t},\ldots,\hat{a}^{K}_{t}\,|\,o_{\leq t},a_{<t},L,M)\in\{1,\ldots,K\} , passing only the selected action a ^ t k ∗ \hat{a}^{k^{*}}_{t} to the grounding model for execution Yang et al. (2026c) . This sample-then-select paradigm has shown promising results when coupled with look-ahead planning, using a world model to estimate the outcome of each action over a fixed number of time steps. See Appendix D.1 for an overview of world model methods following this approach for CUAs. Each candidate is rolled out for H H steps by alternating the world model and the policy, and the judge selects among candidates based on their rollouts (details in Appendix J ). However, look-ahead planning greatly increases computational cost by requiring multiple policy and world-model executions per step.

sections.heading: 4.2 RAG-PolicyJudge (RAG-PJ)
sections.text: To test if the additional compute for world model is valuable when strong policy guidance is available as a tutorial, we design a simple tutorial-conditioned method, RAG-PolicyJudge (RAG-PJ), shown in Figure 2 . We adapt a two-stage GUI-agent framework, consisting of a policy and a grounding model as described above (§ 4.1 ). Implementation details are in Appendix K .

sections.heading: Policy and Grounding Models.
sections.text: We instantiate the policy π ⁡ ( a ^ t | o ≤ t , a < t , L , M ) \pi(\hat{a}_{t}\,|\,o_{\leq t},a_{<t},L,M) as an MLLM that outputs K K candidate actions in a single call Yang et al. (2026c) . To bound context length, in practice we condition π \pi on o ^ ≤ t \hat{o}_{\leq t} in place of o ≤ t o_{\leq t} , where o ^ ≤ t \hat{o}_{\leq t} consists of: the current observation o t o_{t} ; all previous actions; the chain-of-thought of the five most recent steps; and the screenshots of up to five recent steps. Additionally, the task instruction, CUA-specific policy rules, and the tutorial are always available at each time step. We adopt the action space from Agent-S2 Agashe et al. (2025b) . The policy prompt is available in Appendix L . We adopt UI-Venus-1.5 Venus Team et al. (2026) as it is the state-of-the-art grounding model for CUAs and has been used as the grounding model in prior work Gong et al. (2026) ; Jiang et al. (2025) . The grounding prompt is provided in Appendix N . The grounding model g ⁡ ( a t | a ^ t , o t ) g(a_{t}\,|\,\hat{a}_{t},o_{t}) accesses only the current observation o t o_{t} and the policy action a ^ t \hat{a}_{t} .

sections.heading: Judge Model.
sections.text: The judge j j shares the policy’s MLLM and inputs: K K candidate actions, task instruction, the trajectory encoding o ^ ≤ t \hat{o}_{\leq t} , and tutorials. It ranks the candidates with a ranking prompt (Appendix M ) and sends the top-ranked action to the grounding model for execution.

sections.heading: Evaluation metric: task success rate.
sections.text: We use the task success rate metrics defined by OSWorld-Verified and ScienceBoard. For OSWorld-Verified, the metrics are computed within the original maximum of 15 steps Xie et al. (2024) ; Kuntz et al. (2025) ; Ye et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2025) and the extended 50-step budget adopted in follow-up work Abhyankar et al. (2026) ; OpenAI (2025) ; Jia et al. (2026) . For ScienceBoard, we follow each task’s time limit from the original benchmark Sun et al. (2026) .

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We use the following baselines with the same two-stage policy-grounding framework Gou et al. (2025) , the same harness (rules/guidelines), and the same input/output space as RAG-PJ, allowing us to isolate the effects of the world model, the judge, and the tutorial. We adopt the hyperparameters from their best publicly reported configurations. Details are in Appendix K . In all settings with a judge, the policy proposes K = 3 K=3 candidate actions per step 5 5 5 K = 3 K=3 follows the original codebase of our baselines. and the judge selects one; in Policy Only settings, the policy proposes a single action. – Policy Only drops the judge from RAG-PJ. When including the tutorial, we denote this model as Policy Only + RAG . – Policy + Judge (GTA-1) Yang et al. (2026c) is a policy-judge framework, without a world model or tutorial. – R-WoM H=# is a re-implementation of the recent tutorial-augmented look-ahead method from Mei et al. (2026) described in § 4.1 . R-WoM uses an MLLM-based world model to produce zero-shot text-based next-state descriptions. We set H = 1 , 2 , 3 H{=}1,2,3 to adjust how many steps are rolled out during look-ahead search. Our re-implementation details are in Appendix O . 6 6 6 Without tutorials, our re-implementation reproduces R-WoM’s reported gain over a judge-only baseline, as shown in Table 2 ; we use this as a sanity check that the baseline is functional before adding tutorials. – WebDreamer H=# Gu et al. (2025) is a tutorial-free, text-based world model look-ahead method originally proposed for web agents, which we adapt to CUAs. Similar to R-WoM, we use look-ahead horizons H = 1 , 2 H{=}1,2 . Our re-implementation details are in Appendix P . – (Visual) GT-rollout H=# : an oracle experiment in which we use ground-truth screenshots as future rollouts. 7 7 7 The common usage of the term “world model” is to describe a predictor of the next state given a current state and action. This is separate from planning that might use the world model. In this sense, the visual rollout is extremely accurate except for the stochastic elements described in Appendix S , which are fundamentally unpredictable. We do not imply the system as a whole is the best possible planning system. For each action candidate at a given time step, we save and reset the state of the virtual machine hosting the environment before collecting each rollout. Stochastic mismatches between GT-rollout and live states are rare ( < < 1.0% of completed-task states). These mismatches are mostly distracting webpage changes (color, ads), not inherent environment changes that would require a different policy (Appendix F ). Similar to R-WoM H=# , we use H = 1 , 2 , 3 H{=}1,2,3 look-ahead steps. Prior world-model work Chae et al. (2025) ; Gu et al. (2025) ; Luo et al. (2026) ; Zheng et al. (2026) ; Cao et al. (2026) ; Mei et al. (2026) predicts only one step ahead (rarely two); we evaluate up to three. Details are in Appendix F .

sections.heading: Base MLLMs.
sections.text: We use Qwen3-VL-8B, Qwen3-VL-32B, and Qwen3.8-27B Bai et al. (2025) ; Qwen Team (2026) 8 8 8 Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct-FP8, and Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 from the official Hugging Face versions of Qwen. as the base MLLMs for the policy, judge, and world model in both our method and the baselines. These models are commonly used in recent CUA works Xue et al. (2026) ; Yan et al. (2025) ; Bai et al. (2026) ; Wang et al. (2026) .

sections.heading: 6.1 Can tutorials improve CUAs?
sections.text: Finding 1: Tutorials improve task success rate over non-tutorial baselines. In Table (OSWorld-Tutorial) and Table 9 (ScienceBoard-Tutorial), we show that including tutorials in the policy ( row 2 ) improves over the non-tutorial baseline ( Policy Only , row 1 ) by ∼ \sim 3–12% (Table ) and ∼ \sim 15–21% (Table 9 ). The policy-judge framework with tutorials (RAG-PJ, row 4 ) improves over the non-tutorial baseline ( GTA-1 , row 3 ) by ∼ \sim 5–14% (Table ) and ∼ \sim 18–22% (Table 9 ). These improvements are larger on ScienceBoard (Table 9 ), whose specialized scientific apps are likely less covered in MLLM training data. This suggests tutorials help most where MLLMs lack prior knowledge. Table 6 (Appendix A ) and Tables 7 and 8 (Appendix B ) break results down per category in both benchmarks; the improvement from tutorial conditioning is consistent across all categories. Notably, tutorial conditioning in the policy yields most of the gains, suggesting that guidance for producing action candidates is the main source of improvement. Yet policy conditioning alone ( row 2 , Tables and 9 ) does not account for all of RAG-PJ’s gains, so judge action selection still helps. Finally, rows 3a, 3b vs. row 4 (Table ) show that using tutorials in both policy and judge performs best.

sections.heading: 6.2 Do CUAs benefit from zero-shot text-based world models?
sections.text: Finding 2: Given a tutorial, CUAs gain no benefit from zero-shot text-based world models. As shown in Tables (OSWorld-Tutorial) and 9 (ScienceBoard-Tutorial) and their breakdowns in Appendix A , we find that R-WoM does not improve over a judge without world model rollout ( RAG-PJ ). R-WoM without policy-side tutorial conditioning ( rows 5--7 , Table ) matches or underperforms the Policy + RAG Judge without rollout ( row 3a , Table ) at different horizons ( H = 1 , 2 , 3 ) (H{=}1,2,3) . Appendix O.2 traces this to hallucination in rollouts. When policy-side RAG is added ( rows 8--10 , Tables and 9 ), R-WoM is worse than or statistically similar to RAG-PJ ( row 4 ) on both benchmarks. This indicates that gains from R-WoM come from tutorial conditioning and the judge, rather than text-based rollouts. Further, we observe no consistent trend across rollout horizons: longer horizons ( H = 2 , 3 H{=}2,3 ) do not always improve over H = 1 H{=}1 , and in some settings longer horizons slightly degrade performance. This suggests compounding errors across simulated steps add noise to the judge.

sections.heading: 6.3 Do CUAs benefit from ground-truth visual rollouts?
sections.text: Motivated by the observation that text-based rollouts failed to improve over RAG-PJ, we consider an oracle visual rollout ( GT-rollout ) to establish an upper bound on world model performance. Mean ± \pm sample std. over 3 completed runs. Parentheses: change (pp) over Policy + Judge ( row 1 ). Finding 3: Given oracle or noisy MLLM-generated tutorials, zero-shot MLLM judges gain little from ground-truth visual rollouts. In Table (OSWorld-Tutorial) and Table 9 (ScienceBoard-Tutorial), with tutorials, GT-rollout clearly improves over text-based R-WoM ( rows 11--13 vs. 8--10 ) but is not significantly better than RAG-PJ on either benchmark, for both human-verified and MLLM-generated tutorials (Appendix A ). As before, the judge can already decide well from tutorials without reasoning over future consequences. Without tutorials, GT-rollout does help: H = 2 H{=}2 improves over Policy+Judge by ∼ \sim 3–4% (Table 2 , row 7 vs. row 1 ). With noisy MLLM-generated tutorials, GT-rollout gives small nominal gains over RAG-PJ in some settings (Tables 3 and 9 ). In 40 sampled tasks that RAG-PJ fails but GT-rollout solves, the tutorials are partially correct but miss steps. GT-rollout helps the judge recover when: – the horizon is too short for RAG-PJ to try the alternative steps the tutorial suggests, e.g., ScienceBoard categories with only 5 steps; – the action’s effect is visually obvious in the next state, e.g., opening a website or creating a file. This matters more in ScienceBoard-Tutorial, whose scientific software is less familiar to the judge, so it is harder to infer the effect from the tutorial text alone. Per-category results are in Appendices A and B . Finding 4: Agents fail to use ground-truth future information due to poor understanding of task success and progress. To understand why ground-truth visual rollouts do not improve success, we analyze failed tasks in OSWorld-Tutorial with the help of Gemini 3.8 Flash Google DeepMind (2026) and summarize failure reasons and their frequency in Figure 3 . The most frequent failure category is the agent (both the policy and the judge) failing to understand task success: whether the current state satisfies the task instruction . For instance, a task is not completed in the current state, yet the policy and the judge predict that the current state already satisfies the instruction. The judge therefore selects the action that ends the task prematurely. The second most frequently tagged category is the judge failing to reason over the future information about task progress: what has been done and what is left to do . Even if the policy generates good action candidates, the judge fails to select the one that leads to task progress. The judge often repeats the same failed action instead of recognizing the failure and choosing other candidates. We show examples of these failures in Figures 29 , 33 , and 30 . Overall, most failures stem from the judge’s inability to reason over future states generated by world models , not from world-model quality. Examples of other less significant failure reasons and the error-analysis implementation are shown in Appendix R . Implication: CUAs need not only better world models but also better mechanisms for reasoning over future rollouts. Improving world-model fidelity alone may therefore be insufficient for look-ahead planning. Current world-model methods for CUAs lack reward prediction for rollout states, which the judge needs to compare candidates by their futures, and judges need better ways to reason over rollouts, e.g., via prompting or training. This is consistent with Qian et al. (2026) , who find that even a ground-truth world model does not improve embodied agents, as using future information is the main bottleneck.

Tutorial-free baselines shown once. Mean ± \pm sample std. over 3 completed runs. Without an available online tutorial for a given task, can MLLM systems with web search synthesize equally useful ones? Since Tables 4 and 5 (Appendix A ) suggest that tasks with MLLM-generated tutorials may be harder, we use OSWorld-Tutorial to compare both tutorial types on the same tasks . Specifically, we select 110 tasks with human-verified online tutorials. We use our dataset pipeline (described in § 3 ) to create MLLM-generated tutorials for these tasks. We then evaluate both RAG-PJ and the ground-truth visual rollout method under each tutorial condition and report the results in Table 3 . Finding 5: Task-specific tutorials written by a search-grounded frontier MLLM are as useful to the policy and judge as human-verified online tutorials. In Table 3 , we find no statistically significant difference between the two tutorial types, in RAG-PJ ( row 4 ) or in GT-rollout ( rows 5--7 ). This is likely because OSWorld-Tutorial tasks involve common software with abundant online tutorials. We provide examples of MLLM-generated vs. human-verified tutorial pairs and an analysis of a sample of 20 pairs in Appendix E . In this sample, a human verifier judges every MLLM-generated tutorial as correct or partially correct, and prefers it over its human-verified counterpart in 17 of 20 pairs. MLLM-generated tutorials are task-conditioned , naming the on-screen objects and values the task requires, whereas human-verified online tutorials describe an application feature in general, leaving the CUA to ground each action on the current screen.

sections.heading: 7 Limitations
sections.text: Our study has several limitations: First, our MLLM-generated tutorials (Gemini 3.8 Flash with web search) cover noisy online retrieval, but we do not evaluate offline settings, where a local retriever over a smaller corpus (e.g., local documentation) may yield noisier or missing tutorials, which could change the relative benefit of look-ahead planning. Second, both benchmarks run desktop applications in Linux VMs. ScienceBoard-Tutorial has only MLLM-generated tutorials, so our human vs. MLLM tutorial comparison (Finding 5) covers only 110 general-purpose OSWorld-Tutorial tasks. Third, all models come from one MLLM family (Qwen3-VL-8B, Qwen3-VL-32B, Qwen3.8-27B), and all judges are zero-shot prompted; other model families, larger frontier MLLMs, or judges trained to reason over rollouts may use future states more effectively. Fourth, our error analysis (Figure 3 ) uses Gemini 3.8 Flash rather than human annotators to categorize failures, so the categories may carry labeling noise or MLLM biases.

sections.heading: Compute used.
sections.text: We used 272 GPU-hours in total on NVIDIA H100/H200 GPUs, plus about 1,080 hours on an NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10).

sections.heading: Risks.
sections.text: Like all assistive technologies, advances in computer-use agents make it easier for individuals to take action—both good and ill. Given how modern infrastructure relies on digital interfaces, this may pose significant risks for personal digital security, coordinated astroturfing, or model errors causing users harm.

sections.heading: Appendix A Results on OSWorld-Tutorial per category of tutorials
Statistical tests.
sections.text: We use Hierarchical bootstrap, sign-flip permutation, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests over tasks in Table , 5 , and 4 to test whether ground-truth visual rollouts and R-WoM improve over RAG-PJ on OSWorld-Tutorial.

sections.heading: Per-task-category analysis.
sections.text: To understand when and why the agent gains or loses a benefit from ground-truth visual rollout (GT rollouts), we break down the results of Qwen3-VL-32B in Table by task category in Table 6 . We inspected 40 cases where GT rollouts succeeded but RAG-PJ failed. In these cases, candidate actions produced clear, visible changes in the next state, such as opening a new website or creating a file. These visible effects make the correct action easier for the judge to spot, which matters most when there is little time to recover from a mistake. These gains do not generalize to other task categories. Applications like VS Code and GIMP have denser interfaces, so the effect of an action is often less visually clear. In one failure case, the judge misread a VS Code workspace with unwanted Explorer folders as a success—consistent with our earlier finding that the judge misinterprets task success even from perfect future screenshots. The agent simply has more time to observe the consequences of its actions and recover from mistakes without needing look-ahead.

sections.heading: Appendix B Results on ScienceBoard per application
Significance tests.
sections.text: We test whether ground-truth visual rollouts improve over RAG-PJ on ScienceBoard (Table 9 , rows 11--13 vs. row 4 ) with task-level tests. For Qwen3-VL-32B ( H = 1 / 2 / 3 H{=}1/2/3 ): hierarchical bootstrap p = 0.62 / 0.97 / 0.32 p{=}0.62/0.97/0.32 , sign-flip permutation p = 0.58 / 1.00 / 0.24 p{=}0.58/1.00/0.24 , Wilcoxon signed-rank p = 0.51 / 0.99 / 0.20 p{=}0.51/0.99/0.20 . For Qwen3.8-27B ( H = 1 / 2 / 3 H{=}1/2/3 ): sign-flip permutation p = 0.20 / 0.20 / 0.11 p{=}0.20/0.20/0.11 , Wilcoxon signed-rank p = 0.20 / 0.15 / 0.14 p{=}0.20/0.15/0.14 . Welch’s t t -test on run-level totals gives p = 0.43 / 0.73 / 0.18 p{=}0.43/0.73/0.18 (32B) and p = 0.013 / 0.001 / 0.052 p{=}0.013/0.001/0.052 (27B), but it ignores per-task variation, so we do not treat the 27B differences as significant.

sections.heading: Why do GT rollouts help in Celestia and GrassGIS?
sections.text: GT visual rollouts improve performance over RAG-PJ in Celestia and GrassGIS across the evaluated horizons. We sample 40 cases where GT rollouts succeeded but RAG-PJ failed. The common reason is that the tutorials given to agents are only partially correct. They omit steps that the task needs in the current application state, and they present options as equivalent when only some of them work. For example, in Celestia task B-02 (Figure 4 ) the instruction is “Go to Neptune in Celestia.” RAG-PJ executes Method 1 of the retrieved tutorial, and tries to follow the highlighted step in its tutorial. In that step, the tutorial proposes three options to travel to Neptune: pressing G , right-clicking, or double-clicking. RAG-PJ then executes the first option, pressing G , but it fails to travel to Neptune. sections.heading: Appendix C Policy + Judge with visual rollout, without tutorials
sections.text: Figure 6: Success rate with vs. without tutorials (Qwen3-VL-32B). Green arrows: gap from the judge-only reference (dashed) to the best rollout method. Without tutorials, rollout beats the judge by up to 4.2 4.2 %; with tutorials, the gap nearly vanishes. Numbers from Tables 2 and . We note down the differences between WebDreamer and R-WoM, which are both text-based world model look-ahead methods. While WebDreamer and R-WoM both use greedy policy in rollout states, they differ in how rollouts are generated and scored. In WebDreamer ( Gu et al., 2025 ) , for each candidate action, the rollout is generated many times with different imagined trajectories. Each trajectory is scored independently, either complete (1), on track (0.5), or incorrect (0). The scores of these trajectories are averaged to produce a score for that candidate action. In R-WoM ( Mei et al., 2026 ) , only one imagined trajectory is generated for each candidate action. All candidate actions are then ranked listwise based on the single trajectory score, and the best candidate action is selected.

sections.heading: D.1 World models for CUAs
sections.text: Recent work explores world models Ha and Schmidhuber (2018) for CUA planning, which predict future states in one of two forms: (1) textual descriptions of the next state Chae et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2025) ; Cao et al. (2026) ; Mei et al. (2026) ; Zuo et al. (2026) , or (2) visual predictions of the next state, either by generating images directly Luo et al. (2026) ; Xiang et al. (2025) or by generating code that renders them Zheng et al. (2026) ; Han and Qian (2026) . Most recently, Yang et al. (2026b) show that pretrained image generators can act as visual world models, iteratively editing screenshots to synthesize action-grounded training trajectories without deploying the software. In this work, we evaluate whether CUAs with an MLLM-as-a-judge can leverage both forms of world models: text-based rollouts and oracle visual rollouts, an upper bound for visual world models, when given access to task-relevant tutorials.

sections.heading: D.2 Agents that use tutorials (manuals)
sections.text: Tutorials or manuals can describe both step-by-step instructions ( what to do ) and how an environment changes over time (the dynamics of the environment ). Many works study how agents can use tutorials in different domains, including (1) games Nguyen and Lee (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2024) ; Lin et al. (2024) ; Dainese et al. (2023) ; Chen et al. (2024c) , (2) robotics Zhang et al. (2025a) ; Ren et al. (2023) , and (3) embodied environments Chen et al. (2024b) . While our work targets the Computer-use Agent (CUA) domain, some of these works share a similar goal: using tutorials at inference time to help agents handle new tasks or environments. In particular, our work is closely related to Nguyen and Lee (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2024) ; Dainese et al. (2023) . However, these works focus on symbolic 2D environments, where language is restricted to a single sentence per entity—typically 3–5 sentences total—and covers only environmental dynamics. Meanwhile, we focus on real-world GUI environments with longer tutorials that cover both task instructions and environmental dynamics.

sections.heading: D.3 Comparison with RAG-GUI
sections.text: While RAG-GUI Xu et al. (2025a) shares with us the same motivation of using tutorials for GUI agents at inference time, we highlight several key differences between RAG-GUI and our method (RAG-PJ): • RAG-GUI discards visual information in tutorials. RAG-GUI uses a lightweight VLM to judge whether each retrieved multimodal tutorial is relevant and then generates a “concise textual guidance summary” for the VLM. This removes visual information that might be necessary for GUI agents to complete a given task, e.g., clicking on an icon of a button shown in the tutorial. Meanwhile, our method (RAG-PJ) uses raw multimodal tutorials and directly feeds them to the LLM-as-judge to judge the policy’s action, thus potentially taking advantage of visual clues in tutorials. • RAG-GUI is challenging to reproduce and compare. RAG-GUI does not publish its implementation or its dataset (tutorials). Further, it requires extensive training. This makes it challenging for us to directly compare our method (RAG-PJ) with RAG-GUI. Meanwhile, one of our contributions is that we publish our dataset and implementation to foster further research in CUA / GUI agents with tutorials. • RAG-GUI does not have tutorial-used baselines. RAG-GUI does not compare with other GUI / CUA methods that use tutorials. Thus, it is hard to know if RAG-GUI’s design choice is the best way to use tutorials. Meanwhile, we compare against other tutorial-using methods that involve planning ahead with world models. • RAG-GUI focuses on retrieving tutorials, whereas we focus on how to use a given tutorial. RAG-GUI develops a retrieval module to obtain the most relevant tutorials for a given task. Meanwhile, we do not focus on the retrieval part, and offload this retrieval role to frontier LLMs acting as an LLM-augmented retriever, such as Gemini. Retrieval-focused methods like RAG-GUI would be more suitable for CUA settings that involve local software / domain knowledge, where the agent needs a retrieval module that can run locally. Meanwhile, our method (RAG-PJ) is more relevant to general-purpose CUA that can access the internet and frontier LLMs.

Within branch k k , the first action is executed and the rollout may continue for a horizon of up to H H real environment transitions. sections.heading: Initial pool construction.
sections.text: At a decision step, the system checkpoints the main VM before any candidate action is committed. The checkpoint is a QEMU snapshot-save : disk state goes into an internal qcow2 snapshot of the main disk, and CPU, memory, and device state go into an external vmstate image on host shared memory. Snapshot creation runs on a background thread and overlaps policy inference. If the policy returns a single unique candidate, no rollout or judge is run. For the first parallel rollout, the system copies the disk image and the vmstate image once per candidate and cold-launches one rollout VM per candidate from its private copy. Each rollout VM therefore begins with the same disk, memory, device, and interface state. The system captures a settled pre-action screenshot for every candidate and executes the corresponding first grounded action. It then continues each branch on the same VM for up to H H steps, conditioning later actions on that branch’s actions and observations and recording the settled state after every transition. A branch stops early when the policy emits a terminal action ( done , fail , or answer ), when its action cannot be generated or grounded, or when no screenshot can be captured; a terminal first action is not executed. Instead of terminating these VMs after selection, the system transfers them to the warm pool for reuse.

sections.heading: Warm refresh.
sections.text: At every later decision step, all candidates must start from the new live state. The refresh is prepared in the background while the policy runs, and its protocol is: 1. checkpoint the main VM and pause the warm rollout VMs; 2. make K K full copies of the main disk image and of the vmstate image, one per branch; 3. switch each paused warm VM’s active disk to its branch copy at the block layer, attach its vmstate copy, and restore it with a QMP snapshot-load in the same QEMU process; 4. detach and delete the vmstate copy, verify the active disk, resume and recover each rollout VM until its screen is stable, and compare the pre-action states across branches; and 5. execute the K K branch trajectories concurrently, with transitions within each branch proceeding sequentially for up to H H steps. Refreshing an existing pool avoids repeated VM process creation and guest bootstrapping. The refresh still replaces each branch’s complete disk and execution state, ensuring that no disk or memory changes from a previous candidate survive into the next decision step. After a restore, the guest network state is repaired, since the restored TCP connections are stale.

sections.heading: Snapshot isolation.
sections.text: Each branch receives an independent full copy of the disk image and of the vmstate image. Thin copy-on-write overlays on a shared base are not used: the snapshot load restores every writable qcow2 device in the VM, so every branch disk must carry the main disk’s internal snapshot table. Sharing mutable snapshot state between branches can also introduce interference: restoring or modifying one candidate may alter another candidate that has already been restored. Per-candidate copies eliminate this dependency and allow all restores and action executions to proceed concurrently. All copies are kept in host shared memory ( /dev/shm ), and each vmstate copy is deleted as soon as its VM has loaded it. Before a run, a resource preflight checks that host memory and shared-memory space can hold the main VMs, the K K rollout VMs per worker, and their copies; before each copy, a host-wide admission check confirms that enough free space remains.

sections.heading: Selection and state invariants.
sections.text: Before action execution, every rollout VM should recover to the same State 0 as the checkpointed main VM. The implementation captures stable State 0 images and compares each candidate’s State 0 with that of the first candidate by perceptual (dHash) distance; mismatches are logged and recorded with the trajectory. If the warm refresh fails for any branch, because of a failed disk copy, snapshot load, disk verification, or guest recovery, or because K K changed, the pool is discarded and the K K rollout VMs are cold-launched. The judge receives each high-level candidate together with its real rollout trajectory: the later actions and the screenshots of State 1 through State H k H_{k} . While the judge runs, the main VM is reloaded to State 0 in parallel. After it selects k ⋆ k^{\star} , the grounded first action a k ⋆ ( 1 ) a_{k^{\star}}^{(1)} from the selected rollout is dispatched to the live environment without re-grounding; later actions of the selected branch are discarded, and the next step proposes new candidates from scratch. The warm pool persists across the steps of a task until the candidate count changes, recovery fails, the task ends, or the worker shuts down.

sections.heading: Resource accounting and recorded evidence.
sections.text: For W W task workers, the method requires W W main VMs and W ​ K WK rollout VMs, together with their checkpoint copies. Increasing either W W or K K therefore raises memory and shared-memory use substantially. For every step, the trajectory stores the candidate actions, grounded actions, rollout actions and thoughts, State 0 screenshots, and per-horizon rollout screenshots. These artifacts permit visual inspection that all branches began from a common state and that the judge’s evidence corresponds to actual VM execution.

To robustly evaluate the impact of tutorials, we construct the OSWorld-Tutorial dataset by augmenting 360 tasks from the OSWorld-Verified benchmark Xie et al. (2024) . 10 10 10 We use OSWorld-Verified at commit 83e8534 . We recruit three student annotators with experience in software tasks similar to those in OSWorld to collect a tutorial for each task. For each task, we first launch it in a virtual machine and provide the task instruction together with the initial screenshot to the tutorial-generation prompt shown in Figure 13 . We submit this prompt to Google Gemini 3.8 Flash Google DeepMind (2026) . It searches the web for relevant tutorials and synthesizes a comprehensive summary over the retrieved results. The annotators then review the retrieved tutorials and select the most helpful one for each task. To verify tutorials from publicly available articles, they follow the article’s instructions to complete the task and confirm that it is correct and helpful. We find that many OSWorld tasks require combining multiple tutorials, while others have no relevant tutorials available online. For these tasks, we use the response generated by Google Gemini 3.8 Flash directly as the tutorial. We do not verify the correctness of AI-synthesized tutorials. Appendix J Problem formulation We cast the computer-use task as a standard finite-horizon partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) ⟨ S , O , A , T , R , L , M ⟩ \langle S,O,A,T,R,L,M\rangle , conditioned on the task instruction L L and a multimodal tutorial M M . The computing environment itself (typically a virtual machine) serves as a mostly-deterministic 11 11 11 In our setting, T T is deterministic for most tasks. For examples of non-deterministic tasks, see Appendix S . transition function T : S × A → S T:S\times A\to S . As the agent only accesses the environment visually, the observation o t ∈ O o_{t}\in O at each time step t t is simply the current screenshot. Actions correspond to movements or clicks of the mouse and keystrokes as well as stop actions (more details in Figure 19 ). The reward function R : S × A → { 0 , 1 } R:S\times A\to\{0,1\} is sparse and indicates task success when the agent issues stop actions or reaches the horizon H H . We consider a CUA to be a stochastic policy π ⁡ ( a t | o ≤ t , a < t , L , M ) \pi(a_{t}\,|\,o_{\leq t},a_{<t},L,M) , which produces a distribution over actions a t a_{t} given previous observations o ≤ t o_{\leq t} , prior actions a < t a_{<t} , the instruction L L , and the tutorial M M . We want to find a policy which achieves high expected cumulative reward (i.e., task success) over CUA tasks. Look-ahead rollouts. Specifically, given a world model w : O × A → O w:O\times A\to O that predicts the next observation given past observations and the current action, the outcome of each of the K K candidate actions can be estimated as o ~ t 1 , … , o ~ t K \tilde{o}^{1}_{t},...,\tilde{o}^{K}_{t} in a one-step look-ahead. Following Mei et al. (2026) , the policy π \pi is then executed with greedy decoding to generate a single next action a ^ t + 1 j = arg ⁡ max a ^ ⁡ π ⁡ ( a ^ | o ~ t + 1 j ) \hat{a}_{t+1}^{j}=\arg\max_{\hat{a}}\pi(\hat{a}\,|\,\tilde{o}_{t+1}^{j}) for each predicted observation o ~ t + 1 j \tilde{o}_{t+1}^{j} . This loop can be executed until some fixed look-ahead horizon is reached to generate a rollout trajectory ξ j = ( o t , a ^ t j , o ~ t + 1 j , a ^ t + 1 j , … , o ~ t + k j ) \xi^{j}=(o_{t},\hat{a}_{t}^{j},\tilde{o}_{t+1}^{j},\hat{a}_{t+1}^{j},\ldots,\tilde{o}_{t+k}^{j}) for each action candidate a ^ t j \hat{a}_{t}^{j} . The judge model can then select between actions based on their rollout trajectories. Appendix K RAG-PJ implementation details History information. Following GTA-1 Yang et al. (2026c) 12 12 12 Note that the official implementation of GTA-1 https://github.com/Yan98/GTA1 is different from GTA-1’s paper description. In the implementation, it only uses thought tokens and actions, and does not use observation caption descriptions for history information. We follow the implementation instead of the paper description. , the policy and the judge receive the same execution history. It includes the actions of all previous steps, the intermediate thought tokens of the five most recent steps, and the screenshots of up to five recent steps. The screenshot window drops the oldest steps four at a time instead of one per step, so the prompt prefix can be reused across steps. When the history text grows too long, the oldest steps outside the screenshot window are replaced by a single line noting that they were omitted. We find that including intermediate thought tokens for these steps does not significantly improve performance, while it does increase the input length and inference time for both the policy and the judge. Appendix O R-WoM reimplementation O.1 Implementation details We reimplement the R-WoM method based on the description in the paper. We make the following implementation changes to R-WoM to ensure compatibility with our environment and comparability with other baselines for a more controlled comparison. Changes 1, 3 and 4 below are shared by every method in Table , including ours, and are required for a controlled comparison. Change 2 fixes a format violation in the original rollout prompt that left the ranker with malformed input. Table 2 shows the re-implementation reproduces R-WoM’s gain over a judge-only baseline without tutorials. 1. We use the action space defined by Agent-S2 Agashe et al. (2025b) , instead of the original action space of OSWorld Xie et al. (2024) used in R-WoM. This action space makes the agent act more effectively and is more widely adopted in other GUI-agent works, such as the baseline GTA-1 Yang et al. (2026c) , Agent-S family Agashe et al. (2025b) ; Gonzalez-Pumariega et al. (2026) and UITAR1.5 Qin et al. (2025) . 2. We notice that the text-based rollout of R-WoM does not produce a well-structured rollout that follows the rules in the prompt, which makes it hard for the R-WoM judge (ranker) to judge from the rollout. For example, given the horizon H = 2 H{=}2 , it does not stop at the state 2 as required, and it stops at rollout actions instead. Therefore, we design a new rollout prompt with stricter rules and a more structured output format, as shown in the rollout prompt in Figure 23 . 3. To make it fair to compare R-WoM with other baselines such as GTA-1 Yang et al. (2026c) , we add judge rules from GTA-1 to the R-WoM judge prompt. 4. We keep the GTA-1 Yang et al. (2026c) policy rules and action space but adopt R-WoM’s policy output format: a shared observation and a separate thought for each action candidate. O.2 R-WoM error analysis To better understand the limitations of R-WoM, we manually analyzed more than 30 rollout samples. We found that its failures primarily arise from two sources. • Because R-WoM originally does not have RAG policy, policy can propose wrong actions and therefore the judge does not have a good candidate among proposed candidates. For example, if the tutorial already says “Infeasible”, the agent’s policy should produce “agent.fail()” to end the task. However, its policy does not produce this action, instead proposing different plans to complete the task and hallucinating that the task is completed. • R-WoM hallucinates or fails to produce high-quality text-based rollouts, making it difficult for (1) the policy to produce good rollout actions and/or (2) the judge to select the correct action. These failures range from outright incorrect descriptions to inadequate descriptions of the next state. To improve the R-WoM baseline and allow for fair comparison, we extended R-WoM with a RAG policy. We show that the performance of R-WoM + RAG policy improves over R-WoM, confirming R-WoM’s policy limitation in the first source of error. Appendix P WebDreamer reimplementation We run WebDreamer ( Gu et al., 2025 ) from its released code (commit e589411 ), pinned as a read-only submodule. Its multi-step imagination loop and pointwise scoring are unchanged: for each of the K = 3 K{=}3 policy candidates we draw 3 independent simulations of planning horizon H H ; each simulation predicts the state change of the candidate action and then, for up to H − 1 H{-}1 further imagined steps (stopping early if a proposed action is stop ), proposes the next action and predicts its state change. A value function scores each simulation with 10 samples (success = 1 =1 , on the right track = 0.5 =0.5 , otherwise 0 0 ); the candidate with the highest mean score is executed. We adapt the prompts to the desktop (web wording becomes desktop wording, the web operation list becomes our desktop operation list, and the current URL is dropped) and pass the current screenshot as the policy’s encoded image. Both components also receive the real executed-step history, so that WebDreamer sees the same history as the other baselines. When steps have already been executed, each world-model user message starts with the text-only step history used by the R-WoM rollout, under the header “Steps already executed before the screenshot below (real history, text only; not part of PREVIOUS ACTIONS)”; the released code gives the world model no history. Instead of the trajectory’s screenshots and an action list, the value function receives the same history as the policy+judge judge (older steps as text, recent steps with screenshots), followed by the current screenshot under the heading “Current state of the screen” and the simulated steps. The value prompt also gains one rule: a simulation whose first action is agent.fail() counts as a success only when the history and the screen prove the task impossible, mirroring the policy+judge judge’s rule for infeasible tasks. World-model and value calls use the judge model (Qwen3-VL-32B, as for the policy) instead of GPT-4o, with OpenAI’s default sampling (temperature 1.0, top- p p 1.0, no top- k k ). The world model generates at most 2048 new tokens, the released code’s cap for its Claude path (its GPT-4o path sets none). The value function generates at most 1024 new tokens instead of the released 256, because Qwen’s longer reasoning was otherwise cut off before the Status: line on about 10–16% of samples, which then scored 0. We simulate all K = 3 K{=}3 candidates and do not apply the optional LLM filter that prunes candidates before simulation. We first save a QEMU snapshot of the current VM state before evaluating any candidate action. This snapshot saves the exact state of the VM, including the screen, memory, and disk, allowing us to restore it to this state after each candidate action is executed. We then execute each candidate action one at a time on the same VM, wait for the interface to settle, and capture the resulting screenshot as that candidate’s ground-truth next state. After each candidate is executed, the VM is restored back to the saved snapshot, so the next candidate starts from the exact same screen state. This makes the comparison fair and deterministic on most of the tasks, with a few exceptions when the task involves internet access and the content on the screen may change (e.g., Google search results). See more details in Appendix S . Appendix R Ground-Truth Error Analysis We follow the same procedure described in Qian et al. (2026) to analyze errors in the ground-truth visual rollout. In total, we collect 2,116 failed trajectories from all runs with ground-truth rollouts. We first sample 30 tasks and manually go through trajectory data: screenshots, policy "thought" tokens, judge "thought" tokens, and proposed actions. We then identify and summarize the following core categories of errors that lead to agent failure: 1. The judge fails to understand task success : We find a notable portion of cases where the GT-rollout judge fails to understand task success, which is a more specific failure mode. GT-rollout judges fail to understand whether future states satisfy the task instruction. We show an example of this case in Figure 30 . 2. The judge fails to reason over future states : GT-rollout judges can fail to reason over future states to wrongly judge the progress of the task. We show an example of this case in Figure 33 and Figure 29 . 3. Wrong MLLM-generated tutorial : MLLM-generated tutorials are not correct and the agent doesn’t know how to recover from wrong steps in the tutorial. We show an example of this case in Figure 26 . 4. Incomplete tutorial : The tutorial does not provide fine-grained enough steps to complete the task, and the policy fails to propose the missing steps by itself. 5. Policy fails to follow the tutorial correctly : The policy itself misunderstands, skips, contradicts, or wrongly executes a tutorial step. We show an example of this case in Figure 27 . 6. Grounding error : The grounding model maps the same action description to different regions in the visual input, which leads to wrong grounding and thus failure. We show an example of this case in Figure 32 . 7. Observation hallucination in policy : The policy misreads the current state and thus reasons toward a wrong action. We show an example of this case in Figure 31 . 8. Web server error : The web server hosting the task environment has issues, such as the target website being down. This is an external factor that can lead to failure, and it is not caused by the agent’s decision-making process. 9. Agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps : The agent is following a correct path but reaches the 15-step or 50-step limit before completing the task. We show an example of this case in Figure 34 . We then use an MLLM (Gemini 3.8 Flash Google DeepMind (2026) ) to annotate the rest of the failed tasks. Given the trajectory data of a task, we prompt it (see Figure 39 ) to classify failure reasons into the categories above. Because a failed task might have many root causes, we follow Qian et al. (2026) and ask the MLLM to classify potential errors into: (1) a primary reason and (2) mentioned (secondary) reasons. Note that mentioned reasons cannot be duplicated with the primary reason. To assess the reliability of this MLLM-as-a-judge framework, we run the MLLM on the manually annotated examples above and find that the agreement rate for the primary reason reaches 90%. Furthermore, we randomly sample 20 examples from MLLM results to examine manually. All of the results are reasonable and aligned with our predefined categories of error. Based on the MLLM’s results, we plot the number of primary and mentioned reasons in Figure 3 . sections.heading: Overview.
sections.text: To robustly evaluate the impact of tutorials, we construct the OSWorld-Tutorial dataset by augmenting 360 tasks from the OSWorld-Verified benchmark Xie et al. (2024) . 10 10 10 We use OSWorld-Verified at commit 83e8534 . We recruit three student annotators with experience in software tasks similar to those in OSWorld to collect a tutorial for each task. For each task, we first launch it in a virtual machine and provide the task instruction together with the initial screenshot to the tutorial-generation prompt shown in Figure 13 . We submit this prompt to Google Gemini 3.8 Flash Google DeepMind (2026) . It searches the web for relevant tutorials and synthesizes a comprehensive summary over the retrieved results. The annotators then review the retrieved tutorials and select the most helpful one for each task. To verify tutorials from publicly available articles, they follow the article’s instructions to complete the task and confirm that it is correct and helpful. We find that many OSWorld tasks require combining multiple tutorials, while others have no relevant tutorials available online. For these tasks, we use the response generated by Google Gemini 3.8 Flash directly as the tutorial. We do not verify the correctness of AI-synthesized tutorials. Figures 14 and 15 show examples of retrieved publicly available tutorials and MLLM-generated tutorials. Each figure shows task instruction, initial screenshot, and the corresponding tutorial content. Task instruction. Enable the “Do Not Track” feature in Chrome to enhance online privacy. Turn “Do Not Track” on or off When browsing the web on computers or Android devices, users can send a request to websites not to collect or track browsing data. The setting is turned off by default. However, what happens to the data depends on how a website responds to the request. Many websites still collect and use browsing data for security, content, services, ads, recommendations, and reporting statistics. Most websites and web services, including Google’s, do not change their behavior when they receive a Do Not Track request. 1. On your computer, open Chrome. 2. At the top right, select More Settings. 3. Select Privacy and security Third-party cookies. 4. Turn Send a “Do not track” request with your browsing traffic on or off. Figure 14: Chrome task example with a retrieved web tutorial. The top panel shows the initial screenshot; the lower panel shows the retrieved markdown tutorial with inline images preserved. Task ID: 030eeff7-b492-4218-b312-701ec99ee0cc . Source: Google Chrome Help . Task instruction. Could you assist me in placing my photo on the desktop and renaming it to export.jpg ? Category: gimp . GIMP treats standard image formats such as .jpg as exports rather than saves. 1. In the top menu, go to File > Export As… or press Ctrl+Shift+E. 2. In the Name box at the top, delete the existing text and type export.jpg . 3. On the left-hand sidebar, under Places, click Desktop to ensure it is being saved to the right spot. 4. Click the Export button in the bottom right. 5. An “Export Image as JPEG” window will pop up. Click Export again to confirm the settings. Figure 15: GIMP task example with an MLLM-synthesized tutorial. The top panel shows the initial screenshot; the lower panel shows the synthesized tutorial for exporting the image as export.jpg on the desktop. Task ID: 77b8ab4d-994f-43ac-8930-8ca087d7c4b4 .

sections.heading: Statistics.
sections.text: In total, we collect 360 tasks with verified tutorials, covering all eight OSWorld task categories. Among these, 110 tasks have human-verified tutorials retrieved from the web (31%), while the remaining 69% are synthesized by Google Gemini 3.8 Flash. We follow Agent-S3 Gonzalez-Pumariega et al. (2026) and OSWorld-MPC Jia et al. (2026) to exclude eight Google Drive tasks. Recently, these tasks have presented technical challenges in using Google accounts and Google Drive credentials in the sandbox. We notice that some web tasks have just been upgraded to use more aggressive bot detection systems, which block automated access even through residential proxies provided by OSWorld. We therefore exclude one task that is blocked by website-level bot-detection or access restrictions, as listed by task ID in Figure 16 . # Excluded task IDs -- one per line, comments start with # # tripadvisor.com -- "Access is temporarily restricted" behavioral bot detection. b7895e80-f4d1-4648-bee0-4eb45a6f1fa8 Figure 16: Excluded task IDs for websites that block automated access through bot detection, CAPTCHAs, or access-denial systems.

sections.heading: Appendix J Problem formulation
sections.text: We cast the computer-use task as a standard finite-horizon partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) ⟨ S , O , A , T , R , L , M ⟩ \langle S,O,A,T,R,L,M\rangle , conditioned on the task instruction L L and a multimodal tutorial M M . The computing environment itself (typically a virtual machine) serves as a mostly-deterministic 11 11 11 In our setting, T T is deterministic for most tasks. For examples of non-deterministic tasks, see Appendix S . transition function T : S × A → S T:S\times A\to S . As the agent only accesses the environment visually, the observation o t ∈ O o_{t}\in O at each time step t t is simply the current screenshot. Actions correspond to movements or clicks of the mouse and keystrokes as well as stop actions (more details in Figure 19 ). The reward function R : S × A → { 0 , 1 } R:S\times A\to\{0,1\} is sparse and indicates task success when the agent issues stop actions or reaches the horizon H H . We consider a CUA to be a stochastic policy π ⁡ ( a t | o ≤ t , a < t , L , M ) \pi(a_{t}\,|\,o_{\leq t},a_{<t},L,M) , which produces a distribution over actions a t a_{t} given previous observations o ≤ t o_{\leq t} , prior actions a < t a_{<t} , the instruction L L , and the tutorial M M . We want to find a policy which achieves high expected cumulative reward (i.e., task success) over CUA tasks.

sections.heading: Look-ahead rollouts.
sections.text: Specifically, given a world model w : O × A → O w:O\times A\to O that predicts the next observation given past observations and the current action, the outcome of each of the K K candidate actions can be estimated as o ~ t 1 , … , o ~ t K \tilde{o}^{1}_{t},...,\tilde{o}^{K}_{t} in a one-step look-ahead. Following Mei et al. (2026) , the policy π \pi is then executed with greedy decoding to generate a single next action a ^ t + 1 j = arg ⁡ max a ^ ⁡ π ⁡ ( a ^ | o ~ t + 1 j ) \hat{a}_{t+1}^{j}=\arg\max_{\hat{a}}\pi(\hat{a}\,|\,\tilde{o}_{t+1}^{j}) for each predicted observation o ~ t + 1 j \tilde{o}_{t+1}^{j} . This loop can be executed until some fixed look-ahead horizon is reached to generate a rollout trajectory ξ j = ( o t , a ^ t j , o ~ t + 1 j , a ^ t + 1 j , … , o ~ t + k j ) \xi^{j}=(o_{t},\hat{a}_{t}^{j},\tilde{o}_{t+1}^{j},\hat{a}_{t+1}^{j},\ldots,\tilde{o}_{t+k}^{j}) for each action candidate a ^ t j \hat{a}_{t}^{j} . The judge model can then select between actions based on their rollout trajectories.

sections.heading: History information.
sections.text: Following GTA-1 Yang et al. (2026c) 12 12 12 Note that the official implementation of GTA-1 https://github.com/Yan98/GTA1 is different from GTA-1’s paper description. In the implementation, it only uses thought tokens and actions, and does not use observation caption descriptions for history information. We follow the implementation instead of the paper description. , the policy and the judge receive the same execution history. It includes the actions of all previous steps, the intermediate thought tokens of the five most recent steps, and the screenshots of up to five recent steps. The screenshot window drops the oldest steps four at a time instead of one per step, so the prompt prefix can be reused across steps. When the history text grows too long, the oldest steps outside the screenshot window are replaced by a single line noting that they were omitted. We find that including intermediate thought tokens for these steps does not significantly improve performance, while it does increase the input length and inference time for both the policy and the judge. We include the ablation study on the effect of including intermediate thought tokens in the execution history in Table 12 . MLLM base 15 steps w/ thought w/o thought Qwen3-VL-8B 28.5% ± \pm 1.6% 28.1% ± \pm 1.2% Qwen3-VL-32B 39.0% ± \pm 1.2% 38.8% ± \pm 0.4% Table 12: Ablation of including intermediate thought tokens in the execution history. We use the setting vanilla policy without tutorial retrieval. Each result is mean and sample std. over 3 completed runs. We find that including intermediate thought tokens does not significantly improve performance.

sections.heading: Appendix L Policy Prompt
sections.text: The listing below shows the fixed- K K variant used when adaptive policy is disabled before the final step. Appendix O R-WoM reimplementation O.1 Implementation details We reimplement the R-WoM method based on the description in the paper. We make the following implementation changes to R-WoM to ensure compatibility with our environment and comparability with other baselines for a more controlled comparison. Changes 1, 3 and 4 below are shared by every method in Table , including ours, and are required for a controlled comparison. Change 2 fixes a format violation in the original rollout prompt that left the ranker with malformed input. Table 2 shows the re-implementation reproduces R-WoM’s gain over a judge-only baseline without tutorials. 1. We use the action space defined by Agent-S2 Agashe et al. (2025b) , instead of the original action space of OSWorld Xie et al. (2024) used in R-WoM. This action space makes the agent act more effectively and is more widely adopted in other GUI-agent works, such as the baseline GTA-1 Yang et al. (2026c) , Agent-S family Agashe et al. (2025b) ; Gonzalez-Pumariega et al. (2026) and UITAR1.5 Qin et al. (2025) . 2. We notice that the text-based rollout of R-WoM does not produce a well-structured rollout that follows the rules in the prompt, which makes it hard for the R-WoM judge (ranker) to judge from the rollout. For example, given the horizon H = 2 H{=}2 , it does not stop at the state 2 as required, and it stops at rollout actions instead. Therefore, we design a new rollout prompt with stricter rules and a more structured output format, as shown in the rollout prompt in Figure 23 . 3. To make it fair to compare R-WoM with other baselines such as GTA-1 Yang et al. (2026c) , we add judge rules from GTA-1 to the R-WoM judge prompt. 4. We keep the GTA-1 Yang et al. (2026c) policy rules and action space but adopt R-WoM’s policy output format: a shared observation and a separate thought for each action candidate. O.2 R-WoM error analysis To better understand the limitations of R-WoM, we manually analyzed more than 30 rollout samples. We found that its failures primarily arise from two sources. • Because R-WoM originally does not have RAG policy, policy can propose wrong actions and therefore the judge does not have a good candidate among proposed candidates. For example, if the tutorial already says “Infeasible”, the agent’s policy should produce “agent.fail()” to end the task. However, its policy does not produce this action, instead proposing different plans to complete the task and hallucinating that the task is completed. • R-WoM hallucinates or fails to produce high-quality text-based rollouts, making it difficult for (1) the policy to produce good rollout actions and/or (2) the judge to select the correct action. These failures range from outright incorrect descriptions to inadequate descriptions of the next state. To improve the R-WoM baseline and allow for fair comparison, we extended R-WoM with a RAG policy. We show that the performance of R-WoM + RAG policy improves over R-WoM, confirming R-WoM’s policy limitation in the first source of error. Appendix P WebDreamer reimplementation We run WebDreamer ( Gu et al., 2025 ) from its released code (commit e589411 ), pinned as a read-only submodule. Its multi-step imagination loop and pointwise scoring are unchanged: for each of the K = 3 K{=}3 policy candidates we draw 3 independent simulations of planning horizon H H ; each simulation predicts the state change of the candidate action and then, for up to H − 1 H{-}1 further imagined steps (stopping early if a proposed action is stop ), proposes the next action and predicts its state change. A value function scores each simulation with 10 samples (success = 1 =1 , on the right track = 0.5 =0.5 , otherwise 0 0 ); the candidate with the highest mean score is executed. We adapt the prompts to the desktop (web wording becomes desktop wording, the web operation list becomes our desktop operation list, and the current URL is dropped) and pass the current screenshot as the policy’s encoded image. Both components also receive the real executed-step history, so that WebDreamer sees the same history as the other baselines. When steps have already been executed, each world-model user message starts with the text-only step history used by the R-WoM rollout, under the header “Steps already executed before the screenshot below (real history, text only; not part of PREVIOUS ACTIONS)”; the released code gives the world model no history. Instead of the trajectory’s screenshots and an action list, the value function receives the same history as the policy+judge judge (older steps as text, recent steps with screenshots), followed by the current screenshot under the heading “Current state of the screen” and the simulated steps. The value prompt also gains one rule: a simulation whose first action is agent.fail() counts as a success only when the history and the screen prove the task impossible, mirroring the policy+judge judge’s rule for infeasible tasks. World-model and value calls use the judge model (Qwen3-VL-32B, as for the policy) instead of GPT-4o, with OpenAI’s default sampling (temperature 1.0, top- p p 1.0, no top- k k ). The world model generates at most 2048 new tokens, the released code’s cap for its Claude path (its GPT-4o path sets none). The value function generates at most 1024 new tokens instead of the released 256, because Qwen’s longer reasoning was otherwise cut off before the Status: line on about 10–16% of samples, which then scored 0. We simulate all K = 3 K{=}3 candidates and do not apply the optional LLM filter that prunes candidates before simulation. We first save a QEMU snapshot of the current VM state before evaluating any candidate action. This snapshot saves the exact state of the VM, including the screen, memory, and disk, allowing us to restore it to this state after each candidate action is executed. We then execute each candidate action one at a time on the same VM, wait for the interface to settle, and capture the resulting screenshot as that candidate’s ground-truth next state. After each candidate is executed, the VM is restored back to the saved snapshot, so the next candidate starts from the exact same screen state. This makes the comparison fair and deterministic on most of the tasks, with a few exceptions when the task involves internet access and the content on the screen may change (e.g., Google search results). Appendix R Ground-Truth Error Analysis We follow the same procedure described in Qian et al. (2026) to analyze errors in the ground-truth visual rollout. In total, we collect 2,116 failed trajectories from all runs with ground-truth rollouts. We first sample 30 tasks and manually go through trajectory data: screenshots, policy "thought" tokens, judge "thought" tokens, and proposed actions. We then identify and summarize the following core categories of errors that lead to agent failure: 1. The judge fails to understand task success : We find a notable portion of cases where the GT-rollout judge fails to understand task success, which is a more specific failure mode. GT-rollout judges fail to understand whether future states satisfy the task instruction. We show an example of this case in Figure 30 . 2. The judge fails to reason over future states : GT-rollout judges can fail to reason over future states to wrongly judge the progress of the task. We show an example of this case in Figure 33 and Figure 29 . 3. Wrong MLLM-generated tutorial : MLLM-generated tutorials are not correct and the agent doesn’t know how to recover from wrong steps in the tutorial. We show an example of this case in Figure 26 . 4. Incomplete tutorial : The tutorial does not provide fine-grained enough steps to complete the task, and the policy fails to propose the missing steps by itself. 5. Policy fails to follow the tutorial correctly : The policy itself misunderstands, skips, contradicts, or wrongly executes a tutorial step. We show an example of this case in Figure 27 . 6. Grounding error : The grounding model maps the same action description to different regions in the visual input, which leads to wrong grounding and thus failure. We show an example of this case in Figure 32 . 7. Observation hallucination in policy : The policy misreads the current state and thus reasons toward a wrong action. We show an example of this case in Figure 31 . 8. Web server error : The web server hosting the task environment has issues, such as the target website being down. This is an external factor that can lead to failure, and it is not caused by the agent’s decision-making process. 9. Agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps : The agent is following a correct path but reaches the 15-step or 50-step limit before completing the task. We show an example of this case in Figure 34 . We then use an MLLM (Gemini 3.8 Flash Google DeepMind (2026) ) to annotate the rest of the failed tasks. Given the trajectory data of a task, we prompt it (see Figure 39 ) to classify failure reasons into the categories above. Because a failed task might have many root causes, we follow Qian et al. (2026) and ask the MLLM to classify potential errors into: (1) a primary reason and (2) mentioned (secondary) reasons. Note that mentioned reasons cannot be duplicated with the primary reason. To assess the reliability of this MLLM-as-a-judge framework, we run the MLLM on the manually annotated examples above and find that the agreement rate for the primary reason reaches 90%. Furthermore, we randomly sample 20 examples from MLLM results to examine manually. All of the results are reasonable and aligned with our predefined categories of error. Based on the MLLM’s results, we plot the number of primary and mentioned reasons in Figure 3 .
