Look at the “Replies” column on the right side of the list. The discussion at the very top of this list will be the one with the most replies in FlightAware history. Figure 26: An example of a wrong tutorial. The top panel shows the tutorial given to the agent, and the bottom panel shows the screenshot where the agent fails. Task ID: eb303e01-261e-4972-8c07-c9b4e7a4922a Task. Tomorrow, I am scheduled to deliver a talk, and my PowerPoint slides and speaking notes are saved on the desktop. Help me insert my planned remarks for each slide into the “note” section of the PowerPoint as a reminder. I have completed this task for some slides; assist me in completing the remaining part. Failure. The agent should copy the planned remarks from notes.docx and paste them into the active notes area, but instead it hallucinates and types the slide’s own content into the notes section. Tutorial. 3. Enable the Notes View • If the notes input area is not visible at the bottom of the main workspace, go to the top menu and select View > Notes . • Alternatively, you can click the Notes tab located directly above the main slide workspace. 4. Copy and Paste the Remarks • Switch back to the notes.docx window. • Highlight and copy ( Ctrl + C ) the specific text corresponding to the active slide. 4. Copy and Paste the Remarks (continued) • Switch back to the presentation window and click inside the area labeled “Click to add notes” below the slide image. • Paste the text ( Ctrl + V ). 5. Repeat for Remaining Slides • Select the next slide in the sequence from the left pane. • Repeat the copy-paste process for all subsequent slides until all planned remarks from the Word document are successfully transferred to the PowerPoint file. (a) Step 6. (b) Step 7. (c) Step 8. (d) Step 9. Figure 27: Example of agents failing to follow the tutorial correctly (continued on next page). The policy should copy planned remarks from notes.docx and paste them into the PowerPoint notes section, but instead types slide content directly into the notes area. Tutorial-consistent action (should have done): Copy the remaining remarks from notes.docx , return to the presentation, and paste them into the active notes area. Executed action at Step 9: agent.type(element_description="the ‘Click to add Notes’ area", text="Course Essentials\n... Student can...", enter=True) Other candidate actions: agent.switch_applications(app_code="libreoffice-writer") agent.done() Policy thought at Step 9. The Notes area for Slide 2 is active and ready for pasting the remarks. I have already copied the text for Slide 2 from the notes.docx file in a previous step. The next logical action is to paste the text into this active Notes area using Ctrl+V. This aligns with the tutorial’s instruction to paste the text after switching back to the presentation window. Figure 28: Example of agents failing to follow the tutorial correctly (continued). Task ID: 7b7617bd-57cc-468e-9c91-40c4ec2bcb3d Judge tokens. GT-Rollout judge: The goal is to set the minimum number of undo steps to 100. The current screenshot shows the “Document History” section, but the specific “Minimal number of undo levels” setting is not visible. Previous scrolling attempts have not revealed it. The “Document History” section might need to be expanded or further scrolled to locate the setting. However, the hotkey action did not yield any visible progress toward the goal. The best course of action is to continue scrolling within the “Document History” section to locate the desired setting. (a) Current state. Chosen Action. agent.scroll(instruction="at the center of the windows Preference", clicks=-5) (b) GT future state. Figure 29: An example where the judge fails to reason about task progress using the future state. The judge recommends continued scrolling from the current state, even when it realizes the GT future state does not show progress. Example: Fail to find the target state. Task ID: 06fe7178-4491-4589-810f-2e2bc9502122 Task. Can you make my computer bring back the last tab I shut down? (a) State 1. Chosen Action 1. agent.hotkey(keys=[’ctrl’, ’shift’, ’t’]) (b) State 2. Index 0 (should have chosen): agent.done() Index 1 (chosen): agent.hotkey(keys=[’ctrl’, ’shift’, ’t’]) Index 2: agent.click(instruction="the ’Tripadvisor’ tab in the browser", num_clicks=1, button_type=’left’, hold_keys=[]) Judge tokens. GT-Rollout judge: The task is to restore the last closed tab. The tutorial confirms that Ctrl+Shift+T is the correct method. Candidate 1 successfully executed this shortcut and brought up the history page, which indicates the tab was restored. Candidate 0 does nothing and is not useful. Candidate 2 clicks on the current tab, which does not restore a closed tab. Therefore, Candidate 1 is the best choice as it directly fulfills the task. Figure 30: An example where the judge fails to understand task success. The judge selects the restore-tab shortcut in State 1, observes State 2 after that action, and still selects the highlighted restore-tab option again. Example: Wrong reasoning over the current state. Task ID: 82bc8d6a-36eb-4d2d-8801-ef714fb1e55a Task. On next Monday, look up a flight from Mumbai to Stockholm. Policy thought. The current date selected is May 21, 2026, which is a Wednesday. The task requires selecting the upcoming Monday. The next Monday after May 21 is May 26, 2026. I need to click on May 26 in the calendar to set the correct departure date. Figure 31: Wrong reasoning over the current state. The policy misreads the currently selected departure date and reasons toward an incorrect next-Monday target. Example: Wrong grounding. Task ID: 37608790-6147-45d0-9f20-1137bb35703d Task. The information is mixed in one field. Help me split them and fill in the columns of First Name, Last Name and Rank. Finish the work and don’t touch the original data. Grounded action. agent.drag_and_drop( starting_description=‘the fill handle of cell B2’, ending_description=‘cell B22’, hold_keys=[]) (a) Grounding visualization. (b) Resulting state after the grounded action. Figure 32: Wrong grounding example. The grounding model maps the drag-and-drop action to an incorrect spreadsheet region, selecting the wrong range in the resulting state. Example: Failure to reason over future states. Task ID: 67890eb6-6ce5-4c00-9e3d-fb4972699b06 Task. I am an NLP researcher. Check out the best long paper awards of ACL from 2019 to 2022 and record the title , year , author list , and PDF link into table best_awards_acl.xlsx on the desktop. Separate authors only by commas, use official ACL Anthology URLs, not arXiv, and sort rows by year in descending order. (a) State 1. (b) State 2. Index 0 (should have chosen): agent.type(element_description="the search bar on the ACL Anthology website", text="ACL 2021", enter=True) Index 1 (chosen): agent.switch_applications( app_code="libreoffice-calc") Index 2: agent.hotkey(keys=["ctrl", "s"]) Judge tokens. GT-Rollout judge: Candidate 1 switches to LibreOffice Calc, showing the spreadsheet best_awards_acl.xlsx with data already entered for the 2022 award, which directly progresses the task of recording award information. Candidate 0 results in a failed search, and Candidate 2 triggers a save dialog unrelated to the task. Selected: 1. (c) State 2 future. Figure 33: The judge fails to reason over the future. The judge selects the candidate that returns to the partially completed spreadsheet because it observes existing 2022 data, instead of preferring the candidate that continues searching for missing ACL award entries. Example: Agent runs out of max steps. Task ID: 6f4073b8-d8ea-4ade-8a18-c5d1d5d5aa9a Task. I now want to count the meeting cities of the three machine learning conferences in the past ten years from 2013 to 2019 (including 2013 and 2019). I have listed the names and years of the conferences in Excel. Please fill in the vacant locations. Failure step. Step 50. Figure 34: An example where an agent runs out of steps. The agent is still working on the spreadsheet at step 50 but has not completed all missing conference locations before reaching the step limit. In these cases, the screenshot captured in the rollout VM differs from the screenshot captured in the real VM after executing the same action. (A) Screenshot captured in a rollout VM. (B) Screenshot captured in a real VM. Figure 35: Rollout vs. real VM (case 0). (A) Screenshot captured in a rollout VM. (B) Screenshot captured in a live VM. Figure 36: Rollout vs. live VM (case 1). (A) Screenshot captured in a rollout VM. (B) Screenshot captured in a live VM. Figure 37: Rollout vs. live VM (case 2). (A) Screenshot captured in a rollout VM. (B) Screenshot captured in a live VM. Figure 38: Rollout vs. live VM (case 3). Appendix T GT-Rollout Failure Analysis Prompt \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝You are an expert desktop UI-agent and GT-rollout failure analyst. \iow_now:Ne ˝Return JSON only with this exact top-level shape: \iow_now:Ne ˝{ \iow_now:Ne ˝ "primary_reason": { \iow_now:Ne ˝ "category": "grounding error" | "tutorial error" | "tutorial is not completed" | "observation hallucination in policy thought" | "agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps" | "web server error, agent cannot connect" | "the judge fails to reason over the future state" | "the judge fails to reason over the future state, fails to understand task success" | "agents fail to follow the tutorial correctly", \iow_now:Ne ˝ "error_step": integer or null, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "details": string \iow_now:Ne ˝ }, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "mentioned_reasons": [ \iow_now:Ne ˝ { \iow_now:Ne ˝ "category": "grounding error" | "tutorial error" | "tutorial is not completed" | "observation hallucination in policy thought" | "agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps" | "web server error, agent cannot connect" | "the judge fails to reason over the future state" | "the judge fails to reason over the future state, fails to understand task success" | "agents fail to follow the tutorial correctly", \iow_now:Ne ˝ "has_reason": true, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "error_step": integer or null, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "details": string \iow_now:Ne ˝ } \iow_now:Ne ˝ ], \iow_now:Ne ˝ "step_evidence": [ \iow_now:Ne ˝ { \iow_now:Ne ˝ "step": integer or null, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "screenshot_ids": [integer], \iow_now:Ne ˝ "action": string, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "grounded_action": string, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "details": string \iow_now:Ne ˝ } \iow_now:Ne ˝ ], \iow_now:Ne ˝ "reason_presence": { \iow_now:Ne ˝ "grounding error": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "tutorial error": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "tutorial is not completed": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "observation hallucination in policy thought": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "web server error, agent cannot connect": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "the judge fails to reason over the future state": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "the judge fails to reason over the future state, fails to understand task success": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "agents fail to follow the tutorial correctly": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ } \iow_now:Ne ˝} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Use only category strings exactly as listed. \iow_now:Ne ˝Category definitions: \iow_now:Ne ˝- grounding error: The high-level action or selected candidate is correct, but the grounded UI operation targets with (x,y) coordinate are wrong, maybe wrong coordinates, window, field, or application state. For example, the agent outputs "click the ’Submit’ button", but the grounded UI operation clicks on a wrong position that is not the ’Submit’ button. \iow_now:Ne ˝- tutorial error: tutorials are not correct and the agent doesn’t know how to recover from wrong steps in tutorials. \iow_now:Ne ˝- tutorial is not completed: the tutorial doesn’t provide enough fine-grained actions to complete the task, and the agent fails to propose these fine-grained actions correctly by itself. \iow_now:Ne ˝- observation hallucination in policy thought: policy hallucinates wrong observation in its thought process, which leads to wrong next action. For example, the policy hallucinates that it has already opened the target application and thus tries to interact with the application, which leads to failure in completing the task. \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps: The agent appears to be following a valid path and has not made a decisive wrong action, but the task remains incomplete because the run reaches the configured max step limit, including either 15-step or 50-step runs. This can be caused by any of the above reasons or by other unknown reasons; use it as primary only when exhausting the step budget is the latest decisive failure. \iow_now:Ne ˝- web server error, agent cannot connect: the web server hosting the task environment has issues, such as a website being down. \iow_now:Ne ˝- the judge fails to reason over the future state: Use when the GT-rollout judge/selector is the decisive failing component: it selects, approves, or keeps preferring a wrong candidate/action because it misreads the current screenshot, candidate rollout screenshots, or future/resulting state. If the policy proposed a correct tutorial-following action but the judge chose a different candidate by hallucinating that the wrong future state was successful, this category should be primary, not tutorial-following failure. In mentioned_reasons, this category is mutually exclusive with the more specific task-success category below. \iow_now:Ne ˝- the judge fails to reason over the future state, fails to understand task success: The policy or GT-rollout judge fails to understand whether the current/future state satisfies the task instruction, especially when it terminates with agent.done() despite visible evidence that the task is still incorrect. Use this more specific category instead of the broader judge future-state category when task-success or termination evidence is involved; if this category appears in mentioned_reasons, do not also include the broader judge future-state category. \iow_now:Ne ˝- agents fail to follow the tutorial correctly: Use when the policy/agent itself misunderstands, skips, contradicts, or wrongly executes a tutorial step, and that policy/agent behavior is the decisive cause of failure. Do not use this as primary when the policy/proposed actions include the correct tutorial-following action but the GT-rollout judge selects a different wrong candidate; in that case use the judge future-state reasoning category as primary. \iow_now:Ne ˝Do not output "other", "unknown", "unclear", or any category not listed above. If no category fits perfectly, choose the closest listed category and explain the mismatch in details. \iow_now:Ne ˝The primary_reason must be the latest decisive reason that directly explains the final failed outcome, usually associated with steps near the end of the trajectory. Earlier mistakes should be secondary mentioned_reasons unless there is no later decision that preserves or confirms the failure. \iow_now:Ne ˝Critical distinction between tutorial-following failure and judge future-state failure: \iow_now:Ne ˝- Use the tutorial-following category only when the policy/agent itself misunderstands, skips, contradicts, or wrongly executes a tutorial step, and that policy/agent action is the decisive cause. \iow_now:Ne ˝- Use the judge future-state reasoning category when the GT-rollout judge selects, approves, or keeps preferring a wrong candidate/action because it misreads the current screenshot, misreads candidate/future screenshots, or hallucinates that an incorrect future state satisfies the task. \iow_now:Ne ˝- If a correct tutorial-following candidate/action was available or proposed, but the judge chose a different candidate by claiming its resulting state was correct, the primary_reason must be the judge future-state reasoning category. The tutorial-following category may be mentioned only if the policy/agent also independently failed to follow the tutorial. \iow_now:Ne ˝If the final or near-final step marks the task done even though screenshots/evaluator evidence show the task is not successful, prefer the task-success/termination category as primary over earlier action or grounding errors. \iow_now:Ne ˝mentioned_reasons must include only secondary categories with evidence in the trajectory. Do not include the same category as primary_reason in mentioned_reasons. \iow_now:Ne ˝The two judge future-state categories are mutually exclusive in mentioned_reasons. If "the judge fails to reason over the future state, fails to understand task success" applies anywhere, do not include "the judge fails to reason over the future state" in mentioned_reasons; use only the more specific task-success category for judge evidence. \iow_now:Ne ˝reason_presence must contain every allowed category with true or false. \iow_now:Ne ˝Keep the JSON compact: primary_reason.details and each mentioned_reasons.details must be one short sentence. \iow_now:Ne ˝Return at most 6 mentioned_reasons entries, only for categories with concrete evidence. \iow_now:Ne ˝Return at most 6 step_evidence entries total, prioritizing the primary reason step and the latest decisive evidence near the end. \iow_now:Ne ˝step_evidence must cite screenshot IDs from the provided Image index. Do not invent screenshot IDs. Do not generate screenshots. The renderer will embed the referenced images. \iow_now:Ne ˝For each step_evidence item, include the trajectory step, the high-level action proposed by the policy, the grounded/executed action from traj.jsonl or pre_grounded fields, and one short sentence explaining why the screenshot/action matters. \iow_now:Ne ˝Use the evaluation JSON and result details as the source of truth for the final failed state. \iow_now:Ne ˝Use GT-rollout candidate images/actions to decide whether the failure came from policy proposal, grounding, rollout prediction, selection, tutorial conditioning, evaluator issues, or termination behavior. \iow_now:Ne ˝Do not invent evidence. If evidence is weak, say so in details. \iow_now:Ne ˝No markdown fences. No prose outside JSON. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Analyze this failed OSWorld GT-rollout task. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝You are given the full task/evaluation bundle, the full traj.jsonl text, and every raster image referenced by the trajectory. Images have been preprocessed with max_image_pixels={max_image_pixels}; they are not raw screenshots. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Task instruction: \iow_now:Ne ˝{task_instruction} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Image index: \iow_now:Ne ˝{image_index} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Classify the primary failure reason and every category that is mentioned by evidence in the trajectory. \iow_now:Ne ˝Also produce compact step_evidence entries for the screenshots/steps that justify the classification. Refer to screenshots by Image number only. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Task bundle and full trajectory: \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝{bundle_markdown} Figure 39: Gemini prompt used to classify failed GT-rollout trajectories and extract compact evidence for the failure analysis. Appendix U LLM Usage Statement The authors used LLM-based assistants for limited editorial and technical support, including grammar and clarity edits, LaTeX debugging, and draft phrasing for non-substantive text. We also use LLM-assisted programming like Claude Code and Codex to implement infrastructure code for ground-truth visual rollouts and other baselines. All LLM-assisted text and code changes were inspected and revised by the authors. The authors are responsible for the final manuscript, including all claims, analyses, tables, figures, citations, and conclusions.

sections.heading: Appendix M Judge Prompt
sections.text: The system message starts with the same one-line introduction as the policy’s (Appendix L ), followed by a compact action space ( AGENT_METHODS_LIST : one line per method instead of the policy’s full signatures and docstrings) and the judge role text JUDGE_ROLE_PROMPT ; the user message is JUDGE_USER_PROMPT . \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝[SYSTEM MESSAGE] \iow_now:Ne ˝Ubuntu desktop computer-use agent (1920x1080; internet available). The user message gives the task, an optional tutorial, step history, and screenshots, then names your role. Follow only the rules and output format of that role. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# ACTION SPACE \iow_now:Ne ˝Use only these exact methods/arguments; no right_click/double_click: \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.click(instruction, num_clicks=1, button_type=’left’, hold_keys=[]) # button_type=’right’|’middle’; double-click=num_clicks=2 \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.done(return_value=None) \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.drag_and_drop(starting_description, ending_description, hold_keys=[]) \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.fail() # proven impossible: CAPTCHA/login/missing required user account credentials/unavailable site/absent required setting or option \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.highlight_text_span(starting_phrase, ending_phrase) \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.hover(instruction) \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.hold_and_press(hold_keys, press_keys) \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.hotkey(keys) \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.open(app_or_filename) # closed app/file; filename, not path; switch if open. Only Google Chrome, LibreOffice Writer/Calc/Impress, Thunderbird, VSCode, VLC Media Player, GIMP; no other programs \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.scroll(instruction, clicks, shift=False) # +up/-down; shift=horizontal; 1˜3 lines; small=1-5, section=5-10, long=10-20; max=50 \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.set_cell_values(cell_values, app_name, sheet_name) # ALWAYS for sheet cells; formulas start "="; max 30 cells/call; app=title filename, sheet=tab \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.switch_applications(app_code) \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.type(element_description=None, text=”, overwrite=False, enter=False) # omit element_description only when keyboard focus/caret is known unchanged from history or immediately preceding focus action; pointer!=focus; click/app switch/dialog/restore uncertainty requires grounding; overwrite=True replaces, False appends intentionally; in a multi-line text/code editor overwrite=True erases the whole document, so select the part to replace (highlight_text_span) and type over it without element_description; overwrite=True for a single-line GUI input still showing old text (calculator/command line, rename field; not terminals); if it is already selected, omit element_description; console commands: no nested single quotes; Enter only submits (click live-filter results) \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.wait(time) # visible progress/load only \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# ROLE: JUDGE \iow_now:Ne ˝Evaluate the candidate actions and rank them by how well each advances the overall goal. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# EVALUATION CRITERIA: \iow_now:Ne ˝Screenshots are ground truth; tutorials are guidance unless they start with ’Infeasible’. \iow_now:Ne ˝1. Feasibility - Target must be visible now; after-screenshots/rollouts must prove the action worked. \iow_now:Ne ˝2. Exactness - Advance the task without extra steps. \iow_now:Ne ˝3. Effectiveness - Make visible progress toward the final state. \iow_now:Ne ˝4. Completion - Use agent.done() only when already complete. \iow_now:Ne ˝5. Tutorial alignment - Prefer feasible tutorial actions, but trust pixels when they differ. \iow_now:Ne ˝6. No regression - Reject broken state, navigation away, or lost progress. \iow_now:Ne ˝7. Terminal evidence - Consider agent.done()/agent.fail() only with hard screenshot/history proof. Prefer any visible action needed to complete, save, apply, close a required dialog, or verify the final artifact. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# REQUIRED DECISION PROCESS \iow_now:Ne ˝Before deciding: \iow_now:Ne ˝1. Derive exact task-specific success conditions from the task instruction. \iow_now:Ne ˝2. Apply all applicable named evaluation criteria to every candidate. \iow_now:Ne ˝3. Judge progress toward the overall goal, not mere action execution. \iow_now:Ne ˝4. Compare observed or expected resulting states and cumulative progress across candidates. \iow_now:Ne ˝5. Decide only after that comparison. \iow_now:Ne ˝In ‘thought‘, connect screenshot/history evidence to success conditions and criteria; do not merely narrate screenshots. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# TUTORIAL GROUNDING GUIDANCE (IF TUTORIAL IS PROVIDED): \iow_now:Ne ˝Prefer feasible tutorial operations that reach task milestones. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# RULES: \iow_now:Ne ˝(1) **OVERRIDE - Infeasible tutorial**: If a tutorial is provided and starts with ’Infeasible’, agent.fail() is the only correct action. \iow_now:Ne ˝(2) Prefer terminal over GUI, then hotkeys over multiple clicks. \iow_now:Ne ˝(3) ANTI-LOOP: If current and latest HISTORY screenshots are substantially unchanged, reject any candidate matching an action’s method+target from the last 3 steps. If all feasible candidates repeat failures, prefer a different agent.* method family and explain the rejection. \iow_now:Ne ˝(4) Do not treat agent.done(return_value=…) as an infeasibility report; prefer agent.fail() for proven impossibility. \iow_now:Ne ˝(5) On the LAST step, only agent.done() or agent.fail() can succeed. \iow_now:Ne ˝(6) Google Chrome is the ONLY available browser. \iow_now:Ne ˝(7) TEXT-SELECTION METHOD PREFERENCE: For the same text range, prefer agent.highlight_text_span(…) over agent.drag_and_drop(…) unless anchors are not visible or the target is non-text. Do not reject highlight_text_span as unsupported for multi-line selection. \iow_now:Ne ˝(8) FOCUSED TEXT ENTRY: Omit element_description only when current keyboard focus/caret is known and unchanged. Then agent.type(text=…, overwrite=…, enter=…) intentionally skips grounding and clicking. History or the current screenshot must establish the intended focus; any intervening click, app switch, dialog transition, or restore uncertainty changes the rule. Do not reject omitted element_description solely when focus evidence is strong. If focus is uncertain, the target is another field, or only the mouse pointer is over the field, require agent.type(element_description=…, …) so grounding can locate it. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# EVIDENCE-FIRST VERIFICATION: \iow_now:Ne ˝Candidate prose, rationale, tutorials, and simulated/text-only trajectories are hypotheses, not execution evidence. Simulated/text-only trajectories may be FEASIBLE, REJECTED, or UNKNOWN, never VERIFIED. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝- Check exact requested conditions: values, text, counts, range endpoints, selection boundaries, dates, names, file paths, source/provenance, and persistence; generic change is insufficient. \iow_now:Ne ˝- Compare the latest HISTORY action with the current screenshot first. Missing expected effect is failure. \iow_now:Ne ˝- For each unexecuted candidate, require a visible target and preconditions; mark FEASIBLE; never claim execution or mark VERIFIED. \iow_now:Ne ˝- For rollouts, inspect screenshots state by state only for actual executed actions. Mark VERIFIED only when an actual state visibly proves the effect; cite it (e.g. ‘Candidate 1 State 2‘). \iow_now:Ne ˝- Missing, ambiguous, or unreadable evidence is UNKNOWN, never success. \iow_now:Ne ˝- Visible proof: selection shows highlight/handles/caret/status; saving shows a completed dialog plus visible target/location or explicit saved/applied history; formatting shows values; persistence shows Save/Apply/OK or reopen/check. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝- DONE: If any candidate is ‘agent.done(…)‘, ‘thought‘ MUST begin ‘DONE_CHECK: <condition> = MET | NOT-MET; …‘, cover every requested final condition, then give ‘CANDIDATE_CHECKS‘. MET means the requested end state holds (a removal/hide goal is MET when the item is gone) and requires direct current-screen proof or explicit saved/applied confirmation; dialogs, highlights, menus, and partial edits are not completion. Select done only when every condition is MET. Missing/incomplete DONE_CHECK, UNKNOWN, or NOT-MET rejects done; choose progress addressing the missing condition. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Selection rules: \iow_now:Ne ˝- Prefer verification for required UNKNOWN evidence; prefer recovery after two failures in the current GUI branch. \iow_now:Ne ˝- Do not reject all candidates when one can safely reveal missing evidence or recover. Appendix O R-WoM reimplementation O.1 Implementation details We reimplement the R-WoM method based on the description in the paper. We make the following implementation changes to R-WoM to ensure compatibility with our environment and comparability with other baselines for a more controlled comparison. Changes 1, 3 and 4 below are shared by every method in Table , including ours, and are required for a controlled comparison. Change 2 fixes a format violation in the original rollout prompt that left the ranker with malformed input. Table 2 shows the re-implementation reproduces R-WoM’s gain over a judge-only baseline without tutorials. 1. We use the action space defined by Agent-S2 Agashe et al. (2025b) , instead of the original action space of OSWorld Xie et al. (2024) used in R-WoM. This action space makes the agent act more effectively and is more widely adopted in other GUI-agent works, such as the baseline GTA-1 Yang et al. (2026c) , Agent-S family Agashe et al. (2025b) ; Gonzalez-Pumariega et al. (2026) and UITAR1.5 Qin et al. (2025) . 2. We notice that the text-based rollout of R-WoM does not produce a well-structured rollout that follows the rules in the prompt, which makes it hard for the R-WoM judge (ranker) to judge from the rollout. For example, given the horizon H = 2 H{=}2 , it does not stop at the state 2 as required, and it stops at rollout actions instead. Therefore, we design a new rollout prompt with stricter rules and a more structured output format, as shown in the rollout prompt in Figure 23 . 3. To make it fair to compare R-WoM with other baselines such as GTA-1 Yang et al. (2026c) , we add judge rules from GTA-1 to the R-WoM judge prompt. 4. We keep the GTA-1 Yang et al. (2026c) policy rules and action space but adopt R-WoM’s policy output format: a shared observation and a separate thought for each action candidate. O.2 R-WoM error analysis To better understand the limitations of R-WoM, we manually analyzed more than 30 rollout samples. We found that its failures primarily arise from two sources. • Because R-WoM originally does not have RAG policy, policy can propose wrong actions and therefore the judge does not have a good candidate among proposed candidates. For example, if the tutorial already says “Infeasible”, the agent’s policy should produce “agent.fail()” to end the task. However, its policy does not produce this action, instead proposing different plans to complete the task and hallucinating that the task is completed. • R-WoM hallucinates or fails to produce high-quality text-based rollouts, making it difficult for (1) the policy to produce good rollout actions and/or (2) the judge to select the correct action. These failures range from outright incorrect descriptions to inadequate descriptions of the next state. To improve the R-WoM baseline and allow for fair comparison, we extended R-WoM with a RAG policy. We show that the performance of R-WoM + RAG policy improves over R-WoM, confirming R-WoM’s policy limitation in the first source of error. Appendix P WebDreamer reimplementation We run WebDreamer ( Gu et al., 2025 ) from its released code (commit e589411 ), pinned as a read-only submodule. Its multi-step imagination loop and pointwise scoring are unchanged: for each of the K = 3 K{=}3 policy candidates we draw 3 independent simulations of planning horizon H H ; each simulation predicts the state change of the candidate action and then, for up to H − 1 H{-}1 further imagined steps (stopping early if a proposed action is stop ), proposes the next action and predicts its state change. A value function scores each simulation with 10 samples (success = 1 =1 , on the right track = 0.5 =0.5 , otherwise 0 0 ); the candidate with the highest mean score is executed. We adapt the prompts to the desktop (web wording becomes desktop wording, the web operation list becomes our desktop operation list, and the current URL is dropped) and pass the current screenshot as the policy’s encoded image. Both components also receive the real executed-step history, so that WebDreamer sees the same history as the other baselines. When steps have already been executed, each world-model user message starts with the text-only step history used by the R-WoM rollout, under the header “Steps already executed before the screenshot below (real history, text only; not part of PREVIOUS ACTIONS)”; the released code gives the world model no history. Instead of the trajectory’s screenshots and an action list, the value function receives the same history as the policy+judge judge (older steps as text, recent steps with screenshots), followed by the current screenshot under the heading “Current state of the screen” and the simulated steps. The value prompt also gains one rule: a simulation whose first action is agent.fail() counts as a success only when the history and the screen prove the task impossible, mirroring the policy+judge judge’s rule for infeasible tasks. World-model and value calls use the judge model (Qwen3-VL-32B, as for the policy) instead of GPT-4o, with OpenAI’s default sampling (temperature 1.0, top- p p 1.0, no top- k k ). The world model generates at most 2048 new tokens, the released code’s cap for its Claude path (its GPT-4o path sets none). The value function generates at most 1024 new tokens instead of the released 256, because Qwen’s longer reasoning was otherwise cut off before the Status: line on about 10–16% of samples, which then scored 0. We simulate all K = 3 K{=}3 candidates and do not apply the optional LLM filter that prunes candidates before simulation. We first save a QEMU snapshot of the current VM state before evaluating any candidate action. This snapshot saves the exact state of the VM, including the screen, memory, and disk, allowing us to restore it to this state after each candidate action is executed. We then execute each candidate action one at a time on the same VM, wait for the interface to settle, and capture the resulting screenshot as that candidate’s ground-truth next state. After each candidate is executed, the VM is restored back to the saved snapshot, so the next candidate starts from the exact same screen state. This makes the comparison fair and deterministic on most of the tasks, with a few exceptions when the task involves internet access and the content on the screen may change (e.g., Google search results). Appendix R Ground-Truth Error Analysis We follow the same procedure described in Qian et al. (2026) to analyze errors in the ground-truth visual rollout. In total, we collect 2,116 failed trajectories from all runs with ground-truth rollouts. We first sample 30 tasks and manually go through trajectory data: screenshots, policy "thought" tokens, judge "thought" tokens, and proposed actions. We then identify and summarize the following core categories of errors that lead to agent failure: 1. The judge fails to understand task success : We find a notable portion of cases where the GT-rollout judge fails to understand task success, which is a more specific failure mode. GT-rollout judges fail to understand whether future states satisfy the task instruction. We show an example of this case in Figure 30 . 2. The judge fails to reason over future states : GT-rollout judges can fail to reason over future states to wrongly judge the progress of the task. We show an example of this case in Figure 33 and Figure 29 . 3. Wrong MLLM-generated tutorial : MLLM-generated tutorials are not correct and the agent doesn’t know how to recover from wrong steps in the tutorial. We show an example of this case in Figure 26 . 4. Incomplete tutorial : The tutorial does not provide fine-grained enough steps to complete the task, and the policy fails to propose the missing steps by itself. 5. Policy fails to follow the tutorial correctly : The policy itself misunderstands, skips, contradicts, or wrongly executes a tutorial step. We show an example of this case in Figure 27 . 6. Grounding error : The grounding model maps the same action description to different regions in the visual input, which leads to wrong grounding and thus failure. We show an example of this case in Figure 32 . 7. Observation hallucination in policy : The policy misreads the current state and thus reasons toward a wrong action. We show an example of this case in Figure 31 . 8. Web server error : The web server hosting the task environment has issues, such as the target website being down. This is an external factor that can lead to failure, and it is not caused by the agent’s decision-making process. 9. Agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps : The agent is following a correct path but reaches the 15-step or 50-step limit before completing the task. We show an example of this case in Figure 34 . We then use an MLLM (Gemini 3.8 Flash Google DeepMind (2026) ) to annotate the rest of the failed tasks. Given the trajectory data of a task, we prompt it (see Figure 39 ) to classify failure reasons into the categories above. Because a failed task might have many root causes, we follow Qian et al. (2026) and ask the MLLM to classify potential errors into: (1) a primary reason and (2) mentioned (secondary) reasons. Note that mentioned reasons cannot be duplicated with the primary reason. To assess the reliability of this MLLM-as-a-judge framework, we run the MLLM on the manually annotated examples above and find that the agreement rate for the primary reason reaches 90%. Furthermore, we randomly sample 20 examples from MLLM results to examine manually. All of the results are reasonable and aligned with our predefined categories of error. Based on the MLLM’s results, we plot the number of primary and mentioned reasons in Figure 3 . future state, fails to understand task success": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "agents fail to follow the tutorial correctly": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ } \iow_now:Ne ˝} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Use only category strings exactly as listed. \iow_now:Ne ˝Category definitions: \iow_now:Ne ˝- grounding error: The high-level action or selected candidate is correct, but the grounded UI operation targets with (x,y) coordinate are wrong, maybe wrong coordinates, window, field, or application state. For example, the agent outputs "click the ’Submit’ button", but the grounded UI operation clicks on a wrong position that is not the ’Submit’ button. \iow_now:Ne ˝- tutorial error: tutorials are not correct and the agent doesn’t know how to recover from wrong steps in tutorials. \iow_now:Ne ˝- tutorial is not completed: the tutorial doesn’t provide enough fine-grained actions to complete the task, and the agent fails to propose these fine-grained actions correctly by itself. \iow_now:Ne ˝- observation hallucination in policy thought: policy hallucinates wrong observation in its thought process, which leads to wrong next action. For example, the policy hallucinates that it has already opened the target application and thus tries to interact with the application, which leads to failure in completing the task. \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps: The agent appears to be following a valid path and has not made a decisive wrong action, but the task remains incomplete because the run reaches the configured max step limit, including either 15-step or 50-step runs. This can be caused by any of the above reasons or by other unknown reasons; use it as primary only when exhausting the step budget is the latest decisive failure. \iow_now:Ne ˝- web server error, agent cannot connect: the web server hosting the task environment has issues, such as a website being down. \iow_now:Ne ˝- the judge fails to reason over the future state: Use when the GT-rollout judge/selector is the decisive failing component: it selects, approves, or keeps preferring a wrong candidate/action because it misreads the current screenshot, candidate rollout screenshots, or future/resulting state. If the policy proposed a correct tutorial-following action but the judge chose a different candidate by hallucinating that the wrong future state was successful, this category should be primary, not tutorial-following failure. In mentioned_reasons, this category is mutually exclusive with the more specific task-success category below. \iow_now:Ne ˝- the judge fails to reason over the future state, fails to understand task success: The policy or GT-rollout judge fails to understand whether the current/future state satisfies the task instruction, especially when it terminates with agent.done() despite visible evidence that the task is still incorrect. Use this more specific category instead of the broader judge future-state category when task-success or termination evidence is involved; if this category appears in mentioned_reasons, do not also include the broader judge future-state category. \iow_now:Ne ˝- agents fail to follow the tutorial correctly: Use when the policy/agent itself misunderstands, skips, contradicts, or wrongly executes a tutorial step, and that policy/agent behavior is the decisive cause of failure. Do not use this as primary when the policy/proposed actions include the correct tutorial-following action but the GT-rollout judge selects a different wrong candidate; in that case use the judge future-state reasoning category as primary. \iow_now:Ne ˝Do not output "other", "unknown", "unclear", or any category not listed above. If no category fits perfectly, choose the closest listed category and explain the mismatch in details. \iow_now:Ne ˝The primary_reason must be the latest decisive reason that directly explains the final failed outcome, usually associated with steps near the end of the trajectory. Earlier mistakes should be secondary mentioned_reasons unless there is no later decision that preserves or confirms the failure. \iow_now:Ne ˝Critical distinction between tutorial-following failure and judge future-state failure: \iow_now:Ne ˝- Use the tutorial-following category only when the policy/agent itself misunderstands, skips, contradicts, or wrongly executes a tutorial step, and that policy/agent action is the decisive cause. \iow_now:Ne ˝- Use the judge future-state reasoning category when the GT-rollout judge selects, approves, or keeps preferring a wrong candidate/action because it misreads the current screenshot, misreads candidate/future screenshots, or hallucinates that an incorrect future state satisfies the task. \iow_now:Ne ˝- If a correct tutorial-following candidate/action was available or proposed, but the judge chose a different candidate by claiming its resulting state was correct, the primary_reason must be the judge future-state reasoning category. The tutorial-following category may be mentioned only if the policy/agent also independently failed to follow the tutorial. \iow_now:Ne ˝If the final or near-final step marks the task done even though screenshots/evaluator evidence show the task is not successful, prefer the task-success/termination category as primary over earlier action or grounding errors. \iow_now:Ne ˝mentioned_reasons must include only secondary categories with evidence in the trajectory. Do not include the same category as primary_reason in mentioned_reasons. \iow_now:Ne ˝The two judge future-state categories are mutually exclusive in mentioned_reasons. If "the judge fails to reason over the future state, fails to understand task success" applies anywhere, do not include "the judge fails to reason over the future state" in mentioned_reasons; use only the more specific task-success category for judge evidence. \iow_now:Ne ˝reason_presence must contain every allowed category with true or false. \iow_now:Ne ˝Keep the JSON compact: primary_reason.details and each mentioned_reasons.details must be one short sentence. \iow_now:Ne ˝Return at most 6 mentioned_reasons entries, only for categories with concrete evidence. \iow_now:Ne ˝Return at most 6 step_evidence entries total, prioritizing the primary reason step and the latest decisive evidence near the end. \iow_now:Ne ˝step_evidence must cite screenshot IDs from the provided Image index. Do not invent screenshot IDs. Do not generate screenshots. The renderer will embed the referenced images. \iow_now:Ne ˝For each step_evidence item, include the trajectory step, the high-level action proposed by the policy, the grounded/executed action from traj.jsonl or pre_grounded fields, and one short sentence explaining why the screenshot/action matters. \iow_now:Ne ˝Use the evaluation JSON and result details as the source of truth for the final failed state. \iow_now:Ne ˝Use GT-rollout candidate images/actions to decide whether the failure came from policy proposal, grounding, rollout prediction, selection, tutorial conditioning, evaluator issues, or termination behavior. \iow_now:Ne ˝Do not invent evidence. If evidence is weak, say so in details. \iow_now:Ne ˝No markdown fences. Appendix U LLM Usage Statement The authors used LLM-based assistants for limited editorial and technical support, including grammar and clarity edits, LaTeX debugging, and draft phrasing for non-substantive text. We also use LLM-assisted programming like Claude Code and Codex to implement infrastructure code for ground-truth visual rollouts and other baselines. All LLM-assisted text and code changes were inspected and revised by the authors. The authors are responsible for the final manuscript, including all claims, analyses, tables, figures, citations, and conclusions.

Examine the screenshot carefully, think step by step about which element matches, then provide the coordinate. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Match the requested semantic label, not merely a similar-looking icon. In LibreOffice Calc, "Background Color", "Fill Color", or "paint bucket" means the cell background/fill-color bucket control, not the funnel-shaped AutoFilter icon. The output should just be the coordinates of a point, in the format [x,y]. Additionally, if the task is infeasible (e.g., the task is not related to the image), the output should be [-1,-1]. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# Task instruction: \iow_now:Ne ˝{}. \iow_now:Ne ˝ Figure 21: Grounding prompt used by UI-Venus-1.5 to localize UI elements from grounding instructions and screenshots. Appendix O R-WoM reimplementation O.1 Implementation details We reimplement the R-WoM method based on the description in the paper. We make the following implementation changes to R-WoM to ensure compatibility with our environment and comparability with other baselines for a more controlled comparison. Changes 1, 3 and 4 below are shared by every method in Table , including ours, and are required for a controlled comparison. Change 2 fixes a format violation in the original rollout prompt that left the ranker with malformed input. Table 2 shows the re-implementation reproduces R-WoM’s gain over a judge-only baseline without tutorials. 1. We use the action space defined by Agent-S2 Agashe et al. (2025b) , instead of the original action space of OSWorld Xie et al. (2024) used in R-WoM. This action space makes the agent act more effectively and is more widely adopted in other GUI-agent works, such as the baseline GTA-1 Yang et al. (2026c) , Agent-S family Agashe et al. (2025b) ; Gonzalez-Pumariega et al. (2026) and UITAR1.5 Qin et al. (2025) . 2. We notice that the text-based rollout of R-WoM does not produce a well-structured rollout that follows the rules in the prompt, which makes it hard for the R-WoM judge (ranker) to judge from the rollout. For example, given the horizon H = 2 H{=}2 , it does not stop at the state 2 as required, and it stops at rollout actions instead. Therefore, we design a new rollout prompt with stricter rules and a more structured output format, as shown in the rollout prompt in Figure 23 . 3. To make it fair to compare R-WoM with other baselines such as GTA-1 Yang et al. (2026c) , we add judge rules from GTA-1 to the R-WoM judge prompt. 4. We keep the GTA-1 Yang et al. (2026c) policy rules and action space but adopt R-WoM’s policy output format: a shared observation and a separate thought for each action candidate. O.2 R-WoM error analysis To better understand the limitations of R-WoM, we manually analyzed more than 30 rollout samples. We found that its failures primarily arise from two sources. • Because R-WoM originally does not have RAG policy, policy can propose wrong actions and therefore the judge does not have a good candidate among proposed candidates. For example, if the tutorial already says “Infeasible”, the agent’s policy should produce “agent.fail()” to end the task. However, its policy does not produce this action, instead proposing different plans to complete the task and hallucinating that the task is completed. • R-WoM hallucinates or fails to produce high-quality text-based rollouts, making it difficult for (1) the policy to produce good rollout actions and/or (2) the judge to select the correct action. These failures range from outright incorrect descriptions to inadequate descriptions of the next state. To improve the R-WoM baseline and allow for fair comparison, we extended R-WoM with a RAG policy. We show that the performance of R-WoM + RAG policy improves over R-WoM, confirming R-WoM’s policy limitation in the first source of error. Appendix P WebDreamer reimplementation We run WebDreamer ( Gu et al., 2025 ) from its released code (commit e589411 ), pinned as a read-only submodule. Its multi-step imagination loop and pointwise scoring are unchanged: for each of the K = 3 K{=}3 policy candidates we draw 3 independent simulations of planning horizon H H ; each simulation predicts the state change of the candidate action and then, for up to H − 1 H{-}1 further imagined steps (stopping early if a proposed action is stop ), proposes the next action and predicts its state change. A value function scores each simulation with 10 samples (success = 1 =1 , on the right track = 0.5 =0.5 , otherwise 0 0 ); the candidate with the highest mean score is executed. We adapt the prompts to the desktop (web wording becomes desktop wording, the web operation list becomes our desktop operation list, and the current URL is dropped) and pass the current screenshot as the policy’s encoded image. Both components also receive the real executed-step history, so that WebDreamer sees the same history as the other baselines. When steps have already been executed, each world-model user message starts with the text-only step history used by the R-WoM rollout, under the header “Steps already executed before the screenshot below (real history, text only; not part of PREVIOUS ACTIONS)”; the released code gives the world model no history. Instead of the trajectory’s screenshots and an action list, the value function receives the same history as the policy+judge judge (older steps as text, recent steps with screenshots), followed by the current screenshot under the heading “Current state of the screen” and the simulated steps. The value prompt also gains one rule: a simulation whose first action is agent.fail() counts as a success only when the history and the screen prove the task impossible, mirroring the policy+judge judge’s rule for infeasible tasks. World-model and value calls use the judge model (Qwen3-VL-32B, as for the policy) instead of GPT-4o, with OpenAI’s default sampling (temperature 1.0, top- p p 1.0, no top- k k ). The world model generates at most 2048 new tokens, the released code’s cap for its Claude path (its GPT-4o path sets none). The value function generates at most 1024 new tokens instead of the released 256, because Qwen’s longer reasoning was otherwise cut off before the Status: line on about 10–16% of samples, which then scored 0. We simulate all K = 3 K{=}3 candidates and do not apply the optional LLM filter that prunes candidates before simulation. Appendix R Ground-Truth Error Analysis We follow the same procedure described in Qian et al. (2026) to analyze errors in the ground-truth visual rollout. In total, we collect 2,116 failed trajectories from all runs with ground-truth rollouts. We first sample 30 tasks and manually go through trajectory data: screenshots, policy "thought" tokens, judge "thought" tokens, and proposed actions. We then identify and summarize the following core categories of errors that lead to agent failure: 1. The judge fails to understand task success : We find a notable portion of cases where the GT-rollout judge fails to understand task success, which is a more specific failure mode. GT-rollout judges fail to understand whether future states satisfy the task instruction. We show an example of this case in Figure 30 . 2. The judge fails to reason over future states : GT-rollout judges can fail to reason over future states to wrongly judge the progress of the task. We show an example of this case in Figure 33 and Figure 29 . 3. Wrong MLLM-generated tutorial : MLLM-generated tutorials are not correct and the agent doesn’t know how to recover from wrong steps in the tutorial. We show an example of this case in Figure 26 . 4. Incomplete tutorial : The tutorial does not provide fine-grained enough steps to complete the task, and the policy fails to propose the missing steps by itself. 5. Policy fails to follow the tutorial correctly : The policy itself misunderstands, skips, contradicts, or wrongly executes a tutorial step. We show an example of this case in Figure 27 . 6. Grounding error : The grounding model maps the same action description to different regions in the visual input, which leads to wrong grounding and thus failure. We show an example of this case in Figure 32 . 7. Observation hallucination in policy : The policy misreads the current state and thus reasons toward a wrong action. We show an example of this case in Figure 31 . 8. Web server error : The web server hosting the task environment has issues, such as the target website being down. This is an external factor that can lead to failure, and it is not caused by the agent’s decision-making process. 9. Agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps : The agent is following a correct path but reaches the 15-step or 50-step limit before completing the task. We show an example of this case in Figure 34 . We then use an MLLM (Gemini 3.8 Flash Google DeepMind (2026) ) to annotate the rest of the failed tasks. Given the trajectory data of a task, we prompt it (see Figure 39 ) to classify failure reasons into the categories above. Because a failed task might have many root causes, we follow Qian et al. (2026) and ask the MLLM to classify potential errors into: (1) a primary reason and (2) mentioned (secondary) reasons. Note that mentioned reasons cannot be duplicated with the primary reason. To assess the reliability of this MLLM-as-a-judge framework, we run the MLLM on the manually annotated examples above and find that the agreement rate for the primary reason reaches 90%. Furthermore, we randomly sample 20 examples from MLLM results to examine manually. All of the results are reasonable and aligned with our predefined categories of error. Based on the MLLM’s results, we plot the number of primary and mentioned reasons in Figure 3 . sections.heading: O.1 Implementation details
sections.text: We reimplement the R-WoM method based on the description in the paper. We make the following implementation changes to R-WoM to ensure compatibility with our environment and comparability with other baselines for a more controlled comparison. Changes 1, 3 and 4 below are shared by every method in Table , including ours, and are required for a controlled comparison. Change 2 fixes a format violation in the original rollout prompt that left the ranker with malformed input. Table 2 shows the re-implementation reproduces R-WoM’s gain over a judge-only baseline without tutorials. 1. We use the action space defined by Agent-S2 Agashe et al. (2025b) , instead of the original action space of OSWorld Xie et al. (2024) used in R-WoM. This action space makes the agent act more effectively and is more widely adopted in other GUI-agent works, such as the baseline GTA-1 Yang et al. (2026c) , Agent-S family Agashe et al. (2025b) ; Gonzalez-Pumariega et al. (2026) and UITAR1.5 Qin et al. (2025) . 2. We notice that the text-based rollout of R-WoM does not produce a well-structured rollout that follows the rules in the prompt, which makes it hard for the R-WoM judge (ranker) to judge from the rollout. For example, given the horizon H = 2 H{=}2 , it does not stop at the state 2 as required, and it stops at rollout actions instead. Therefore, we design a new rollout prompt with stricter rules and a more structured output format, as shown in the rollout prompt in Figure 23 . 3. To make it fair to compare R-WoM with other baselines such as GTA-1 Yang et al. (2026c) , we add judge rules from GTA-1 to the R-WoM judge prompt. 4. We keep the GTA-1 Yang et al. (2026c) policy rules and action space but adopt R-WoM’s policy output format: a shared observation and a separate thought for each action candidate.

sections.heading: O.2 R-WoM error analysis
sections.text: To better understand the limitations of R-WoM, we manually analyzed more than 30 rollout samples. We found that its failures primarily arise from two sources. • Because R-WoM originally does not have RAG policy, policy can propose wrong actions and therefore the judge does not have a good candidate among proposed candidates. For example, if the tutorial already says “Infeasible”, the agent’s policy should produce “agent.fail()” to end the task. However, its policy does not produce this action, instead proposing different plans to complete the task and hallucinating that the task is completed. • R-WoM hallucinates or fails to produce high-quality text-based rollouts, making it difficult for (1) the policy to produce good rollout actions and/or (2) the judge to select the correct action. These failures range from outright incorrect descriptions to inadequate descriptions of the next state. To improve the R-WoM baseline and allow for fair comparison, we extended R-WoM with a RAG policy. We show that the performance of R-WoM + RAG policy improves over R-WoM, confirming R-WoM’s policy limitation in the first source of error.

sections.heading: O.3 Policy prompt
sections.text: The R-WoM policy uses the GTA-1 policy prompt (Figure 19 ) with the same system introduction, action space, policy rules, action requirements, and tutorial rules. Only the output section changes, to follow the R-WoM policy format: one shared observation, then a separate thought inside each action candidate. The structured-output JSON schema matches: it requires observation and a thought in every candidate, with no shared thought. Each candidate’s thought is passed to its world-model rollout and to the judge, and the selected candidate’s thought is stored in the history. Without tutorial evidence, the Tutorial Reference parts are omitted as in the GTA-1 prompt. Appendix P WebDreamer reimplementation We run WebDreamer ( Gu et al., 2025 ) from its released code (commit e589411 ), pinned as a read-only submodule. Its multi-step imagination loop and pointwise scoring are unchanged: for each of the K = 3 K{=}3 policy candidates we draw 3 independent simulations of planning horizon H H ; each simulation predicts the state change of the candidate action and then, for up to H − 1 H{-}1 further imagined steps (stopping early if a proposed action is stop ), proposes the next action and predicts its state change. A value function scores each simulation with 10 samples (success = 1 =1 , on the right track = 0.5 =0.5 , otherwise 0 0 ); the candidate with the highest mean score is executed. We adapt the prompts to the desktop (web wording becomes desktop wording, the web operation list becomes our desktop operation list, and the current URL is dropped) and pass the current screenshot as the policy’s encoded image. Both components also receive the real executed-step history, so that WebDreamer sees the same history as the other baselines. When steps have already been executed, each world-model user message starts with the text-only step history used by the R-WoM rollout, under the header “Steps already executed before the screenshot below (real history, text only; not part of PREVIOUS ACTIONS)”; the released code gives the world model no history. Instead of the trajectory’s screenshots and an action list, the value function receives the same history as the policy+judge judge (older steps as text, recent steps with screenshots), followed by the current screenshot under the heading “Current state of the screen” and the simulated steps. The value prompt also gains one rule: a simulation whose first action is agent.fail() counts as a success only when the history and the screen prove the task impossible, mirroring the policy+judge judge’s rule for infeasible tasks. World-model and value calls use the judge model (Qwen3-VL-32B, as for the policy) instead of GPT-4o, with OpenAI’s default sampling (temperature 1.0, top- p p 1.0, no top- k k ). The world model generates at most 2048 new tokens, the released code’s cap for its Claude path (its GPT-4o path sets none). The value function generates at most 1024 new tokens instead of the released 256, because Qwen’s longer reasoning was otherwise cut off before the Status: line on about 10–16% of samples, which then scored 0. We simulate all K = 3 K{=}3 candidates and do not apply the optional LLM filter that prunes candidates before simulation. We first save a QEMU snapshot of the current VM state before evaluating any candidate action. This snapshot saves the exact state of the VM, including the screen, memory, and disk, allowing us to restore it to this state after each candidate action is executed. We then execute each candidate action one at a time on the same VM, wait for the interface to settle, and capture the resulting screenshot as that candidate’s ground-truth next state. After each candidate is executed, the VM is restored back to the saved snapshot, so the next candidate starts from the exact same screen state. This makes the comparison fair and deterministic on most of the tasks, with a few exceptions when the task involves internet access and the content on the screen may change (e.g., Google search results). See more details in Appendix S . Appendix R Ground-Truth Error Analysis We follow the same procedure described in Qian et al. (2026) to analyze errors in the ground-truth visual rollout. In total, we collect 2,116 failed trajectories from all runs with ground-truth rollouts. We first sample 30 tasks and manually go through trajectory data: screenshots, policy "thought" tokens, judge "thought" tokens, and proposed actions. We then identify and summarize the following core categories of errors that lead to agent failure: 1. The judge fails to understand task success : We find a notable portion of cases where the GT-rollout judge fails to understand task success, which is a more specific failure mode. GT-rollout judges fail to understand whether future states satisfy the task instruction. We show an example of this case in Figure 30 . 2. The judge fails to reason over future states : GT-rollout judges can fail to reason over future states to wrongly judge the progress of the task. We show an example of this case in Figure 33 and Figure 29 . 3. Wrong MLLM-generated tutorial : MLLM-generated tutorials are not correct and the agent doesn’t know how to recover from wrong steps in the tutorial. We show an example of this case in Figure 26 . 4. Incomplete tutorial : The tutorial does not provide fine-grained enough steps to complete the task, and the policy fails to propose the missing steps by itself. 5. Policy fails to follow the tutorial correctly : The policy itself misunderstands, skips, contradicts, or wrongly executes a tutorial step. We show an example of this case in Figure 27 . 6. Grounding error : The grounding model maps the same action description to different regions in the visual input, which leads to wrong grounding and thus failure. We show an example of this case in Figure 32 . 7. Observation hallucination in policy : The policy misreads the current state and thus reasons toward a wrong action. We show an example of this case in Figure 31 . 8. Web server error : The web server hosting the task environment has issues, such as the target website being down. This is an external factor that can lead to failure, and it is not caused by the agent’s decision-making process. 9. Agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps : The agent is following a correct path but reaches the 15-step or 50-step limit before completing the task. We show an example of this case in Figure 34 . We then use an MLLM (Gemini 3.8 Flash Google DeepMind (2026) ) to annotate the rest of the failed tasks. Given the trajectory data of a task, we prompt it (see Figure 39 ) to classify failure reasons into the categories above. Because a failed task might have many root causes, we follow Qian et al. (2026) and ask the MLLM to classify potential errors into: (1) a primary reason and (2) mentioned (secondary) reasons. Note that mentioned reasons cannot be duplicated with the primary reason. To assess the reliability of this MLLM-as-a-judge framework, we run the MLLM on the manually annotated examples above and find that the agreement rate for the primary reason reaches 90%. Furthermore, we randomly sample 20 examples from MLLM results to examine manually. All of the results are reasonable and aligned with our predefined categories of error. Based on the MLLM’s results, we plot the number of primary and mentioned reasons in Figure 3 .
