The next logical action is to paste the text into this active Notes area using Ctrl+V. This aligns with the tutorial’s instruction to paste the text after switching back to the presentation window. Figure 28: Example of agents failing to follow the tutorial correctly (continued). Task ID: 7b7617bd-57cc-468e-9c91-40c4ec2bcb3d Judge tokens. GT-Rollout judge: The goal is to set the minimum number of undo steps to 100. The current screenshot shows the “Document History” section, but the specific “Minimal number of undo levels” setting is not visible. Previous scrolling attempts have not revealed it. The “Document History” section might need to be expanded or further scrolled to locate the setting. However, the hotkey action did not yield any visible progress toward the goal. The best course of action is to continue scrolling within the “Document History” section to locate the desired setting. (a) Current state. Chosen Action. agent.scroll(instruction="at the center of the windows Preference", clicks=-5) (b) GT future state. Figure 29: An example where the judge fails to reason about task progress using the future state. The judge recommends continued scrolling from the current state, even when it realizes the GT future state does not show progress. Example: Fail to find the target state. Task ID: 06fe7178-4491-4589-810f-2e2bc9502122 Task. Can you make my computer bring back the last tab I shut down? (a) State 1. Chosen Action 1. agent.hotkey(keys=[’ctrl’, ’shift’, ’t’]) (b) State 2. Index 0 (should have chosen): agent.done() Index 1 (chosen): agent.hotkey(keys=[’ctrl’, ’shift’, ’t’]) Index 2: agent.click(instruction="the ’Tripadvisor’ tab in the browser", num_clicks=1, button_type=’left’, hold_keys=[]) Judge tokens. GT-Rollout judge: The task is to restore the last closed tab. The tutorial confirms that Ctrl+Shift+T is the correct method. Candidate 1 successfully executed this shortcut and brought up the history page, which indicates the tab was restored. Candidate 0 does nothing and is not useful. Candidate 2 clicks on the current tab, which does not restore a closed tab. Therefore, Candidate 1 is the best choice as it directly fulfills the task. Figure 30: An example where the judge fails to understand task success. The judge selects the restore-tab shortcut in State 1, observes State 2 after that action, and still selects the highlighted restore-tab option again. Example: Wrong reasoning over the current state. Task ID: 82bc8d6a-36eb-4d2d-8801-ef714fb1e55a Task. On next Monday, look up a flight from Mumbai to Stockholm. Policy thought. The current date selected is May 21, 2026, which is a Wednesday. The task requires selecting the upcoming Monday. The next Monday after May 21 is May 26, 2026. I need to click on May 26 in the calendar to set the correct departure date. Figure 31: Wrong reasoning over the current state. The policy misreads the currently selected departure date and reasons toward an incorrect next-Monday target. Example: Wrong grounding. Task ID: 37608790-6147-45d0-9f20-1137bb35703d Task. The information is mixed in one field. Help me split them and fill in the columns of First Name, Last Name and Rank. Finish the work and don’t touch the original data. Grounded action. agent.drag_and_drop( starting_description=‘the fill handle of cell B2’, ending_description=‘cell B22’, hold_keys=[]) (a) Grounding visualization. (b) Resulting state after the grounded action. Figure 32: Wrong grounding example. The grounding model maps the drag-and-drop action to an incorrect spreadsheet region, selecting the wrong range in the resulting state. Example: Failure to reason over future states. Task ID: 67890eb6-6ce5-4c00-9e3d-fb4972699b06 Task. I am an NLP researcher. Check out the best long paper awards of ACL from 2019 to 2022 and record the title , year , author list , and PDF link into table best_awards_acl.xlsx on the desktop. Separate authors only by commas, use official ACL Anthology URLs, not arXiv, and sort rows by year in descending order. (a) State 1. (b) State 2. Index 0 (should have chosen): agent.type(element_description="the search bar on the ACL Anthology website", text="ACL 2021", enter=True) Index 1 (chosen): agent.switch_applications( app_code="libreoffice-calc") Index 2: agent.hotkey(keys=["ctrl", "s"]) Judge tokens. GT-Rollout judge: Candidate 1 switches to LibreOffice Calc, showing the spreadsheet best_awards_acl.xlsx with data already entered for the 2022 award, which directly progresses the task of recording award information. Candidate 0 results in a failed search, and Candidate 2 triggers a save dialog unrelated to the task. Selected: 1. (c) State 2 future. Figure 33: The judge fails to reason over the future. The judge selects the candidate that returns to the partially completed spreadsheet because it observes existing 2022 data, instead of preferring the candidate that continues searching for missing ACL award entries. Example: Agent runs out of max steps. Task ID: 6f4073b8-d8ea-4ade-8a18-c5d1d5d5aa9a Task. I now want to count the meeting cities of the three machine learning conferences in the past ten years from 2013 to 2019 (including 2013 and 2019). I have listed the names and years of the conferences in Excel. Please fill in the vacant locations. Failure step. Step 50. Figure 34: An example where an agent runs out of steps. The agent is still working on the spreadsheet at step 50 but has not completed all missing conference locations before reaching the step limit. Appendix S Example of stochastic dynamics in OSWorld environment We provide examples of rollout mismatch issues in the OSWorld environment in Figures 35 – 38 . In these cases, the screenshot captured in the rollout VM differs from the screenshot captured in the real VM after executing the same action. (A) Screenshot captured in a rollout VM. (B) Screenshot captured in a real VM. Figure 35: Rollout vs. real VM (case 0). (A) Screenshot captured in a rollout VM. (B) Screenshot captured in a live VM. Figure 36: Rollout vs. live VM (case 1). (A) Screenshot captured in a rollout VM. (B) Screenshot captured in a live VM. Figure 37: Rollout vs. live VM (case 2). (A) Screenshot captured in a rollout VM. (B) Screenshot captured in a live VM. Figure 38: Rollout vs. live VM (case 3). Appendix T GT-Rollout Failure Analysis Prompt \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝You are an expert desktop UI-agent and GT-rollout failure analyst. \iow_now:Ne ˝Return JSON only with this exact top-level shape: \iow_now:Ne ˝{ \iow_now:Ne ˝ "primary_reason": { \iow_now:Ne ˝ "category": "grounding error" | "tutorial error" | "tutorial is not completed" | "observation hallucination in policy thought" | "agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps" | "web server error, agent cannot connect" | "the judge fails to reason over the future state" | "the judge fails to reason over the future state, fails to understand task success" | "agents fail to follow the tutorial correctly", \iow_now:Ne ˝ "error_step": integer or null, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "details": string \iow_now:Ne ˝ }, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "mentioned_reasons": [ \iow_now:Ne ˝ { \iow_now:Ne ˝ "category": "grounding error" | "tutorial error" | "tutorial is not completed" | "observation hallucination in policy thought" | "agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps" | "web server error, agent cannot connect" | "the judge fails to reason over the future state" | "the judge fails to reason over the future state, fails to understand task success" | "agents fail to follow the tutorial correctly", \iow_now:Ne ˝ "has_reason": true, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "error_step": integer or null, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "details": string \iow_now:Ne ˝ } \iow_now:Ne ˝ ], \iow_now:Ne ˝ "step_evidence": [ \iow_now:Ne ˝ { \iow_now:Ne ˝ "step": integer or null, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "screenshot_ids": [integer], \iow_now:Ne ˝ "action": string, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "grounded_action": string, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "details": string \iow_now:Ne ˝ } \iow_now:Ne ˝ ], \iow_now:Ne ˝ "reason_presence": { \iow_now:Ne ˝ "grounding error": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "tutorial error": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "tutorial is not completed": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "observation hallucination in policy thought": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "web server error, agent cannot connect": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "the judge fails to reason over the future state": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "the judge fails to reason over the future state, fails to understand task success": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "agents fail to follow the tutorial correctly": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ } \iow_now:Ne ˝} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Use only category strings exactly as listed. \iow_now:Ne ˝Category definitions: \iow_now:Ne ˝- grounding error: The high-level action or selected candidate is correct, but the grounded UI operation targets with (x,y) coordinate are wrong, maybe wrong coordinates, window, field, or application state. For example, the agent outputs "click the ’Submit’ button", but the grounded UI operation clicks on a wrong position that is not the ’Submit’ button. \iow_now:Ne ˝- tutorial error: tutorials are not correct and the agent doesn’t know how to recover from wrong steps in tutorials. \iow_now:Ne ˝- tutorial is not completed: the tutorial doesn’t provide enough fine-grained actions to complete the task, and the agent fails to propose these fine-grained actions correctly by itself. \iow_now:Ne ˝- observation hallucination in policy thought: policy hallucinates wrong observation in its thought process, which leads to wrong next action. For example, the policy hallucinates that it has already opened the target application and thus tries to interact with the application, which leads to failure in completing the task. \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps: The agent appears to be following a valid path and has not made a decisive wrong action, but the task remains incomplete because the run reaches the configured max step limit, including either 15-step or 50-step runs. This can be caused by any of the above reasons or by other unknown reasons; use it as primary only when exhausting the step budget is the latest decisive failure. \iow_now:Ne ˝- web server error, agent cannot connect: the web server hosting the task environment has issues, such as a website being down. \iow_now:Ne ˝- the judge fails to reason over the future state: Use when the GT-rollout judge/selector is the decisive failing component: it selects, approves, or keeps preferring a wrong candidate/action because it misreads the current screenshot, candidate rollout screenshots, or future/resulting state. If the policy proposed a correct tutorial-following action but the judge chose a different candidate by hallucinating that the wrong future state was successful, this category should be primary, not tutorial-following failure. In mentioned_reasons, this category is mutually exclusive with the more specific task-success category below. \iow_now:Ne ˝- the judge fails to reason over the future state, fails to understand task success: The policy or GT-rollout judge fails to understand whether the current/future state satisfies the task instruction, especially when it terminates with agent.done() despite visible evidence that the task is still incorrect. Use this more specific category instead of the broader judge future-state category when task-success or termination evidence is involved; if this category appears in mentioned_reasons, do not also include the broader judge future-state category. \iow_now:Ne ˝- agents fail to follow the tutorial correctly: Use when the policy/agent itself misunderstands, skips, contradicts, or wrongly executes a tutorial step, and that policy/agent behavior is the decisive cause of failure. Do not use this as primary when the policy/proposed actions include the correct tutorial-following action but the GT-rollout judge selects a different wrong candidate; in that case use the judge future-state reasoning category as primary. \iow_now:Ne ˝Do not output "other", "unknown", "unclear", or any category not listed above. If no category fits perfectly, choose the closest listed category and explain the mismatch in details. \iow_now:Ne ˝The primary_reason must be the latest decisive reason that directly explains the final failed outcome, usually associated with steps near the end of the trajectory. Earlier mistakes should be secondary mentioned_reasons unless there is no later decision that preserves or confirms the failure. \iow_now:Ne ˝Critical distinction between tutorial-following failure and judge future-state failure: \iow_now:Ne ˝- Use the tutorial-following category only when the policy/agent itself misunderstands, skips, contradicts, or wrongly executes a tutorial step, and that policy/agent action is the decisive cause. \iow_now:Ne ˝- Use the judge future-state reasoning category when the GT-rollout judge selects, approves, or keeps preferring a wrong candidate/action because it misreads the current screenshot, misreads candidate/future screenshots, or hallucinates that an incorrect future state satisfies the task. \iow_now:Ne ˝- If a correct tutorial-following candidate/action was available or proposed, but the judge chose a different candidate by claiming its resulting state was correct, the primary_reason must be the judge future-state reasoning category. The tutorial-following category may be mentioned only if the policy/agent also independently failed to follow the tutorial. \iow_now:Ne ˝If the final or near-final step marks the task done even though screenshots/evaluator evidence show the task is not successful, prefer the task-success/termination category as primary over earlier action or grounding errors. \iow_now:Ne ˝mentioned_reasons must include only secondary categories with evidence in the trajectory. Do not include the same category as primary_reason in mentioned_reasons. \iow_now:Ne ˝The two judge future-state categories are mutually exclusive in mentioned_reasons. If "the judge fails to reason over the future state, fails to understand task success" applies anywhere, do not include "the judge fails to reason over the future state" in mentioned_reasons; use only the more specific task-success category for judge evidence. \iow_now:Ne ˝reason_presence must contain every allowed category with true or false. \iow_now:Ne ˝Keep the JSON compact: primary_reason.details and each mentioned_reasons.details must be one short sentence. \iow_now:Ne ˝Return at most 6 mentioned_reasons entries, only for categories with concrete evidence. \iow_now:Ne ˝Return at most 6 step_evidence entries total, prioritizing the primary reason step and the latest decisive evidence near the end. \iow_now:Ne ˝step_evidence must cite screenshot IDs from the provided Image index. Do not invent screenshot IDs. Do not generate screenshots. The renderer will embed the referenced images. \iow_now:Ne ˝For each step_evidence item, include the trajectory step, the high-level action proposed by the policy, the grounded/executed action from traj.jsonl or pre_grounded fields, and one short sentence explaining why the screenshot/action matters. \iow_now:Ne ˝Use the evaluation JSON and result details as the source of truth for the final failed state. \iow_now:Ne ˝Use GT-rollout candidate images/actions to decide whether the failure came from policy proposal, grounding, rollout prediction, selection, tutorial conditioning, evaluator issues, or termination behavior. \iow_now:Ne ˝Do not invent evidence. If evidence is weak, say so in details. \iow_now:Ne ˝No markdown fences. No prose outside JSON. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Analyze this failed OSWorld GT-rollout task. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝You are given the full task/evaluation bundle, the full traj.jsonl text, and every raster image referenced by the trajectory. Images have been preprocessed with max_image_pixels={max_image_pixels}; they are not raw screenshots. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Task instruction: \iow_now:Ne ˝{task_instruction} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Image index: \iow_now:Ne ˝{image_index} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Classify the primary failure reason and every category that is mentioned by evidence in the trajectory. \iow_now:Ne ˝Also produce compact step_evidence entries for the screenshots/steps that justify the classification. Refer to screenshots by Image number only. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Task bundle and full trajectory: \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝{bundle_markdown} Figure 39: Gemini prompt used to classify failed GT-rollout trajectories and extract compact evidence for the failure analysis. Appendix U LLM Usage Statement The authors used LLM-based assistants for limited editorial and technical support, including grammar and clarity edits, LaTeX debugging, and draft phrasing for non-substantive text. We also use LLM-assisted programming like Claude Code and Codex to implement infrastructure code for ground-truth visual rollouts and other baselines. All LLM-assisted text and code changes were inspected and revised by the authors. The authors are responsible for the final manuscript, including all claims, analyses, tables, figures, citations, and conclusions.

sections.heading: O.4 Rollout prompt
sections.text: The TUTORIAL USAGE GUIDELINE block is included only when tutorial evidence exists; when no tutorial evidence is available, the runtime removes this block from the rollout prefix. Plain text is from the original R-WoM paper or implementation. In the unified diff below, red “-” lines are original text removed or replaced, green “+” lines are current runtime additions or replacements, and black lines are unchanged context; --- and +++ identify the compared versions. Only word-level semantic changes are colored; capitalization, Markdown markers, list markers, punctuation, and symbol-only differences are normalized and not treated as changes. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝— ORIGINAL R-WoM PROMPT \iow_now:Ne ˝+++ OUR CURRENT RUNTIME PROMPT \iow_now:Ne ˝You are a world-model assistant with extensive knowledge of desktop and web UIs. Given the task \iow_now:Ne ˝objective, the candidate action, and the observation before the candidate action, you must "simulate \iow_now:Ne ˝the future" and describe the plausible future states. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝(*@-Available actions \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝-# Action space definition@*) \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝(*&+# ACTION SPACE \iow_now:Ne ˝+Use only these exact methods/arguments; no right_click/double_click: \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.click(instruction, num_clicks=1, button_type=’left’, hold_keys=[]) # button_type=’right’|’middle’; double-click=num_clicks=2 \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.done(return_value=None) \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.drag_and_drop(starting_description, ending_description, hold_keys=[]) \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.fail() # proven impossible: CAPTCHA/login/missing required user account credentials/unavailable site/absent required setting or option \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.highlight_text_span(starting_phrase, ending_phrase) \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.hover(instruction) \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.hold_and_press(hold_keys, press_keys) \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.hotkey(keys) \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.open(app_or_filename) # closed app/file; filename, not path; switch if open. Only Google Chrome, LibreOffice Writer/Calc/Impress, Thunderbird, VSCode, VLC Media Player, GIMP; no other programs \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.scroll(instruction, clicks, shift=False) # +up/-down; shift=horizontal; 1˜3 lines; small=1-5, section=5-10, long=10-20; max=50 \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.set_cell_values(cell_values, app_name, sheet_name) # ALWAYS for sheet cells; formulas start "="; max 30 cells/call; app=title filename, sheet=tab \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.switch_applications(app_code) \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.type(element_description=None, text=”, overwrite=False, enter=False) # omit element_description only when keyboard focus/caret is known unchanged from history or immediately preceding focus action; pointer!=focus; click/app switch/dialog/restore uncertainty requires grounding; overwrite=True replaces, False appends intentionally; in a multi-line text/code editor overwrite=True erases the whole document, so select the part to replace (highlight_text_span) and type over it without element_description; overwrite=True for a single-line GUI input still showing old text (calculator/command line, rename field; not terminals); if it is already selected, omit element_description; console commands: no nested single quotes; Enter only submits (click live-filter results) \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.wait(time) # visible progress/load only&*) \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# TUTORIAL USAGE GUIDELINE \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝1. Use the tutorials to identify efficient workflow patterns that should be predicted as likely outcomes. \iow_now:Ne ˝2. Provide a reference to the tutorial if the current situation matches the standard operations in the tutorials. If the current situation does not align with tutorials, rely on internal world knowledge instead. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# Environment awareness checklist \iow_now:Ne ˝- Visible UI elements: text, icons, menus, modals, tooltips \iow_now:Ne ˝- Element states: enabled/disabled, focused/hovered, loading progress \iow_now:Ne ˝- Hidden or off-screen affordances revealed by scrolling or clicking \iow_now:Ne ˝- Cursor position, caret position, selection highlights \iow_now:Ne ˝- Global context: file system changes, network requests, OS dialogs \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# Output Format \iow_now:Ne ˝(*@-Produce an ordered chain from STATE 0 (current) up to STATE n (1 <= n <= {k}); you may stop early \iow_now:Ne ˝-if no further prediction is useful.@*) \iow_now:Ne ˝(*&+Produce an ordered chain from ACTION 0 up to STATE {k_steps}. \iow_now:Ne ˝+ \iow_now:Ne ˝+Strict rules: \iow_now:Ne ˝+- Do NOT describe the current state. The reader already has the current screenshot; restating it wastes tokens and risks contradicting the pixels. Never output a STATE 0 line. \iow_now:Ne ˝+- Start with ACTION 0: followed by the candidate action exactly as provided in the user message. \iow_now:Ne ˝+- The highest allowed STATE index is {k_steps}. Never output STATE {k_steps} + 1 or any larger index. \iow_now:Ne ˝+- Between every two consecutive states, you MUST output an ACTION line. Every STATE i (for 1 <= i < {k_steps}) MUST be followed by ACTION i: before STATE i+1. There is no STATE 0, so ACTION 0 is the first line of the response. \iow_now:Ne ˝+- Describe only what the action would CHANGE, relative to the current screenshot. Do not re-describe unchanged UI. \iow_now:Ne ˝+- Keyboard shortcuts: predict the effect of the shortcut’s real default binding in this application, not the effect the candidate intends. If you are not sure what the shortcut does here, write "effect uncertain" instead of assuming success. \iow_now:Ne ˝+- Repeated actions: if HISTORY shows the same method on the same target was already executed and the current screenshot does not show its expected effect, that action did not work here. Predict that it again causes no visible change, unless the screen now differs in a way that removes the reason it failed (e.g., a blocking dialog has closed or the needed focus or selection now exists). \iow_now:Ne ˝+- STOP IMMEDIATELY after STATE {k_steps}. Do NOT output ACTION {k_steps} or any text after the last STATE. The response must end with STATE {k_steps}: <description>. \iow_now:Ne ˝+- Do not add explanations, code fences, headings, or extra text before or after the rollout. \iow_now:Ne ˝+ \iow_now:Ne ˝+# EXAMPLE OUTPUT (FOR K_STEPS={k_steps}): \iow_now:Ne ˝+{rollout_example} \iow_now:Ne ˝+ \iow_now:Ne ˝+WRONG (do NOT do this): \iow_now:Ne ˝+STATE {k_steps}: <description> \iow_now:Ne ˝+ACTION {k_steps}: <any action here> <- FORBIDDEN, response must end at STATE {k_steps}&*) \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# CANDIDATE THOUGHT AND ACTION \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Thought: {thought} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Action: {action_code} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# YOUR TASK \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Simulate the plausible future states after executing the candidate action. Follow the rollout-length limit from the system prompt exactly. Do not output extra states or actions after the final STATE line. Use the output format specified above. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# CURRENT STEP \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝You are on step {current_step} of maximum {max_steps} steps. R-WoM rollout prompt Figure 23: Unified diff of the original R-WoM rollout prompt and our current runtime prompt. Rollout Example, K=1 \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝ROLLOUT_EXAMPLE_K1 = """ACTION 0: agent.typewrite(text="downloads") \iow_now:Ne ˝STATE 1: The search field contains "downloads", and matching download-related settings are visible.""" Rollout Example, K=2 \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝ROLLOUT_EXAMPLE_K2 = """ACTION 0: agent.typewrite(text="downloads") \iow_now:Ne ˝STATE 1: The search field contains "downloads", and matching download-related settings are visible. \iow_now:Ne ˝ACTION 1: agent.click(instruction="Click the Change button for download location") \iow_now:Ne ˝STATE 2: A file chooser dialog opens with folder choices and Cancel and Select buttons.""" Rollout Example, K=3 \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝ROLLOUT_EXAMPLE_K3 = """ACTION 0: agent.typewrite(text="downloads") \iow_now:Ne ˝STATE 1: The search field contains "downloads", and matching download-related settings are visible. \iow_now:Ne ˝ACTION 1: agent.click(instruction="Click the Change button for download location") \iow_now:Ne ˝STATE 2: A file chooser dialog opens with folder choices and Cancel and Select buttons. \iow_now:Ne ˝ACTION 2: agent.click(instruction="Select the Documents folder") \iow_now:Ne ˝STATE 3: The Documents folder is highlighted in the file chooser, ready to be selected as the new download location.""" We use different examples with different rollout lengths. O.5 R-WoM judge Plain text is from the original R-WoM paper or implementation. Appendix P WebDreamer reimplementation We run WebDreamer ( Gu et al., 2025 ) from its released code (commit e589411 ), pinned as a read-only submodule. Its multi-step imagination loop and pointwise scoring are unchanged: for each of the K = 3 K{=}3 policy candidates we draw 3 independent simulations of planning horizon H H ; each simulation predicts the state change of the candidate action and then, for up to H − 1 H{-}1 further imagined steps (stopping early if a proposed action is stop ), proposes the next action and predicts its state change. A value function scores each simulation with 10 samples (success = 1 =1 , on the right track = 0.5 =0.5 , otherwise 0 0 ); the candidate with the highest mean score is executed. We adapt the prompts to the desktop (web wording becomes desktop wording, the web operation list becomes our desktop operation list, and the current URL is dropped) and pass the current screenshot as the policy’s encoded image. Both components also receive the real executed-step history, so that WebDreamer sees the same history as the other baselines. When steps have already been executed, each world-model user message starts with the text-only step history used by the R-WoM rollout, under the header “Steps already executed before the screenshot below (real history, text only; not part of PREVIOUS ACTIONS)”; the released code gives the world model no history. Instead of the trajectory’s screenshots and an action list, the value function receives the same history as the policy+judge judge (older steps as text, recent steps with screenshots), followed by the current screenshot under the heading “Current state of the screen” and the simulated steps. The value prompt also gains one rule: a simulation whose first action is agent.fail() counts as a success only when the history and the screen prove the task impossible, mirroring the policy+judge judge’s rule for infeasible tasks. World-model and value calls use the judge model (Qwen3-VL-32B, as for the policy) instead of GPT-4o, with OpenAI’s default sampling (temperature 1.0, top- p p 1.0, no top- k k ). The world model generates at most 2048 new tokens, the released code’s cap for its Claude path (its GPT-4o path sets none). The value function generates at most 1024 new tokens instead of the released 256, because Qwen’s longer reasoning was otherwise cut off before the Status: line on about 10–16% of samples, which then scored 0. We simulate all K = 3 K{=}3 candidates and do not apply the optional LLM filter that prunes candidates before simulation. We first save a QEMU snapshot of the current VM state before evaluating any candidate action. This snapshot saves the exact state of the VM, including the screen, memory, and disk, allowing us to restore it to this state after each candidate action is executed. We then execute each candidate action one at a time on the same VM, wait for the interface to settle, and capture the resulting screenshot as that candidate’s ground-truth next state. After each candidate is executed, the VM is restored back to the saved snapshot, so the next candidate starts from the exact same screen state. This makes the comparison fair and deterministic on most of the tasks, with a few exceptions when the task involves internet access and the content on the screen may change (e.g., Google search results). Appendix R Ground-Truth Error Analysis We follow the same procedure described in Qian et al. (2026) to analyze errors in the ground-truth visual rollout. In total, we collect 2,116 failed trajectories from all runs with ground-truth rollouts. We first sample 30 tasks and manually go through trajectory data: screenshots, policy "thought" tokens, judge "thought" tokens, and proposed actions. We then identify and summarize the following core categories of errors that lead to agent failure: 1. The judge fails to understand task success : We find a notable portion of cases where the GT-rollout judge fails to understand task success, which is a more specific failure mode. GT-rollout judges fail to understand whether future states satisfy the task instruction. We show an example of this case in Figure 30 . 2. The judge fails to reason over future states : GT-rollout judges can fail to reason over future states to wrongly judge the progress of the task. We show an example of this case in Figure 33 and Figure 29 . 3. Wrong MLLM-generated tutorial : MLLM-generated tutorials are not correct and the agent doesn’t know how to recover from wrong steps in the tutorial. We show an example of this case in Figure 26 . 4. Incomplete tutorial : The tutorial does not provide fine-grained enough steps to complete the task, and the policy fails to propose the missing steps by itself. 5. Policy fails to follow the tutorial correctly : The policy itself misunderstands, skips, contradicts, or wrongly executes a tutorial step. We show an example of this case in Figure 27 . 6. Grounding error : The grounding model maps the same action description to different regions in the visual input, which leads to wrong grounding and thus failure. We show an example of this case in Figure 32 . 7. Observation hallucination in policy : The policy misreads the current state and thus reasons toward a wrong action. We show an example of this case in Figure 31 . 8. Web server error : The web server hosting the task environment has issues, such as the target website being down. This is an external factor that can lead to failure, and it is not caused by the agent’s decision-making process. 9. Agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps : The agent is following a correct path but reaches the 15-step or 50-step limit before completing the task. We show an example of this case in Figure 34 . We then use an MLLM (Gemini 3.8 Flash Google DeepMind (2026) ) to annotate the rest of the failed tasks. Given the trajectory data of a task, we prompt it (see Figure 39 ) to classify failure reasons into the categories above. Because a failed task might have many root causes, we follow Qian et al. (2026) and ask the MLLM to classify potential errors into: (1) a primary reason and (2) mentioned (secondary) reasons. Note that mentioned reasons cannot be duplicated with the primary reason. To assess the reliability of this MLLM-as-a-judge framework, we run the MLLM on the manually annotated examples above and find that the agreement rate for the primary reason reaches 90%. Furthermore, we randomly sample 20 examples from MLLM results to examine manually. All of the results are reasonable and aligned with our predefined categories of error. Based on the MLLM’s results, we plot the number of primary and mentioned reasons in Figure 3 . If no category fits perfectly, choose the closest listed category and explain the mismatch in details. \iow_now:Ne ˝The primary_reason must be the latest decisive reason that directly explains the final failed outcome, usually associated with steps near the end of the trajectory. Earlier mistakes should be secondary mentioned_reasons unless there is no later decision that preserves or confirms the failure. \iow_now:Ne ˝Critical distinction between tutorial-following failure and judge future-state failure: \iow_now:Ne ˝- Use the tutorial-following category only when the policy/agent itself misunderstands, skips, contradicts, or wrongly executes a tutorial step, and that policy/agent action is the decisive cause. \iow_now:Ne ˝- Use the judge future-state reasoning category when the GT-rollout judge selects, approves, or keeps preferring a wrong candidate/action because it misreads the current screenshot, misreads candidate/future screenshots, or hallucinates that an incorrect future state satisfies the task. \iow_now:Ne ˝- If a correct tutorial-following candidate/action was available or proposed, but the judge chose a different candidate by claiming its resulting state was correct, the primary_reason must be the judge future-state reasoning category. The tutorial-following category may be mentioned only if the policy/agent also independently failed to follow the tutorial. \iow_now:Ne ˝If the final or near-final step marks the task done even though screenshots/evaluator evidence show the task is not successful, prefer the task-success/termination category as primary over earlier action or grounding errors. \iow_now:Ne ˝mentioned_reasons must include only secondary categories with evidence in the trajectory. Do not include the same category as primary_reason in mentioned_reasons. \iow_now:Ne ˝The two judge future-state categories are mutually exclusive in mentioned_reasons. If "the judge fails to reason over the future state, fails to understand task success" applies anywhere, do not include "the judge fails to reason over the future state" in mentioned_reasons; use only the more specific task-success category for judge evidence. \iow_now:Ne ˝reason_presence must contain every allowed category with true or false. \iow_now:Ne ˝Keep the JSON compact: primary_reason.details and each mentioned_reasons.details must be one short sentence. \iow_now:Ne ˝Return at most 6 mentioned_reasons entries, only for categories with concrete evidence. \iow_now:Ne ˝Return at most 6 step_evidence entries total, prioritizing the primary reason step and the latest decisive evidence near the end. \iow_now:Ne ˝step_evidence must cite screenshot IDs from the provided Image index. Do not invent screenshot IDs. Do not generate screenshots. The renderer will embed the referenced images. \iow_now:Ne ˝For each step_evidence item, include the trajectory step, the high-level action proposed by the policy, the grounded/executed action from traj.jsonl or pre_grounded fields, and one short sentence explaining why the screenshot/action matters. \iow_now:Ne ˝Use the evaluation JSON and result details as the source of truth for the final failed state. \iow_now:Ne ˝Use GT-rollout candidate images/actions to decide whether the failure came from policy proposal, grounding, rollout prediction, selection, tutorial conditioning, evaluator issues, or termination behavior. \iow_now:Ne ˝Do not invent evidence. If evidence is weak, say so in details. \iow_now:Ne ˝No markdown fences. No prose outside JSON. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Analyze this failed OSWorld GT-rollout task. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝You are given the full task/evaluation bundle, the full traj.jsonl text, and every raster image referenced by the trajectory. Images have been preprocessed with max_image_pixels={max_image_pixels}; they are not raw screenshots. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Task instruction: \iow_now:Ne ˝{task_instruction} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Image index: \iow_now:Ne ˝{image_index} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Classify the primary failure reason and every category that is mentioned by evidence in the trajectory. \iow_now:Ne ˝Also produce compact step_evidence entries for the screenshots/steps that justify the classification. Refer to screenshots by Image number only. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Task bundle and full trajectory: \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝{bundle_markdown} Figure 39: Gemini prompt used to classify failed GT-rollout trajectories and extract compact evidence for the failure analysis. Appendix U LLM Usage Statement The authors used LLM-based assistants for limited editorial and technical support, including grammar and clarity edits, LaTeX debugging, and draft phrasing for non-substantive text. We also use LLM-assisted programming like Claude Code and Codex to implement infrastructure code for ground-truth visual rollouts and other baselines. All LLM-assisted text and code changes were inspected and revised by the authors. The authors are responsible for the final manuscript, including all claims, analyses, tables, figures, citations, and conclusions.

Only word-level semantic changes are colored; capitalization, Markdown markers, list markers, punctuation, and symbol-only differences are normalized and not treated as changes. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝— ORIGINAL R-WoM PROMPT \iow_now:Ne ˝+++ OUR CURRENT RUNTIME PROMPT \iow_now:Ne ˝You are an agent that evaluates actions by considering the observation before the action candidates and the potential outcomes of these actions. \iow_now:Ne ˝(*&+Ubuntu desktop computer-use agent (1920x1080; internet available). \iow_now:Ne ˝+Evaluate the candidate actions and rank them by how well each advances the overall goal.&*) \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝(*&+# ACTION SPACE \iow_now:Ne ˝+Use only these exact methods/arguments; no right_click/double_click: \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.click(instruction, num_clicks=1, button_type=’left’, hold_keys=[]) # button_type=’right’|’middle’; double-click=num_clicks=2 \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.done(return_value=None) \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.drag_and_drop(starting_description, ending_description, hold_keys=[]) \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.fail() # proven impossible: CAPTCHA/login/missing required user account credentials/unavailable site/absent required setting or option \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.highlight_text_span(starting_phrase, ending_phrase) \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.hover(instruction) \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.hold_and_press(hold_keys, press_keys) \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.hotkey(keys) \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.open(app_or_filename) # closed app/file; filename, not path; switch if open. Only Google Chrome, LibreOffice Writer/Calc/Impress, Thunderbird, VSCode, VLC Media Player, GIMP; no other programs \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.scroll(instruction, clicks, shift=False) # +up/-down; shift=horizontal; 1˜3 lines; small=1-5, section=5-10, long=10-20; max=50 \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.set_cell_values(cell_values, app_name, sheet_name) # ALWAYS for sheet cells; formulas start "="; max 30 cells/call; app=title filename, sheet=tab \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.switch_applications(app_code) \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.type(element_description=None, text=”, overwrite=False, enter=False) # omit element_description only when keyboard focus/caret is known unchanged from history or immediately preceding focus action; pointer!=focus; click/app switch/dialog/restore uncertainty requires grounding; overwrite=True replaces, False appends intentionally; in a multi-line text/code editor overwrite=True erases the whole document, so select the part to replace (highlight_text_span) and type over it without element_description; overwrite=True for a single-line GUI input still showing old text (calculator/command line, rename field; not terminals); if it is already selected, omit element_description; console commands: no nested single quotes; Enter only submits (click live-filter results) \iow_now:Ne ˝+- agent.wait(time) # visible progress/load only&*) \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝(*&+# EVALUATION CRITERIA: \iow_now:Ne ˝+Screenshots are ground truth; tutorials are guidance unless they start with ’Infeasible’. \iow_now:Ne ˝+1. Feasibility - Target must be visible now; after-screenshots/rollouts must prove the action worked. \iow_now:Ne ˝+2. Exactness - Advance the task without extra steps. \iow_now:Ne ˝+3. Effectiveness - Make visible progress toward the final state. \iow_now:Ne ˝+4. Completion - Use agent.done() only when already complete. \iow_now:Ne ˝+5. Tutorial alignment - Prefer feasible tutorial actions, but trust pixels when they differ. \iow_now:Ne ˝+6. No regression - Reject broken state, navigation away, or lost progress. \iow_now:Ne ˝+7. Terminal evidence - Consider agent.done()/agent.fail() only with hard screenshot/history proof. Prefer any visible action needed to complete, save, apply, close a required dialog, or verify the final artifact.&*) \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝(*&+# REQUIRED DECISION PROCESS \iow_now:Ne ˝+Before deciding: \iow_now:Ne ˝+1. Derive exact task-specific success conditions from the task instruction. \iow_now:Ne ˝+2. Apply all applicable named evaluation criteria to every candidate. \iow_now:Ne ˝+3. Judge progress toward the overall goal, not mere action execution. \iow_now:Ne ˝+4. Compare observed or expected resulting states and cumulative progress across candidates. \iow_now:Ne ˝+5. Decide only after that comparison. \iow_now:Ne ˝+In ‘thought‘, connect screenshot/history evidence to success conditions and criteria; do not merely narrate screenshots.&*) \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# Tutorial Grounding Guidance (*&+(IF TUTORIAL IS PROVIDED):&*) \iow_now:Ne ˝(*&+Prefer feasible tutorial operations that reach task milestones. &*)Prioritize action sequences that follow the standard operations in the tutorials and have captured the milestones and conditions to make more meaningful progress to achieve the task objective. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝(*&+# RULES: \iow_now:Ne ˝+(1) **OVERRIDE - Infeasible tutorial**: If a tutorial is provided and starts with ’Infeasible’, agent.fail() is the only correct action. \iow_now:Ne ˝+(2) Prefer terminal over GUI, then hotkeys over multiple clicks. \iow_now:Ne ˝+(3) ANTI-LOOP: If current and latest HISTORY screenshots are substantially unchanged, reject any candidate matching an action’s method+target from the last 3 steps. If all feasible candidates repeat failures, prefer a different agent.* method family and explain the rejection. \iow_now:Ne ˝+(4) Do not treat agent.done(return_value=…) as an infeasibility report; prefer agent.fail() for proven impossibility. \iow_now:Ne ˝+(5) On the LAST step, only agent.done() or agent.fail() can succeed. \iow_now:Ne ˝+(6) Google Chrome is the ONLY available browser. \iow_now:Ne ˝+(7) TEXT-SELECTION METHOD PREFERENCE: For the same text range, prefer agent.highlight_text_span(…) over agent.drag_and_drop(…) unless anchors are not visible or the target is non-text. Do not reject highlight_text_span as unsupported for multi-line selection. \iow_now:Ne ˝+(8) FOCUSED TEXT ENTRY: Omit element_description only when current keyboard focus/caret is known and unchanged. Then agent.type(text=…, overwrite=…, enter=…) intentionally skips grounding and clicking. History or the current screenshot must establish the intended focus; any intervening click, app switch, dialog transition, or restore uncertainty changes the rule. Do not reject omitted element_description solely when focus evidence is strong. If focus is uncertain, the target is another field, or only the mouse pointer is over the field, require agent.type(element_description=…, …) so grounding can locate it.&*) \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝(*&+# EVIDENCE-FIRST VERIFICATION: \iow_now:Ne ˝+Candidate prose, rationale, tutorials, and simulated/text-only trajectories are hypotheses, not execution evidence. Simulated/text-only trajectories may be FEASIBLE, REJECTED, or UNKNOWN, never VERIFIED. \iow_now:Ne ˝+ \iow_now:Ne ˝+- Check exact requested conditions: values, text, counts, range endpoints, selection boundaries, dates, names, file paths, source/provenance, and persistence; generic change is insufficient. \iow_now:Ne ˝+- Compare the latest HISTORY action with the current screenshot first. Missing expected effect is failure. \iow_now:Ne ˝+- For each unexecuted candidate, require a visible target and preconditions; mark FEASIBLE; never claim execution or mark VERIFIED. \iow_now:Ne ˝+- For rollouts, inspect screenshots state by state only for actual executed actions. Mark VERIFIED only when an actual state visibly proves the effect; cite it (e.g. ‘Candidate 1 State 2‘). \iow_now:Ne ˝+- Missing, ambiguous, or unreadable evidence is UNKNOWN, never success. \iow_now:Ne ˝+- Visible proof: selection shows highlight/handles/caret/status; saving shows a completed dialog plus visible target/location or explicit saved/applied history; formatting shows values; persistence shows Save/Apply/OK or reopen/check. \iow_now:Ne ˝+ \iow_now:Ne ˝+- DONE: If any candidate is ‘agent.done(…)‘, ‘thought‘ MUST begin ‘DONE_CHECK: <condition> = MET | NOT-MET; …‘, cover every requested final condition, then give ‘CANDIDATE_CHECKS‘. MET means the requested end state holds (a removal/hide goal is MET when the item is gone) and requires direct current-screen proof or explicit saved/applied confirmation; dialogs, highlights, menus, and partial edits are not completion. Select done only when every condition is MET. Missing/incomplete DONE_CHECK, UNKNOWN, or NOT-MET rejects done; choose progress addressing the missing condition. \iow_now:Ne ˝+ \iow_now:Ne ˝+Selection rules: \iow_now:Ne ˝+- Prefer verification for required UNKNOWN evidence; prefer recovery after two failures in the current GUI branch. \iow_now:Ne ˝+- Do not reject all candidates when one can safely reveal missing evidence or recover. If none advances the task, choose the least-irreversible visible verification/recovery; never unsupported done/fail.&*) \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝(*&+# THOUGHT FORMAT \iow_now:Ne ˝+In ‘thought‘, output these fields in order: \iow_now:Ne ˝+TASK_CHECK: <condition> = VERIFIED | FAILED | UNKNOWN (<evidence from the CURRENT SCREENSHOT>); … \iow_now:Ne ˝+LAST_EFFECT: SEEN | NOT-SEEN | UNKNOWN (<evidence from the CURRENT SCREENSHOT>) \iow_now:Ne ˝+CANDIDATE_CHECKS: \iow_now:Ne ˝+0 = FEASIBLE (Feasibility: target visible; Effectiveness: expected effect advances a condition) \iow_now:Ne ˝+1 = REJECTED (Feasibility: target/prerequisite missing; Effectiveness: no task progress) \iow_now:Ne ˝+2 = … \iow_now:Ne ˝+ \iow_now:Ne ˝+LAST_EFFECT reports whether the latest executed action visibly changed the screen. It is about the action already taken, never about a simulation: a rollout can never make LAST_EFFECT SEEN. \iow_now:Ne ˝+If LAST_EFFECT is NOT-SEEN, that action had no effect: REJECT every candidate repeating its method+target however confident its simulation, and prefer a candidate that establishes the missing prerequisite (focus, selection, caret, or an open dialog) or switches to a different agent.* method family. \iow_now:Ne ˝+Judge feasibility against the CURRENT SCREENSHOT; a simulation may only argue about an action’s expected effect, never establish what is on screen now. \iow_now:Ne ˝+ \iow_now:Ne ˝+If any candidate is ‘agent.done(…)‘, ‘thought‘ MUST begin with the ‘DONE_CHECK:‘ line required by the evidence rules above, followed immediately by CANDIDATE_CHECKS, then TASK_CHECK and LAST_EFFECT.&*) \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# Output Format \iow_now:Ne ˝Output your response in the following JSON format: \iow_now:Ne ˝{ \iow_now:Ne ˝(*&+ "thought": "your rationale for the ranking result",&*) \iow_now:Ne ˝ "ranking": [x, x, x] # "indexes of the action candidates, most \iow_now:Ne ˝ promising first" \iow_now:Ne ˝(*@- "thought": "your rationale for the ranking result"@*) \iow_now:Ne ˝} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# TASK INSTRUCTION \iow_now:Ne ˝{instruction} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# TUTORIAL EVIDENCE (IF ANY) \iow_now:Ne ˝{evidence_text} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# STEP HISTORY \iow_now:Ne ˝{step_history} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝(*&+# CURRENT SCREENSHOT \iow_now:Ne ˝+{current_screenshot}&*) \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# SIMULATED ROLLOUT TRAJECTORIES (ONE PER CANDIDATE ACTION) \iow_now:Ne ˝Each block below shows one candidate’s policy thought and its world-model simulation. Evaluate each candidate’s feasibility, correctness, and effectiveness, then rank them. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝{rollouts_block} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# CURRENT STEP \iow_now:Ne ˝You are on step {current_step} of maximum {max_steps} steps. R-WoM judge prompt Figure 24: Unified diff of the original R-WoM judge prompt and our current runtime prompt. Appendix P WebDreamer reimplementation We run WebDreamer ( Gu et al., 2025 ) from its released code (commit e589411 ), pinned as a read-only submodule. Its multi-step imagination loop and pointwise scoring are unchanged: for each of the K = 3 K{=}3 policy candidates we draw 3 independent simulations of planning horizon H H ; each simulation predicts the state change of the candidate action and then, for up to H − 1 H{-}1 further imagined steps (stopping early if a proposed action is stop ), proposes the next action and predicts its state change. A value function scores each simulation with 10 samples (success = 1 =1 , on the right track = 0.5 =0.5 , otherwise 0 0 ); the candidate with the highest mean score is executed. We adapt the prompts to the desktop (web wording becomes desktop wording, the web operation list becomes our desktop operation list, and the current URL is dropped) and pass the current screenshot as the policy’s encoded image. Both components also receive the real executed-step history, so that WebDreamer sees the same history as the other baselines. When steps have already been executed, each world-model user message starts with the text-only step history used by the R-WoM rollout, under the header “Steps already executed before the screenshot below (real history, text only; not part of PREVIOUS ACTIONS)”; the released code gives the world model no history. Instead of the trajectory’s screenshots and an action list, the value function receives the same history as the policy+judge judge (older steps as text, recent steps with screenshots), followed by the current screenshot under the heading “Current state of the screen” and the simulated steps. The value prompt also gains one rule: a simulation whose first action is agent.fail() counts as a success only when the history and the screen prove the task impossible, mirroring the policy+judge judge’s rule for infeasible tasks. World-model and value calls use the judge model (Qwen3-VL-32B, as for the policy) instead of GPT-4o, with OpenAI’s default sampling (temperature 1.0, top- p p 1.0, no top- k k ). The world model generates at most 2048 new tokens, the released code’s cap for its Claude path (its GPT-4o path sets none). The value function generates at most 1024 new tokens instead of the released 256, because Qwen’s longer reasoning was otherwise cut off before the Status: line on about 10–16% of samples, which then scored 0. We simulate all K = 3 K{=}3 candidates and do not apply the optional LLM filter that prunes candidates before simulation. ˝(*@-You are an expert in evaluating the performance of a web navigation agent.@*) \iow_now:Ne ˝(*@-The agent is designed to help a human user navigate a website to complete a task.@*) \iow_now:Ne user intent**.@*) \iow_now:Ne ˝(*&+You are an expert in evaluating the performance of a computer-use agent.&*) \iow_now:Ne ˝(*&+The agent is designed to help a human user operate a computer desktop to complete a task.&*) \iow_now:Ne ˝(*&+Given the user’s intent, the agent’s action history, the current state of the screen, your goal is to decide **whether the simulated steps by the agent indicate a We first save a QEMU snapshot of the current VM state before evaluating any candidate action. This snapshot saves the exact state of the VM, including the screen, memory, and disk, allowing us to restore it to this state after each candidate action is executed. We then execute each candidate action one at a time on the same VM, wait for the interface to settle, and capture the resulting screenshot as that candidate’s ground-truth next state. After each candidate is executed, the VM is restored back to the saved snapshot, so the next candidate starts from the exact same screen state. This makes the comparison fair and deterministic on most of the tasks, with a few exceptions when the task involves internet access and the content on the screen may change (e.g., Google search results). See more details in Appendix S . Appendix R Ground-Truth Error Analysis We follow the same procedure described in Qian et al. (2026) to analyze errors in the ground-truth visual rollout. In total, we collect 2,116 failed trajectories from all runs with ground-truth rollouts. We first sample 30 tasks and manually go through trajectory data: screenshots, policy "thought" tokens, judge "thought" tokens, and proposed actions. We then identify and summarize the following core categories of errors that lead to agent failure: 1. The judge fails to understand task success : We find a notable portion of cases where the GT-rollout judge fails to understand task success, which is a more specific failure mode. GT-rollout judges fail to understand whether future states satisfy the task instruction. We show an example of this case in Figure 30 . 2. The judge fails to reason over future states : GT-rollout judges can fail to reason over future states to wrongly judge the progress of the task. We show an example of this case in Figure 33 and Figure 29 . 3. Wrong MLLM-generated tutorial : MLLM-generated tutorials are not correct and the agent doesn’t know how to recover from wrong steps in the tutorial. We show an example of this case in Figure 26 . 4. Incomplete tutorial : The tutorial does not provide fine-grained enough steps to complete the task, and the policy fails to propose the missing steps by itself. 5. Policy fails to follow the tutorial correctly : The policy itself misunderstands, skips, contradicts, or wrongly executes a tutorial step. We show an example of this case in Figure 27 . 6. Grounding error : The grounding model maps the same action description to different regions in the visual input, which leads to wrong grounding and thus failure. We show an example of this case in Figure 32 . 7. Observation hallucination in policy : The policy misreads the current state and thus reasons toward a wrong action. We show an example of this case in Figure 31 . 8. Web server error : The web server hosting the task environment has issues, such as the target website being down. This is an external factor that can lead to failure, and it is not caused by the agent’s decision-making process. 9. Agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps : The agent is following a correct path but reaches the 15-step or 50-step limit before completing the task. We show an example of this case in Figure 34 . We then use an MLLM (Gemini 3.8 Flash Google DeepMind (2026) ) to annotate the rest of the failed tasks. Given the trajectory data of a task, we prompt it (see Figure 39 ) to classify failure reasons into the categories above. Because a failed task might have many root causes, we follow Qian et al. (2026) and ask the MLLM to classify potential errors into: (1) a primary reason and (2) mentioned (secondary) reasons. Note that mentioned reasons cannot be duplicated with the primary reason. To assess the reliability of this MLLM-as-a-judge framework, we run the MLLM on the manually annotated examples above and find that the agreement rate for the primary reason reaches 90%. Furthermore, we randomly sample 20 examples from MLLM results to examine manually. All of the results are reasonable and aligned with our predefined categories of error. Based on the MLLM’s results, we plot the number of primary and mentioned reasons in Figure 3 . sections.heading: Appendix P WebDreamer reimplementation
sections.text: We run WebDreamer ( Gu et al., 2025 ) from its released code (commit e589411 ), pinned as a read-only submodule. Its multi-step imagination loop and pointwise scoring are unchanged: for each of the K = 3 K{=}3 policy candidates we draw 3 independent simulations of planning horizon H H ; each simulation predicts the state change of the candidate action and then, for up to H − 1 H{-}1 further imagined steps (stopping early if a proposed action is stop ), proposes the next action and predicts its state change. A value function scores each simulation with 10 samples (success = 1 =1 , on the right track = 0.5 =0.5 , otherwise 0 0 ); the candidate with the highest mean score is executed. We adapt the prompts to the desktop (web wording becomes desktop wording, the web operation list becomes our desktop operation list, and the current URL is dropped) and pass the current screenshot as the policy’s encoded image. Both components also receive the real executed-step history, so that WebDreamer sees the same history as the other baselines. When steps have already been executed, each world-model user message starts with the text-only step history used by the R-WoM rollout, under the header “Steps already executed before the screenshot below (real history, text only; not part of PREVIOUS ACTIONS)”; the released code gives the world model no history. Instead of the trajectory’s screenshots and an action list, the value function receives the same history as the policy+judge judge (older steps as text, recent steps with screenshots), followed by the current screenshot under the heading “Current state of the screen” and the simulated steps. The value prompt also gains one rule: a simulation whose first action is agent.fail() counts as a success only when the history and the screen prove the task impossible, mirroring the policy+judge judge’s rule for infeasible tasks. World-model and value calls use the judge model (Qwen3-VL-32B, as for the policy) instead of GPT-4o, with OpenAI’s default sampling (temperature 1.0, top- p p 1.0, no top- k k ). The world model generates at most 2048 new tokens, the released code’s cap for its Claude path (its GPT-4o path sets none). The value function generates at most 1024 new tokens instead of the released 256, because Qwen’s longer reasoning was otherwise cut off before the Status: line on about 10–16% of samples, which then scored 0. We simulate all K = 3 K{=}3 candidates and do not apply the optional LLM filter that prunes candidates before simulation. In the unified diffs below, red “-” lines are original WebDreamer text removed or replaced, green “+” lines are our replacements, and black lines are unchanged.

We first save a QEMU snapshot of the current VM state before evaluating any candidate action. This snapshot saves the exact state of the VM, including the screen, memory, and disk, allowing us to restore it to this state after each candidate action is executed. We then execute each candidate action one at a time on the same VM, wait for the interface to settle, and capture the resulting screenshot as that candidate’s ground-truth next state. After each candidate is executed, the VM is restored back to the saved snapshot, so the next candidate starts from the exact same screen state. If focus is uncertain, the target is another field, or only the mouse pointer is over the field, require agent.type(element_description=…, …) so grounding can locate it. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# EVIDENCE-FIRST VERIFICATION: \iow_now:Ne ˝Candidate prose, rationale, tutorials, and simulated/text-only trajectories are hypotheses, not execution evidence. Simulated/text-only trajectories may be FEASIBLE, REJECTED, or UNKNOWN, never VERIFIED. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝- Check exact requested conditions: values, text, counts, range endpoints, selection boundaries, dates, names, file paths, source/provenance, and persistence; generic change is insufficient. \iow_now:Ne ˝- Compare the latest HISTORY action with the current screenshot first. Appendix R Ground-Truth Error Analysis We follow the same procedure described in Qian et al. (2026) to analyze errors in the ground-truth visual rollout. In total, we collect 2,116 failed trajectories from all runs with ground-truth rollouts. We first sample 30 tasks and manually go through trajectory data: screenshots, policy "thought" tokens, judge "thought" tokens, and proposed actions. We then identify and summarize the following core categories of errors that lead to agent failure: 1. The judge fails to understand task success : We find a notable portion of cases where the GT-rollout judge fails to understand task success, which is a more specific failure mode. GT-rollout judges fail to understand whether future states satisfy the task instruction. We show an example of this case in Figure 30 . 2. The judge fails to reason over future states : GT-rollout judges can fail to reason over future states to wrongly judge the progress of the task. We show an example of this case in Figure 33 and Figure 29 . 3. Wrong MLLM-generated tutorial : MLLM-generated tutorials are not correct and the agent doesn’t know how to recover from wrong steps in the tutorial. We show an example of this case in Figure 26 . 4. Incomplete tutorial : The tutorial does not provide fine-grained enough steps to complete the task, and the policy fails to propose the missing steps by itself. 5. Policy fails to follow the tutorial correctly : The policy itself misunderstands, skips, contradicts, or wrongly executes a tutorial step. We show an example of this case in Figure 27 . 6. Grounding error : The grounding model maps the same action description to different regions in the visual input, which leads to wrong grounding and thus failure. We show an example of this case in Figure 32 . 7. Observation hallucination in policy : The policy misreads the current state and thus reasons toward a wrong action. We show an example of this case in Figure 31 . 8. Web server error : The web server hosting the task environment has issues, such as the target website being down. This is an external factor that can lead to failure, and it is not caused by the agent’s decision-making process. 9. Agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps : The agent is following a correct path but reaches the 15-step or 50-step limit before completing the task. We show an example of this case in Figure 34 . We then use an MLLM (Gemini 3.8 Flash Google DeepMind (2026) ) to annotate the rest of the failed tasks. Given the trajectory data of a task, we prompt it (see Figure 39 ) to classify failure reasons into the categories above. Because a failed task might have many root causes, we follow Qian et al. (2026) and ask the MLLM to classify potential errors into: (1) a primary reason and (2) mentioned (secondary) reasons. Note that mentioned reasons cannot be duplicated with the primary reason. To assess the reliability of this MLLM-as-a-judge framework, we run the MLLM on the manually annotated examples above and find that the agreement rate for the primary reason reaches 90%. Furthermore, we randomly sample 20 examples from MLLM results to examine manually. All of the results are reasonable and aligned with our predefined categories of error. Based on the MLLM’s results, we plot the number of primary and mentioned reasons in Figure 3 . category strings exactly as listed. \iow_now:Ne ˝Category definitions: \iow_now:Ne ˝- grounding error: The high-level action or selected candidate is correct, but the grounded UI operation targets with (x,y) coordinate are wrong, maybe wrong coordinates, window, field, or application state. Do not include the same category as primary_reason in mentioned_reasons. \iow_now:Ne ˝The two judge future-state categories are mutually exclusive in mentioned_reasons. If "the judge fails to reason over the future state, fails to understand task success" applies anywhere, do not include "the judge fails to reason over the future state" in mentioned_reasons; use only the more specific task-success category for judge evidence. \iow_now:Ne ˝reason_presence must contain every allowed category with true or false. \iow_now:Ne ˝Keep the JSON compact: primary_reason.details and each mentioned_reasons.details must be one short sentence. \iow_now:Ne ˝Return at most 6 mentioned_reasons entries, only for categories with concrete evidence. \iow_now:Ne ˝Return at most 6 step_evidence entries total, prioritizing the primary reason step and the latest decisive evidence near the end. \iow_now:Ne ˝step_evidence must cite screenshot IDs from the provided Image index. Do not invent screenshot IDs. Do not generate screenshots. The renderer will embed the referenced images. \iow_now:Ne ˝For each step_evidence item, include the trajectory step, the high-level action proposed by the policy, the grounded/executed action from traj.jsonl or pre_grounded fields, and one short sentence explaining why the screenshot/action matters. \iow_now:Ne ˝Use the evaluation JSON and result details as the source of truth for the final failed state. \iow_now:Ne ˝Use GT-rollout candidate images/actions to decide whether the failure came from policy proposal, grounding, rollout prediction, selection, tutorial conditioning, evaluator issues, or termination behavior. \iow_now:Ne ˝Do not invent evidence. If evidence is weak, say so in details. \iow_now:Ne ˝No markdown fences. Appendix U LLM Usage Statement The authors used LLM-based assistants for limited editorial and technical support, including grammar and clarity edits, LaTeX debugging, and draft phrasing for non-substantive text. All LLM-assisted text and code changes were inspected and revised by the authors.
