understand task success" | "agents fail to follow the tutorial correctly", \iow_now:Ne ˝ "has_reason": true, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "error_step": integer or null, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "details": string \iow_now:Ne ˝ } \iow_now:Ne ˝ ], \iow_now:Ne ˝ "step_evidence": [ \iow_now:Ne ˝ { \iow_now:Ne ˝ "step": integer or null, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "screenshot_ids": [integer], \iow_now:Ne ˝ "action": string, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "grounded_action": string, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "details": string \iow_now:Ne ˝ } \iow_now:Ne ˝ ], \iow_now:Ne ˝ "reason_presence": { \iow_now:Ne ˝ "grounding error": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "tutorial error": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "tutorial is not completed": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "observation hallucination in policy thought": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "web server error, agent cannot connect": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "the judge fails to reason over the future state": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "the judge fails to reason over the future state, fails to understand task success": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ "agents fail to follow the tutorial correctly": boolean, \iow_now:Ne ˝ } \iow_now:Ne ˝} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Use only category strings exactly as listed. \iow_now:Ne ˝Category definitions: \iow_now:Ne ˝- grounding error: The high-level action or selected candidate is correct, but the grounded UI operation targets with (x,y) coordinate are wrong, maybe wrong coordinates, window, field, or application state. For example, the agent outputs "click the ’Submit’ button", but the grounded UI operation clicks on a wrong position that is not the ’Submit’ button. \iow_now:Ne ˝- tutorial error: tutorials are not correct and the agent doesn’t know how to recover from wrong steps in tutorials. \iow_now:Ne ˝- tutorial is not completed: the tutorial doesn’t provide enough fine-grained actions to complete the task, and the agent fails to propose these fine-grained actions correctly by itself. \iow_now:Ne ˝- observation hallucination in policy thought: policy hallucinates wrong observation in its thought process, which leads to wrong next action. For example, the policy hallucinates that it has already opened the target application and thus tries to interact with the application, which leads to failure in completing the task. \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps: The agent appears to be following a valid path and has not made a decisive wrong action, but the task remains incomplete because the run reaches the configured max step limit, including either 15-step or 50-step runs. This can be caused by any of the above reasons or by other unknown reasons; use it as primary only when exhausting the step budget is the latest decisive failure. \iow_now:Ne ˝- web server error, agent cannot connect: the web server hosting the task environment has issues, such as a website being down. \iow_now:Ne ˝- the judge fails to reason over the future state: Use when the GT-rollout judge/selector is the decisive failing component: it selects, approves, or keeps preferring a wrong candidate/action because it misreads the current screenshot, candidate rollout screenshots, or future/resulting state. If the policy proposed a correct tutorial-following action but the judge chose a different candidate by hallucinating that the wrong future state was successful, this category should be primary, not tutorial-following failure. In mentioned_reasons, this category is mutually exclusive with the more specific task-success category below. \iow_now:Ne ˝- the judge fails to reason over the future state, fails to understand task success: The policy or GT-rollout judge fails to understand whether the current/future state satisfies the task instruction, especially when it terminates with agent.done() despite visible evidence that the task is still incorrect. Use this more specific category instead of the broader judge future-state category when task-success or termination evidence is involved; if this category appears in mentioned_reasons, do not also include the broader judge future-state category. \iow_now:Ne ˝- agents fail to follow the tutorial correctly: Use when the policy/agent itself misunderstands, skips, contradicts, or wrongly executes a tutorial step, and that policy/agent behavior is the decisive cause of failure. Do not use this as primary when the policy/proposed actions include the correct tutorial-following action but the GT-rollout judge selects a different wrong candidate; in that case use the judge future-state reasoning category as primary. \iow_now:Ne ˝Do not output "other", "unknown", "unclear", or any category not listed above. If no category fits perfectly, choose the closest listed category and explain the mismatch in details. \iow_now:Ne ˝The primary_reason must be the latest decisive reason that directly explains the final failed outcome, usually associated with steps near the end of the trajectory. Earlier mistakes should be secondary mentioned_reasons unless there is no later decision that preserves or confirms the failure. \iow_now:Ne ˝Critical distinction between tutorial-following failure and judge future-state failure: \iow_now:Ne ˝- Use the tutorial-following category only when the policy/agent itself misunderstands, skips, contradicts, or wrongly executes a tutorial step, and that policy/agent action is the decisive cause. \iow_now:Ne ˝- Use the judge future-state reasoning category when the GT-rollout judge selects, approves, or keeps preferring a wrong candidate/action because it misreads the current screenshot, misreads candidate/future screenshots, or hallucinates that an incorrect future state satisfies the task. \iow_now:Ne ˝- If a correct tutorial-following candidate/action was available or proposed, but the judge chose a different candidate by claiming its resulting state was correct, the primary_reason must be the judge future-state reasoning category. The tutorial-following category may be mentioned only if the policy/agent also independently failed to follow the tutorial. \iow_now:Ne ˝If the final or near-final step marks the task done even though screenshots/evaluator evidence show the task is not successful, prefer the task-success/termination category as primary over earlier action or grounding errors. \iow_now:Ne ˝mentioned_reasons must include only secondary categories with evidence in the trajectory. Do not include the same category as primary_reason in mentioned_reasons. \iow_now:Ne ˝The two judge future-state categories are mutually exclusive in mentioned_reasons. If "the judge fails to reason over the future state, fails to understand task success" applies anywhere, do not include "the judge fails to reason over the future state" in mentioned_reasons; use only the more specific task-success category for judge evidence. \iow_now:Ne ˝reason_presence must contain every allowed category with true or false. \iow_now:Ne ˝Keep the JSON compact: primary_reason.details and each mentioned_reasons.details must be one short sentence. \iow_now:Ne ˝Return at most 6 mentioned_reasons entries, only for categories with concrete evidence. \iow_now:Ne ˝Return at most 6 step_evidence entries total, prioritizing the primary reason step and the latest decisive evidence near the end. \iow_now:Ne ˝step_evidence must cite screenshot IDs from the provided Image index. Do not invent screenshot IDs. Do not generate screenshots. The renderer will embed the referenced images. \iow_now:Ne ˝For each step_evidence item, include the trajectory step, the high-level action proposed by the policy, the grounded/executed action from traj.jsonl or pre_grounded fields, and one short sentence explaining why the screenshot/action matters. \iow_now:Ne ˝Use the evaluation JSON and result details as the source of truth for the final failed state. \iow_now:Ne ˝Use GT-rollout candidate images/actions to decide whether the failure came from policy proposal, grounding, rollout prediction, selection, tutorial conditioning, evaluator issues, or termination behavior. \iow_now:Ne ˝Do not invent evidence. If evidence is weak, say so in details. \iow_now:Ne ˝No markdown fences. No prose outside JSON. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Analyze this failed OSWorld GT-rollout task. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝You are given the full task/evaluation bundle, the full traj.jsonl text, and every raster image referenced by the trajectory. Images have been preprocessed with max_image_pixels={max_image_pixels}; they are not raw screenshots. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Task instruction: \iow_now:Ne ˝{task_instruction} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Image index: \iow_now:Ne ˝{image_index} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Classify the primary failure reason and every category that is mentioned by evidence in the trajectory. \iow_now:Ne ˝Also produce compact step_evidence entries for the screenshots/steps that justify the classification. Refer to screenshots by Image number only. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Task bundle and full trajectory: \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝{bundle_markdown} Figure 39: Gemini prompt used to classify failed GT-rollout trajectories and extract compact evidence for the failure analysis. Appendix U LLM Usage Statement The authors used LLM-based assistants for limited editorial and technical support, including grammar and clarity edits, LaTeX debugging, and draft phrasing for non-substantive text. We also use LLM-assisted programming like Claude Code and Codex to implement infrastructure code for ground-truth visual rollouts and other baselines. All LLM-assisted text and code changes were inspected and revised by the authors. The authors are responsible for the final manuscript, including all claims, analyses, tables, figures, citations, and conclusions.

sections.heading: Appendix Q Visual Ground-Truth implementation details
sections.text: To find the ground-truth screenshot for each step in the serial option, we first use a QEMU virtual machine supported by Singularity as our environment for OSWorld. We first save a QEMU snapshot of the current VM state before evaluating any candidate action. This snapshot saves the exact state of the VM, including the screen, memory, and disk, allowing us to restore it to this state after each candidate action is executed. We then execute each candidate action one at a time on the same VM, wait for the interface to settle, and capture the resulting screenshot as that candidate’s ground-truth next state. After each candidate is executed, the VM is restored back to the saved snapshot, so the next candidate starts from the exact same screen state. This makes the comparison fair and deterministic on most of the tasks, with a few exceptions when the task involves internet access and the content on the screen may change (e.g., Google search results). See more details in Appendix S . For multi-horizon trajectories (depth > 1 >1 ), the runtime inserts the bold notice shown below; single-step runs omit it. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝[SYSTEM MESSAGE] \iow_now:Ne ˝You are a desktop computer agent on Ubuntu with internet access that evaluates actions by considering the observation before the action candidates and the potential outcomes of these actions. Rank the candidate actions by how effectively each advances toward the goal, considering both the current observation and actual executed rollout outcomes. \iow_now:Ne ˝# ACTION SPACE \iow_now:Ne ˝Use only these exact methods/arguments; no right_click/double_click: \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.click(instruction, num_clicks=1, button_type=’left’, hold_keys=[]) # button_type=’right’|’middle’; double-click=num_clicks=2 \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.done(return_value=None) \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.drag_and_drop(starting_description, ending_description, hold_keys=[]) \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.fail() # proven impossible: CAPTCHA/login/missing required user account credentials/unavailable site/absent required setting or option \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.highlight_text_span(starting_phrase, ending_phrase) \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.hover(instruction) \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.hold_and_press(hold_keys, press_keys) \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.hotkey(keys) \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.open(app_or_filename) # closed app/file; filename, not path; switch if open. Only Google Chrome, LibreOffice Writer/Calc/Impress, Thunderbird, VSCode, VLC Media Player, GIMP; no other programs \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.scroll(instruction, clicks, shift=False) # +up/-down; shift=horizontal; 1˜3 lines; small=1-5, section=5-10, long=10-20; max=50 \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.set_cell_values(cell_values, app_name, sheet_name) # ALWAYS for sheet cells; formulas start "="; max 30 cells/call; app=title filename, sheet=tab \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.switch_applications(app_code) \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.type(element_description=None, text=”, overwrite=False, enter=False) # omit element_description only when keyboard focus/caret is known unchanged from history or immediately preceding focus action; pointer!=focus; click/app switch/dialog/restore uncertainty requires grounding; overwrite=True replaces, False appends intentionally; in a multi-line text/code editor overwrite=True erases the whole document, so select the part to replace (highlight_text_span) and type over it without element_description; overwrite=True for a single-line GUI input still showing old text (calculator/command line, rename field; not terminals); if it is already selected, omit element_description; console commands: no nested single quotes; Enter only submits (click live-filter results) \iow_now:Ne ˝- agent.wait(time) # visible progress/load only \iow_now:Ne ˝**Multi-horizon rollout (depth={depth})**: Each candidate shows a trajectory of {depth} steps executed on the real VM. The first action is the candidate’s proposed action; subsequent actions were chosen by the policy model based on the resulting screenshot. Evaluate the FULL trajectory; prefer the candidate whose trajectory makes the most cumulative progress. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# EVALUATION CRITERIA: \iow_now:Ne ˝Screenshots are ground truth; tutorials are guidance unless they start with ’Infeasible’. \iow_now:Ne ˝1. Feasibility - Target must be visible now; after-screenshots/rollouts must prove the action worked. \iow_now:Ne ˝2. Exactness - Advance the task without extra steps. \iow_now:Ne ˝3. Effectiveness - Make visible progress toward the final state. \iow_now:Ne ˝4. Completion - Use agent.done() only when already complete. \iow_now:Ne ˝5. Tutorial alignment - Prefer feasible tutorial actions, but trust pixels when they differ. \iow_now:Ne ˝6. No regression - Reject broken state, navigation away, or lost progress. \iow_now:Ne ˝7. Terminal evidence - Consider agent.done()/agent.fail() only with hard screenshot/history proof. Prefer any visible action needed to complete, save, apply, close a required dialog, or verify the final artifact. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# REQUIRED DECISION PROCESS \iow_now:Ne ˝Before deciding: \iow_now:Ne ˝1. Derive exact task-specific success conditions from the task instruction. \iow_now:Ne ˝2. Apply all applicable named evaluation criteria to every candidate. \iow_now:Ne ˝3. Judge progress toward the overall goal, not mere action execution. \iow_now:Ne ˝4. Compare observed or expected resulting states and cumulative progress across candidates. \iow_now:Ne ˝5. Decide only after that comparison. \iow_now:Ne ˝In ‘thought‘, connect screenshot/history evidence to success conditions and criteria; do not merely narrate screenshots. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# TUTORIAL GROUNDING GUIDANCE (IF TUTORIAL IS PROVIDED): \iow_now:Ne ˝Prefer feasible tutorial operations that reach task milestones. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# RULES: \iow_now:Ne ˝(1) **OVERRIDE - Infeasible tutorial**: If a tutorial is provided and starts with ’Infeasible’, agent.fail() is the only correct action. \iow_now:Ne ˝(2) Prefer terminal over GUI, then hotkeys over multiple clicks. \iow_now:Ne ˝(3) ANTI-LOOP: If current and latest HISTORY screenshots are substantially unchanged, reject any candidate matching an action’s method+target from the last 3 steps. If all feasible candidates repeat failures, prefer a different agent.* method family and explain the rejection. \iow_now:Ne ˝(4) Do not treat agent.done(return_value=…) as an infeasibility report; prefer agent.fail() for proven impossibility. \iow_now:Ne ˝(5) On the LAST step, only agent.done() or agent.fail() can succeed. \iow_now:Ne ˝(6) Google Chrome is the ONLY available browser. \iow_now:Ne ˝(7) TEXT-SELECTION METHOD PREFERENCE: For the same text range, prefer agent.highlight_text_span(…) over agent.drag_and_drop(…) unless anchors are not visible or the target is non-text. Do not reject highlight_text_span as unsupported for multi-line selection. \iow_now:Ne ˝(8) FOCUSED TEXT ENTRY: Omit element_description only when current keyboard focus/caret is known and unchanged. Then agent.type(text=…, overwrite=…, enter=…) intentionally skips grounding and clicking. History or the current screenshot must establish the intended focus; any intervening click, app switch, dialog transition, or restore uncertainty changes the rule. Do not reject omitted element_description solely when focus evidence is strong. If focus is uncertain, the target is another field, or only the mouse pointer is over the field, require agent.type(element_description=…, …) so grounding can locate it. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# EVIDENCE-FIRST VERIFICATION: \iow_now:Ne ˝Candidate prose, rationale, tutorials, and simulated/text-only trajectories are hypotheses, not execution evidence. Simulated/text-only trajectories may be FEASIBLE, REJECTED, or UNKNOWN, never VERIFIED. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝- Check exact requested conditions: values, text, counts, range endpoints, selection boundaries, dates, names, file paths, source/provenance, and persistence; generic change is insufficient. \iow_now:Ne ˝- Compare the latest HISTORY action with the current screenshot first. Missing expected effect is failure. \iow_now:Ne ˝- For each unexecuted candidate, require a visible target and preconditions; mark FEASIBLE; never claim execution or mark VERIFIED. \iow_now:Ne ˝- For rollouts, inspect screenshots state by state only for actual executed actions. Mark VERIFIED only when an actual state visibly proves the effect; cite it (e.g. ‘Candidate 1 State 2‘). \iow_now:Ne ˝- Missing, ambiguous, or unreadable evidence is UNKNOWN, never success. \iow_now:Ne ˝- Visible proof: selection shows highlight/handles/caret/status; saving shows a completed dialog plus visible target/location or explicit saved/applied history; formatting shows values; persistence shows Save/Apply/OK or reopen/check. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝- DONE: If any candidate is ‘agent.done(…)‘, ‘thought‘ MUST begin ‘DONE_CHECK: <condition> = MET | NOT-MET; …‘, cover every requested final condition, then give ‘CANDIDATE_CHECKS‘. MET means the requested end state holds (a removal/hide goal is MET when the item is gone) and requires direct current-screen proof or explicit saved/applied confirmation; dialogs, highlights, menus, and partial edits are not completion. Select done only when every condition is MET. Missing/incomplete DONE_CHECK, UNKNOWN, or NOT-MET rejects done; choose progress addressing the missing condition. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝Selection rules: \iow_now:Ne ˝- Prefer verification for required UNKNOWN evidence; prefer recovery after two failures in the current GUI branch. \iow_now:Ne ˝- Do not reject all candidates when one can safely reveal missing evidence or recover. If none advances the task, choose the least-irreversible visible verification/recovery; never unsupported done/fail. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝- Evaluate each candidate by its full observed trajectory, not just the action text. \iow_now:Ne ˝- Evaluate each candidate independently. Do NOT use the outcome of Candidate A as evidence that Candidate B is complete. \iow_now:Ne ˝- If Candidate B is agent.done(), it has no post-action state, so judge it only from the current screenshot/history. \iow_now:Ne ˝- Prefer the candidate whose resulting state makes the most progress toward the task goal. \iow_now:Ne ˝- For multi-step trajectories, evaluate cumulative progress across ALL steps and focus on the FINAL screenshot. \iow_now:Ne ˝# TASK \iow_now:Ne ˝Based on the ACTUAL screenshots above, rank the candidates from most to least progress toward the task goal. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# THOUGHT FORMAT \iow_now:Ne ˝In ‘thought‘, output these fields in order: \iow_now:Ne ˝TASK_CHECK: <condition> = VERIFIED | FAILED | UNKNOWN (<evidence from the CURRENT SCREENSHOT>); … \iow_now:Ne ˝LAST_EFFECT: SEEN | NOT-SEEN | UNKNOWN (<evidence from the CURRENT SCREENSHOT>) \iow_now:Ne ˝CANDIDATE_CHECKS: 0 = VERIFIED | FEASIBLE | REJECTED | UNKNOWN (<evidence>); … \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝LAST_EFFECT reports whether the latest executed action visibly changed the screen. It is about the action \iow_now:Ne ˝already taken, never about a candidate’s rollout: a rollout can never make LAST_EFFECT SEEN. \iow_now:Ne ˝If LAST_EFFECT is NOT-SEEN, that action had no effect: REJECT every candidate repeating its method+target \iow_now:Ne ˝unless its rollout screenshots visibly show the missing effect, and prefer a candidate that establishes the \iow_now:Ne ˝missing prerequisite (focus, selection, caret, or an open dialog) or switches to a different agent.* method family. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝If any candidate is ‘agent.done(…)‘, ‘thought‘ MUST begin with the ‘DONE_CHECK:‘ line required by the \iow_now:Ne ˝evidence rules above, followed immediately by CANDIDATE_CHECKS, then TASK_CHECK and LAST_EFFECT. \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# OUTPUT FORMAT \iow_now:Ne ˝Output your response in the following JSON format: \iow_now:Ne ˝{ \iow_now:Ne ˝ "thought": "your rationale for the ranking result", \iow_now:Ne ˝ "ranking": [x, x, x] # "indexes of the action candidates, most promising first" \iow_now:Ne ˝} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝[USER MESSAGE] \iow_now:Ne ˝TUTORIAL/REFERENCE: \iow_now:Ne ˝{tutorial} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# TASK INSTRUCTION \iow_now:Ne ˝{instruction} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# HISTORY \iow_now:Ne ˝{step_history} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# CURRENT SCREENSHOT \iow_now:Ne ˝{current_screenshot} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# CANDIDATE ACTIONS \iow_now:Ne ˝{candidate_actions} \iow_now:Ne ˝ \iow_now:Ne ˝# STEP \iow_now:Ne ˝You are on step {current_step} of maximum {max_steps} steps. Appendix R Ground-Truth Error Analysis We follow the same procedure described in Qian et al. (2026) to analyze errors in the ground-truth visual rollout. In total, we collect 2,116 failed trajectories from all runs with ground-truth rollouts. We first sample 30 tasks and manually go through trajectory data: screenshots, policy "thought" tokens, judge "thought" tokens, and proposed actions. We then identify and summarize the following core categories of errors that lead to agent failure: 1. The judge fails to understand task success : We find a notable portion of cases where the GT-rollout judge fails to understand task success, which is a more specific failure mode. GT-rollout judges fail to understand whether future states satisfy the task instruction. We show an example of this case in Figure 30 . 2. The judge fails to reason over future states : GT-rollout judges can fail to reason over future states to wrongly judge the progress of the task. We show an example of this case in Figure 33 and Figure 29 . 3. Wrong MLLM-generated tutorial : MLLM-generated tutorials are not correct and the agent doesn’t know how to recover from wrong steps in the tutorial. We show an example of this case in Figure 26 . 4. Incomplete tutorial : The tutorial does not provide fine-grained enough steps to complete the task, and the policy fails to propose the missing steps by itself. 5. Policy fails to follow the tutorial correctly : The policy itself misunderstands, skips, contradicts, or wrongly executes a tutorial step. We show an example of this case in Figure 27 . 6. Grounding error : The grounding model maps the same action description to different regions in the visual input, which leads to wrong grounding and thus failure. We show an example of this case in Figure 32 . 7. Observation hallucination in policy : The policy misreads the current state and thus reasons toward a wrong action. We show an example of this case in Figure 31 . 8. Web server error : The web server hosting the task environment has issues, such as the target website being down. This is an external factor that can lead to failure, and it is not caused by the agent’s decision-making process. 9. Agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps : The agent is following a correct path but reaches the 15-step or 50-step limit before completing the task. We show an example of this case in Figure 34 . We then use an MLLM (Gemini 3.8 Flash Google DeepMind (2026) ) to annotate the rest of the failed tasks. Given the trajectory data of a task, we prompt it (see Figure 39 ) to classify failure reasons into the categories above. Because a failed task might have many root causes, we follow Qian et al. (2026) and ask the MLLM to classify potential errors into: (1) a primary reason and (2) mentioned (secondary) reasons. Note that mentioned reasons cannot be duplicated with the primary reason. To assess the reliability of this MLLM-as-a-judge framework, we run the MLLM on the manually annotated examples above and find that the agreement rate for the primary reason reaches 90%. Furthermore, we randomly sample 20 examples from MLLM results to examine manually. All of the results are reasonable and aligned with our predefined categories of error. Based on the MLLM’s results, we plot the number of primary and mentioned reasons in Figure 3 . sections.heading: Appendix R Ground-Truth Error Analysis
sections.text: We follow the same procedure described in Qian et al. (2026) to analyze errors in the ground-truth visual rollout. In total, we collect 2,116 failed trajectories from all runs with ground-truth rollouts. We first sample 30 tasks and manually go through trajectory data: screenshots, policy "thought" tokens, judge "thought" tokens, and proposed actions. We then identify and summarize the following core categories of errors that lead to agent failure: 1. The judge fails to understand task success : We find a notable portion of cases where the GT-rollout judge fails to understand task success, which is a more specific failure mode. GT-rollout judges fail to understand whether future states satisfy the task instruction. We show an example of this case in Figure 30 . 2. The judge fails to reason over future states : GT-rollout judges can fail to reason over future states to wrongly judge the progress of the task. We show an example of this case in Figure 33 and Figure 29 . 3. Wrong MLLM-generated tutorial : MLLM-generated tutorials are not correct and the agent doesn’t know how to recover from wrong steps in the tutorial. We show an example of this case in Figure 26 . 4. Incomplete tutorial : The tutorial does not provide fine-grained enough steps to complete the task, and the policy fails to propose the missing steps by itself. 5. Policy fails to follow the tutorial correctly : The policy itself misunderstands, skips, contradicts, or wrongly executes a tutorial step. We show an example of this case in Figure 27 . 6. Grounding error : The grounding model maps the same action description to different regions in the visual input, which leads to wrong grounding and thus failure. We show an example of this case in Figure 32 . 7. Observation hallucination in policy : The policy misreads the current state and thus reasons toward a wrong action. We show an example of this case in Figure 31 . 8. Web server error : The web server hosting the task environment has issues, such as the target website being down. This is an external factor that can lead to failure, and it is not caused by the agent’s decision-making process. 9. Agent doing correctly but runs out of max steps : The agent is following a correct path but reaches the 15-step or 50-step limit before completing the task. We show an example of this case in Figure 34 . We then use an MLLM (Gemini 3.8 Flash Google DeepMind (2026) ) to annotate the rest of the failed tasks. Given the trajectory data of a task, we prompt it (see Figure 39 ) to classify failure reasons into the categories above. Because a failed task might have many root causes, we follow Qian et al. (2026) and ask the MLLM to classify potential errors into: (1) a primary reason and (2) mentioned (secondary) reasons. Note that mentioned reasons cannot be duplicated with the primary reason. To assess the reliability of this MLLM-as-a-judge framework, we run the MLLM on the manually annotated examples above and find that the agreement rate for the primary reason reaches 90%. Furthermore, we randomly sample 20 examples from MLLM results to examine manually. All of the results are reasonable and aligned with our predefined categories of error. Based on the MLLM’s results, we plot the number of primary and mentioned reasons in Figure 3 . text: Computer-Use Agents Gain Little Benefit from a World Model When Conditioned on Tutorials Skip to main content Report GitHub Issue × Title: Content selection saved. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2611.04073v1 [cs.LG] 02 Nov 2026 Computer-Use Agents Gain Little Benefit from a World Model When Conditioned on Tutorials Anh (Joe) Nguyen Tianyi Xu * Phat Tran * Harry Yu * Affiliation: Huazheng Wang Stefan Lee Affiliation: Oregon State University Email: {nguyejoe,xut2,tranphat,yuhar,huazheng.wang,leestef}@oregonstate.edu Abstract Recent work has improved computer-use agents (CUAs) by combining retrieved task-relevant tutorials and look-ahead planning using world models with MLLM judges. However, the contribution of each component—tutorials, the judge, and the world model—to overall improvement has not been evaluated in isolation. To fill this gap, we first construct OSWorld-Tutorial and ScienceBoard-Tutorial: two datasets for CUAs with curated multimodal tutorials, covering everyday and scientific domains. We then propose RAG-PolicyJudge (RAG-PJ), a policy-judge framework for CUAs conditioned on task-specific tutorials: the policy proposes candidate actions, and the judge selects among them. To isolate the effect of world models given tutorials, we compare RAG-PJ with and without common world models: using either zero-shot text-based descriptions of next states or an oracle that returns ground-truth visual observations. We find that RAG-PJ gains little benefit from these rollouts when tutorials are present, even with perfect visual futures . This suggests prior world-model gains in tutorial-conditioned methods come mainly from tutorial understanding and the judge’s ability to select the proposed actions, rather than from predicted rollouts. Error analysis reveals that the bottleneck is not rollout fidelity, but the judge’s ability to reason over future states and recognize task completion. This highlights the need to improve not just next-state prediction in world models, but also reasoning over their predicted rollouts. 1 1 1 Datasets and code are available at github.com/realjoenguyen/RAGPJ-official . * * footnotetext: Equal contribution. 1 Introduction People rely on desktop and web software for day-to-day tasks and scientific workflows. Computer-use agents (CUAs) aim to automate these tasks by interacting with computer interfaces given natural-language user instructions. Modern CUAs are typically built on top of multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) trained on static offline data. As software is updated and user interfaces shift, these MLLM-based CUAs may lack current procedural knowledge about new environments, resulting in degraded performance Ishmam and Marino (2026) . A natural approach to address this gap is to provide CUAs with up-to-date task-specific tutorials. These readily available tutorials, contain environment descriptions and step-by-step instructions in the form of text and screenshots. 2 2 2 An example tutorial is given in Appendix G . Figure 1: Success rate on OSWorld-Tutorial (Qwen3-VL-32B) of RAG-PJ, a policy–judge CUA, whose judge sees no rollout, a predicted text rollout (R-WoM Mei et al. (2026) ), or an oracle visual rollout (real future screenshots). Rollouts help RAG-PJ without a tutorial but add almost nothing with one. Full results in § 6 and Appendix C . Recent work has integrated tutorial retrieval as a component in CUA systems Yang et al. (2026a) ; Xu et al. (2025a) . However, these systems do not compare against alternative tutorial-use approaches, leaving their effectiveness unclear. A parallel body of work has considered test-time scaling for CUAs through a policy-judge approach with look-ahead planning Luo et al. (2026) ; Chae et al. (2025) . These methods use a world model to predict the outcome of action candidates under a policy, over one or many steps. They then use an MLLM-as-a-judge to select the best action among the candidates, conditioned on these predicted rollouts. Recently, tutorial-augmented methods of this approach have been introduced Mei et al. (2026) . However, these methods conflate the contributions of the tutorial, the judge, and world-model rollouts without proper evaluation. To fill this gap, we study the effect of tutorial information on CUAs with and without look-ahead planning, while retaining the MLLM-as-a-judge framework. Intuitively, high-quality tutorials already provide guidance for the policy to generate actions and demonstrations of their effects that can be used by the judge. This can potentially reduce the need for costly world model training and inference. With this motivation, we propose a simple yet effective method: RAG-PolicyJudge (RAG-PJ), a retrieval-augmented policy-judge framework for CUAs. RAG-PJ provides a task-specific tutorial to both (1) the policy, which proposes action candidates, and (2) the judge, which selects the best action among them. To evaluate tutorials for CUAs across domains, we build curated tutorials for existing datasets: OSWorld-Verified for day-to-day tasks Xie et al. (2024) and ScienceBoard for scientific workflows Sun et al. (2026) , resulting in two new tutorial benchmarks: OSWorld-Tutorial and ScienceBoard-Tutorial. The two original datasets are widely adopted for CUAs, facilitating easy adoption and reuse by the research community. To study the effect of world models on policy-judge frameworks in these two tutorial datasets, using the same base MLLM for both the policy and the judge, we compare RAG-PJ with two types of world models for CUAs: text-based and visual. First, zero-shot text-based rollouts Mei et al. (2026) (i.e., the text description of what the predicted next state would look like). Second, oracle visual rollouts (i.e., the real screenshot of the next state). We argue that these oracle rollouts are an upper bound on the next-state fidelity a learned visual world model (like ViMo Luo et al. (2026) ) could achieve. We find that RAG-PJ matches both rollout variants when tutorials are present. This indicates that current zero-shot MLLM-as-a-judge models gain little extra benefit from a world model, even with oracle visual futures, when conditioned on tutorials (Figure 1 ). Analyzing failures of the oracle rollout, we find that the agent’s failure to understand task success and progress , even when the oracle future is available, is a primary bottleneck to higher performance. This suggests that progress in CUAs may require not just better world models, but also stronger reasoning over the futures these world models simulate. In summary, our contributions are as follows: – We introduce RAG-PJ, a simple yet effective tutorial-conditioned policy-judge method for CUAs (§ 4.2 ). – We build OSWorld-Tutorial and ScienceBoard-Tutorial, two curated tutorial datasets with existing tasks from OSWorld Xie et al. (2024) and ScienceBoard Sun et al. (2026) (§ 3 ), facilitating tutorial study for CUAs. – We propose an oracle visual rollout infrastructure for CUAs, providing an important ablation on the effect of visual world-model rollouts with perfect future information (§ 5 , Appendix F ). – We provide a controlled comparison of tutorial-only judging, text-based rollouts, and oracle visual rollouts-demonstrating that current MLLM-as-a-judge models gain little benefit from world models given task-specific tutorials (§ 6 ). 2 Related Work World model evaluation for CUAs. Several works find that zero-shot rollouts from pretrained MLLMs used as world models Ha and Schmidhuber (2018) are not yet faithful or consistent proxies for real environments Li et al. (2026) ; Xu et al. (2026) ; Fu et al. (2026) . Beyond MLLMs as world models, other works use oracle world models to study upper-bound look-ahead performance in embodied tasks Qian et al. (2026) and, at the first step only, in computer-use tasks Gonzalez-Pumariega et al. (2026) . We extend these analyses to (1) oracle image-based rollouts with task-specific tutorials and (2) look-ahead planning at every step of computer-use tasks. Concurrent to our work, Tang et al. (2026) show that code-based visual world model add little benefit if agents can already have a well-trained MLLM-as-a-judge. Our work complements theirs by studying the benefit of world model rollouts against zero-shot MLLM-as-judge, in the presence of task-specific tutorials. Further, we study two types of common world models: we adopt (1) text-based, and build (2) visual ground truths, which is the upper bound of current visual world models. CUAs that use tutorials (or manuals). Prior work uses tutorials either to create training data Ou et al. (2024) ; Xu et al. (2025b) ; Zhang et al. (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2025b) ; Song et al. (2026) ; Lu et al. (2026) or as guidance at inference time Liu et al. (2026b) ; Xu et al. (2025a) ; Agashe et al. (2025a) ; Mei et al. (2026) ; Yang et al. (2026a) , where the tutorial guides action generation (policy) or selection (judge). RAG-GUI Xu et al. (2025a) and Agent S Agashe et al. (2025a) retrieve text-only tutorials to extract guidance for policy-only agents. 3 3 3 See Appendix D.3 for a comparison with RAG-GUI. Liu et al. (2026b) retrieve tutorial videos at inference time as in-context guidance for the policy. Similar to our benchmarks, there are two recent multimodal tutorial datasets for CUA/GUI: WebOne Long et al. (2026) and DocOS Liu et al. (2026a) , where agents must search the open web for documentation before executing a task. However, WebOne is only for web agents and tutorials are not task-conditioned, but rather than software documentation in general. DocOS is not publicly available, preventing direct comparison. In contrast, our work focuses on task-specific multimodal tutorials for general CUAs and test-time scaling approach with a MLLM-as-a-judge, which is evaluated against world model rollout methods. We also release our benchmark and trained agents for reproducibility. Most similar to our approach are OS-Symphony Yang et al. (2026a) and R-WoM Mei et al. (2026) . OS-Symphony couples retrieved tutorials with a multi-agent history-reflection policy, but does not compare against other tutorial-using baselines. Our tutorial-conditioned judge is orthogonal and could be combined with its policy. Like R-WoM, we focus on settings where multimodal task-specific tutorials are available, but R-WoM’s results do not disentangle the tutorial, the MLLM-as-a-judge, and the rollout, and it is evaluated on a non-public subset of ∼ 85 {\sim}85 OSWorld tasks. R-WoM reports that its rollouts improve over a no-tutorial baseline, but never compares against a tutorial-conditioned judge without rollout. We add that comparison with our method RAG-PJ, and find the judge alone matches R-WoM; we further test oracle visual rollouts. See Appendix D for a more detailed discussion of related work. 3 Tutorial datasets Tutorial dataset domains. To evaluate tutorials and tutorial-conditioned CUAs across domains, we pair existing tasks with newly collected tutorials to build two datasets: (1) OSWorld-Tutorial, from general-purpose desktop tasks in OSWorld-Verified Xie et al. (2024) , and (2) ScienceBoard-Tutorial, from scientific-software workflow tasks in ScienceBoard Sun et al. (2026) . General-purpose tasks from OSWorld-Verified reflect everyday computer use, with abundant online tutorials. Scientific software from ScienceBoard is harder on both fronts. First, its applications are niche: step-by-step task tutorials are scarce, and even ScienceBoard’s annotators relied on official documentation (Table 6 of Sun et al. (2026) ). Second, current open MLLMs still struggle on these tasks, with as low as ∼ \sim 30% success rate with Qwen3.8-27B (Table 9 ). This makes it a natural testbed for whether tutorials, even scarce ones, can compensate for limited MLLM familiarity with these specialized domains. Generating tutorials. We pair each task with one multimodal tutorial (text and possibly images) drawn from web sources. The tutorial type depends on what is available online for that task. First, human-verified online tutorials : we search Google with the task instruction, and when a retrieved tutorial covers the task, one of three annotators experienced with Ubuntu environments selects the most helpful one and verifies it by following its instructions to complete the task; we keep the pair only when this succeeds. This accounts for 31% of OSWorld-Tutorial tasks and none of the ScienceBoard-Tutorial tasks, as the latter’s scientific software is niche and lacks task-level tutorials online. These tutorials rule out retrieval errors, letting us measure the effect of tutorials independently of the retrieval pipeline. Second, MLLM-generated tutorials : when no single online tutorial covers the task (none exists, or the task requires combining several), we launch the task in a virtual machine and prompt Google Gemini 3.8 Flash Google DeepMind (2026) with the task instruction, the initial screenshot, and the tutorial-generation prompt in Appendix H ; Gemini searches the web and writes a task-specific tutorial, which we keep without human verification. The screenshot lets it refer to the actual files, columns, and menus of the task instead of inventing names. MLLM-generated tutorials mirror practical real-world guidance: users rarely have a curated tutorial database and instead ask a search-augmented MLLM for task-specific instructions. MLLM-generated tutorials cover 69% of OSWorld-Tutorial tasks and all ScienceBoard-Tutorial tasks. Dataset statistics. We create total 529 tutorials across both original datasets. OSWorld-Tutorial contains 360 existing OSWorld-Verified tasks 4 4 4 OSWorld-Verified at commit 83e8534 (Jun 24, 2026), excluding 9 tasks that require Google Drive credentials or are blocked by website bot detection (Appendix H ). : 110 with human-verified and 250 with MLLM-generated tutorials (examples in Appendix H ). ScienceBoard-Tutorial pairs all 169 existing ScienceBoard tasks with MLLM-generated tutorials (examples in Appendix I ). 4 Tutorial-conditioned CUAs Figure 2: Overview of RAG-PJ. Given the instruction, current screenshot, and trajectory history, a tutorial-conditioned policy proposes candidate actions, a tutorial-conditioned judge selects one, and a grounding model maps it to keyboard/mouse inputs. 4.1 Preliminaries CUA architectures. A CUA is a policy π ⁡ ( a t | o ≤ t , a < t , L , M ) \pi(a_{t}\,|\,o_{\leq t},a_{<t},L,M) over screenshots o o , actions a a , instruction L L , and tutorial M M . See Appendix J for the full problem formulation. Typically, CUA architectures are built on MLLMs. Designs are either end-to-end, with one MLLM mapping inputs directly to actions Qin et al. (2025) , or modular, combining multiple MLLMs and specialized models Agashe et al. (2025b) ; Yang et al. (2026a) . We follow the common two-stage modular design. A policy π ( a ^ t | ⋅ ) \pi(\hat{a}_{t}\,|\,\cdot) outputs a natural-language action (e.g., click(the red button) ). A grounding model g ( a t | a ^ t , ⋅ ) g(a_{t}\,|\,\hat{a}_{t},\cdot) then maps it to a low-level action (e.g., click(731, 244) ). Judges and world models. Other work samples K K action candidates a ^ t 1 , … , a ^ t K ∼ π ( a ^ t | ⋅ ) \hat{a}^{1}_{t},\ldots,\hat{a}^{K}_{t}\sim\pi(\hat{a}_{t}\,|\,\cdot) and introduces a judge model that selects the index of the best candidate, k ∗ = j ( a ^ t 1 , … , a ^ t K | o ≤ t , a < t , L , M ) ∈ { 1 , … , K } k^{*}=j(\hat{a}^{1}_{t},\ldots,\hat{a}^{K}_{t}\,|\,o_{\leq t},a_{<t},L,M)\in\{1,\ldots,K\} , passing only the selected action a ^ t k ∗ \hat{a}^{k^{*}}_{t} to the grounding model for execution Yang et al. (2026c) . This sample-then-select paradigm has shown promising results when coupled with look-ahead planning, using a world model to estimate the outcome of each action over a fixed number of time steps. See Appendix D.1 for an overview of world model methods following this approach for CUAs. Each candidate is rolled out for H H steps by alternating the world model and the policy, and the judge selects among candidates based on their rollouts (details in Appendix J ). However, look-ahead planning greatly increases computational cost by requiring multiple policy and world-model executions per step. 4.2 RAG-PolicyJudge (RAG-PJ) To test if the additional compute for world model is valuable when strong policy guidance is available as a tutorial, we design a simple tutorial-conditioned method, RAG-PolicyJudge (RAG-PJ), shown in Figure 2 . We adapt a two-stage GUI-agent framework, consisting of a policy and a grounding model as described above (§ 4.1 ). Implementation details are in Appendix K . Policy and Grounding Models. We instantiate the policy π ⁡ ( a ^ t | o ≤ t , a < t , L , M ) \pi(\hat{a}_{t}\,|\,o_{\leq t},a_{<t},L,M) as an MLLM that outputs K K candidate actions in a single call Yang et al. (2026c) . To bound context length, in practice we condition π \pi on o ^ ≤ t \hat{o}_{\leq t} in place of o ≤ t o_{\leq t} , where o ^ ≤ t \hat{o}_{\leq t} consists of: the current observation o t o_{t} ; all previous actions; the chain-of-thought of the five most recent steps; and the screenshots of up to five recent steps. Additionally, the task instruction, CUA-specific policy rules, and the tutorial are always available at each time step. We adopt the action space from Agent-S2 Agashe et al. (2025b) . The policy prompt is available in Appendix L . We adopt UI-Venus-1.5 Venus Team et al. (2026) as it is the state-of-the-art grounding model for CUAs and has been used as the grounding model in prior work Gong et al. (2026) ; Jiang et al. (2025) . The grounding prompt is provided in Appendix N . The grounding model g ⁡ ( a t | a ^ t , o t ) g(a_{t}\,|\,\hat{a}_{t},o_{t}) accesses only the current observation o t o_{t} and the policy action a ^ t \hat{a}_{t} . Judge Model. The judge j j shares the policy’s MLLM and inputs: K K candidate actions, task instruction, the trajectory encoding o ^ ≤ t \hat{o}_{\leq t} , and tutorials. It ranks the candidates with a ranking prompt (Appendix M ) and sends the top-ranked action to the grounding model for execution. 5 Experimental Settings Evaluation metric: task success rate. We use the task success rate metrics defined by OSWorld-Verified and ScienceBoard. For OSWorld-Verified, the metrics are computed within the original maximum of 15 steps Xie et al. (2024) ; Kuntz et al. (2025) ; Ye et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2025) and the extended 50-step budget adopted in follow-up work Abhyankar et al. (2026) ; OpenAI (2025) ; Jia et al. (2026) . For ScienceBoard, we follow each task’s time limit from the original benchmark Sun et al. (2026) . Baselines. We use the following baselines with the same two-stage policy-grounding framework Gou et al. (2025) , the same harness (rules/guidelines), and the same input/output space as RAG-PJ, allowing us to isolate the effects of the world model, the judge, and the tutorial. We adopt the hyperparameters from their best publicly reported configurations. Details are in Appendix K . In all settings with a judge, the policy proposes K = 3 K=3 candidate actions per step 5 5 5 K = 3 K=3 follows the original codebase of our baselines. and the judge selects one; in Policy Only settings, the policy proposes a single action. – Policy Only drops the judge from RAG-PJ. When including the tutorial, we denote this model as Policy Only + RAG . – Policy + Judge (GTA-1) Yang et al. (2026c) is a policy-judge framework, without a world model or tutorial. – R-WoM H=# is a re-implementation of the recent tutorial-augmented look-ahead method from Mei et al. (2026) described in § 4.1 . R-WoM uses an MLLM-based world model to produce zero-shot text-based next-state descriptions. We set H = 1 , 2 , 3 H{=}1,2,3 to adjust how many steps are rolled out during look-ahead search. Finding 1: Tutorials improve task success rate over non-tutorial baselines. In Table (OSWorld-Tutorial) and Table 9 (ScienceBoard-Tutorial), we show that including tutorials in the policy ( row 2 ) improves over the non-tutorial baseline ( Policy Only , row 1 ) by ∼ \sim 3–12% (Table ) and ∼ \sim 15–21% (Table 9 ). The policy-judge framework with tutorials (RAG-PJ, row 4 ) improves over the non-tutorial baseline ( GTA-1 , row 3 ) by ∼ \sim 5–14% (Table ) and ∼ \sim 18–22% (Table 9 ). These improvements are larger on ScienceBoard (Table 9 ), whose specialized scientific apps are likely less covered in MLLM training data. This suggests tutorials help most where MLLMs lack prior knowledge. Table 6 (Appendix A ) and Tables 7 and 8 (Appendix B ) break results down per category in both benchmarks; the improvement from tutorial conditioning is consistent across all categories. Notably, tutorial conditioning in the policy yields most of the gains, suggesting that guidance for producing action candidates is the main source of improvement. Yet policy conditioning alone ( row 2 , Tables and 9 ) does not account for all of RAG-PJ’s gains, so judge action selection still helps. Finally, rows 3a, 3b vs. row 4 (Table ) show that using tutorials in both policy and judge performs best. 6.2 Do CUAs benefit from zero-shot text-based world models? Finding 2: Given a tutorial, CUAs gain no benefit from zero-shot text-based world models. As shown in Tables (OSWorld-Tutorial) and 9 (ScienceBoard-Tutorial) and their breakdowns in Appendix A , we find that R-WoM does not improve over a judge without world model rollout ( RAG-PJ ). R-WoM without policy-side tutorial conditioning ( rows 5--7 , Table ) matches or underperforms the Policy + RAG Judge without rollout ( row 3a , Table ) at different horizons ( H = 1 , 2 , 3 ) (H{=}1,2,3) . Appendix O.2 traces this to hallucination in rollouts. When policy-side RAG is added ( rows 8--10 , Tables and 9 ), R-WoM is worse than or statistically similar to RAG-PJ ( row 4 ) on both benchmarks. This indicates that gains from R-WoM come from tutorial conditioning and the judge, rather than text-based rollouts. Further, we observe no consistent trend across rollout horizons: longer horizons ( H = 2 , 3 H{=}2,3 ) do not always improve over H = 1 H{=}1 , and in some settings longer horizons slightly degrade performance. This suggests compounding errors across simulated steps add noise to the judge. 6.3 Do CUAs benefit from ground-truth visual rollouts? Finding 3: Given oracle or noisy MLLM-generated tutorials, zero-shot MLLM judges gain little from ground-truth visual rollouts. In Table (OSWorld-Tutorial) and Table 9 (ScienceBoard-Tutorial), with tutorials, GT-rollout clearly improves over text-based R-WoM ( rows 11--13 vs. 8--10 ) but is not significantly better than RAG-PJ on either benchmark, for both human-verified and MLLM-generated tutorials (Appendix A ). As before, the judge can already decide well from tutorials without reasoning over future consequences. Without tutorials, GT-rollout does help: H = 2 H{=}2 improves over Policy+Judge by ∼ \sim 3–4% (Table 2 , row 7 vs. row 1 ). With noisy MLLM-generated tutorials, GT-rollout gives small nominal gains over RAG-PJ in some settings (Tables 3 and 9 ). In 40 sampled tasks that RAG-PJ fails but GT-rollout solves, the tutorials are partially correct but miss steps. GT-rollout helps the judge recover when: – the horizon is too short for RAG-PJ to try the alternative steps the tutorial suggests, e.g., ScienceBoard categories with only 5 steps; – the action’s effect is visually obvious in the next state, e.g., opening a website or creating a file. This matters more in ScienceBoard-Tutorial, whose scientific software is less familiar to the judge, so it is harder to infer the effect from the tutorial text alone. Per-category results are in Appendices A and B . Finding 4: Agents fail to use ground-truth future information due to poor understanding of task success and progress. To understand why ground-truth visual rollouts do not improve success, we analyze failed tasks in OSWorld-Tutorial with the help of Gemini 3.8 Flash Google DeepMind (2026) and summarize failure reasons and their frequency in Figure 3 . The most frequent failure category is the agent (both the policy and the judge) failing to understand task success: whether the current state satisfies the task instruction . For instance, a task is not completed in the current state, yet the policy and the judge predict that the current state already satisfies the instruction. The judge therefore selects the action that ends the task prematurely. The second most frequently tagged category is the judge failing to reason over the future information about task progress: what has been done and what is left to do . Even if the policy generates good action candidates, the judge fails to select the one that leads to task progress. The judge often repeats the same failed action instead of recognizing the failure and choosing other candidates. We show examples of these failures in Figures 29 , 33 , and 30 . Overall, most failures stem from the judge’s inability to reason over future states generated by world models , not from world-model quality. Examples of other less significant failure reasons and the error-analysis implementation are shown in Appendix R . Implication: CUAs need not only better world models but also better mechanisms for reasoning over future rollouts. Improving world-model fidelity alone may therefore be insufficient for look-ahead planning. Current world-model methods for CUAs lack reward prediction for rollout states, which the judge needs to compare candidates by their futures, and judges need better ways to reason over rollouts, e.g., via prompting or training. This is consistent with Qian et al. (2026) , who find that even a ground-truth world model does not improve embodied agents, as using future information is the main bottleneck. 6.4 Can current MLLM systems synthesize tutorials for CUAs as good as human-verified online tutorials? Without an available online tutorial for a given task, can MLLM systems with web search synthesize equally useful ones? Since Tables 4 and 5 (Appendix A ) suggest that tasks with MLLM-generated tutorials may be harder, we use OSWorld-Tutorial to compare both tutorial types on the same tasks . Specifically, we select 110 tasks with human-verified online tutorials. We use our dataset pipeline (described in § 3 ) to create MLLM-generated tutorials for these tasks. We then evaluate both RAG-PJ and the ground-truth visual rollout method under each tutorial condition and report the results in Table 3 . Finding 5: Task-specific tutorials written by a search-grounded frontier MLLM are as useful to the policy and judge as human-verified online tutorials. In Table 3 , we find no statistically significant difference between the two tutorial types, in RAG-PJ ( row 4 ) or in GT-rollout ( rows 5--7 ). This is likely because OSWorld-Tutorial tasks involve common software with abundant online tutorials. We provide examples of MLLM-generated vs. human-verified tutorial pairs and an analysis of a sample of 20 pairs in Appendix E . In this sample, a human verifier judges every MLLM-generated tutorial as correct or partially correct, and prefers it over its human-verified counterpart in 17 of 20 pairs. MLLM-generated tutorials are task-conditioned , naming the on-screen objects and values the task requires, whereas human-verified online tutorials describe an application feature in general, leaving the CUA to ground each action on the current screen. 7 Limitations Our study has several limitations: First, our MLLM-generated tutorials (Gemini 3.8 Flash with web search) cover noisy online retrieval, but we do not evaluate offline settings, where a local retriever over a smaller corpus (e.g., local documentation) may yield noisier or missing tutorials, which could change the relative benefit of look-ahead planning. Second, both benchmarks run desktop applications in Linux VMs. ScienceBoard-Tutorial has only MLLM-generated tutorials, so our human vs. MLLM tutorial comparison (Finding 5) covers only 110 general-purpose OSWorld-Tutorial tasks. Third, all models come from one MLLM family (Qwen3-VL-8B, Qwen3-VL-32B, Qwen3.8-27B), and all judges are zero-shot prompted; other model families, larger frontier MLLMs, or judges trained to reason over rollouts may use future states more effectively. Fourth, our error analysis (Figure 3 ) uses Gemini 3.8 Flash rather than human annotators to categorize failures, so the categories may carry labeling noise or MLLM biases. 8 Ethical Considerations Compute used. We used 272 GPU-hours in total on NVIDIA H100/H200 GPUs, plus about 1,080 hours on an NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10). Risks. Like all assistive technologies, advances in computer-use agents make it easier for individuals to take action—both good and ill. Given how modern infrastructure relies on digital interfaces, this may pose significant risks for personal digital security, coordinated astroturfing, or model errors causing users harm. We use Hierarchical bootstrap, sign-flip permutation, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests over tasks in Table , 5 , and 4 to test whether ground-truth visual rollouts and R-WoM improve over RAG-PJ on OSWorld-Tutorial. Per-task-category analysis. To understand when and why the agent gains or loses a benefit from ground-truth visual rollout (GT rollouts), we break down the results of Qwen3-VL-32B in Table by task category in Table 6 . We inspected 40 cases where GT rollouts succeeded but RAG-PJ failed. In these cases, candidate actions produced clear, visible changes in the next state, such as opening a new website or creating a file. These visible effects make the correct action easier for the judge to spot, which matters most when there is little time to recover from a mistake. These gains do not generalize to other task categories. Applications like VS Code and GIMP have denser interfaces, so the effect of an action is often less visually clear. In one failure case, the judge misread a VS Code workspace with unwanted Explorer folders as a success—consistent with our earlier finding that the judge misinterprets task success even from perfect future screenshots. The agent simply has more time to observe the consequences of its actions and recover from mistakes without needing look-ahead. Why do GT rollouts help in Celestia and GrassGIS? GT visual rollouts improve performance over RAG-PJ in Celestia and GrassGIS across the evaluated horizons. We sample 40 cases where GT rollouts succeeded but RAG-PJ failed. The common reason is that the tutorials given to agents are only partially correct. They omit steps that the task needs in the current application state, and they present options as equivalent when only some of them work. For example, in Celestia task B-02 (Figure 4 ) the instruction is “Go to Neptune in Celestia.” RAG-PJ executes Method 1 of the retrieved tutorial, and tries to follow the highlighted step in its tutorial. In that step, the tutorial proposes three options to travel to Neptune: pressing G , right-clicking, or double-clicking. RAG-PJ then executes the first option, pressing G , but it fails to travel to Neptune. The reason is that its tutorial fails to include the step that gives the 3D viewport keyboard focus (by clicking on it), right before the step that instructs the user to press G to travel to Neptune. Therefore, it fails to do that step and run out of the 5-step budget of that task, before trying the other options. GT-rollout insteads executes all three options in the tutorial on a copy of the VM, and sees that only the right-click option works, so it chooses that one and completes the task in 4 steps. Numbers from Tables 2 and . We note down the differences between WebDreamer and R-WoM, which are both text-based world model look-ahead methods. While WebDreamer and R-WoM both use greedy policy in rollout states, they differ in how rollouts are generated and scored. In WebDreamer ( Gu et al., 2025 ) , for each candidate action, the rollout is generated many times with different imagined trajectories. Each trajectory is scored independently, either complete (1), on track (0.5), or incorrect (0). The scores of these trajectories are averaged to produce a score for that candidate action. In R-WoM ( Mei et al., 2026 ) , only one imagined trajectory is generated for each candidate action. All candidate actions are then ranked listwise based on the single trajectory score, and the best candidate action is selected.
